en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Salutations to Śrī Nandikeśvara. May there be no obstacles. May all be auspicious.
Herein begins the *Prabhu-liṅga-līlā* in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.

I bow to Śaṅkara, the Lord of all, who is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite, Primordial, and Undecaying; who bestows the realization of the unreality of this world, which is a meaningless illusion, through the *Tātparyārtha*, the commentary on the *Sūtrāvalī*— the established doctrine that unifies the singular intention of the glorious *Vedaśikhā*.
I perpetually worship the Lord’s form as the Liṅga, which transcends the reach of speech and mind. || 1 ||
Once, in the holy Naimiṣa forest, which was filled with hosts of sages and nourished by the magnificent, great flow of the Bhāgīrathī; (2)
Adorned with incomparable, glossy clusters of leaves, flowers, and fruits; filled with dense, flourishing springtime; and exceedingly pleasant and cool. || 3 ||
With *caṃpaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, *caṃdana*, *agaru*, and *tiṃduka* trees;
with *kapittha*, *aśvattha*, *kharjūra*, *nārikela*, and honey-bearing trees. || 4 ||
With *panasa*, *plakṣa*, *kadalī*, *rasāla*, and *bakula* trees;
with *āsana*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, and *vaṭa* trees; and with *jambū*, *jambīra*, and *pāṭala* trees.
With grapes, sugarcane, pomegranates, kunda flowers, bandhujīvaka flowers, and bamboo—
[all] as tender as petals fit for worshiping the lotus feet of Maheśvara.
It was overspread with countless clusters of bilva trees,
along with mallikā, mādhavī, jājī, karavīra, and kuruṇṭaka flowers.
[He was attended] daily by Śyāmantika, Rudraja, Nandyāvarta, Śamīdruma,
and other venerable sages who were peerless and unsurpassed.
With those numerous, sky-scraping trees that illuminated the quarters of the horizon,
their hollow trunks were filled with the flowing sap of ripened fruit.

With bees that were noisy with humming, their limbs dancing upon the tips of branches, and who were intoxicated by the flow of nectar from clusters of flowers that were perfectly clear and translucent; (10)
It resounded with the cries of śārikās, kīras, kirmīras, peacocks, and pikas,
and was adorned with divine mandāra, pārijāta, and kalpaka trees.
It was adorned with lineages headed by the lineage of Santānavṛkṣa,
and graced by royal swans who sported there and were themselves embellished by other royal swans.
It shines with throngs of radiant Apsarases who resemble beds of white water-lilies,
who are adorned with sacred ash and as white as the great silver mountain.

The description of the Naimiṣa forest: with the lofty peaks of its pavilions made of rudrākṣa beads scraping the sky, and with the bark garments dancing upon the tall bamboo poles in the courtyards of the leaf-huts. (14)
It was radiant with the branches of trees draped in rows of saffron robes,
and lofty with the auspicious abodes of ten million upon ten million great liṅgas.
In that place, the quarters were perfumed by the incense rising from the worship of Sadāśiva,
and it was surrounded by yoga-sheds where great yogis practicing with forceful effort (haṭha) performed their exercises.

In that place, which is expanded by the great abyss pervaded by the density of the bliss of absorption (layānanda), and where the sands are formed by the spray of the Ganges shimmering from the practice of mantra-worship; 17.
In the pavilion of the hermitage frequented by the great yogi Śivarāja, which resounded with the sounds of summoning for the sake of honoring guests at all times; 18.

It was crowded with deities who had arrived to receive their sacrificial portions, and it resounded with the chanting of the established doctrines of the Vedas and Vedānta by those reciting them. || 19 ||
In which the lotus-pool is always resounded by the echoing reverberations of the cries of "Hara, Hara."
In that place abounding in many kinds of grass, where wild rice, bulbs, roots, and other such things were plentiful.
It was devoted to the worship of Śiva seated upon a crystal-clear stone slab,
crowded with hundreds of ascetics shining amidst five fires.
It was surrounded by hosts of *parahaṃsas* who meditated upon the words of ultimate reality, and who were solely intent on contemplating the supreme truth of the supreme Lord’s primordial wisdom.
By those initiated into the Mahāpāśupata, Aghora, Śaiva, and Śāmbhava [traditions].
By those endowed with knowledge of the six locations (ṣaṭsthala) and intent upon the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva). || 23 ||
By those established in the rules of conduct prescribed in the Śvetāśvatara branch [of the Veda].
By the devotees of Maheśvara and by those who possess the *liṅga* of life through his grace. || 24 ||
By the best of heroic Māheśvaras, who were endowed with oneness through their refuges.
By those who eat what is offered to Śiva, while turning their backs on what is not offered. || 25 ||

By those who have reached certainty through the realization that "the entire universe consists of Śiva," and who have purified the categories of reality through the connection between the body and the *prāṇaliṅga*, [this state is attained]. || 26 ||
Filled with supreme bliss, free from burdens, and unrestrained;
having abandoned mutual animosity born of caste, they were unperturbed. || 27 ||
It was crowded in one place by cows, tigers, and other creatures eager to seize grass and water, yet it was beautiful in its entirety, bringing about a convergence of all joys.
They were satisfied with food and drink that possessed the essence of the six flavors, served in golden vessels fashioned by the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhuk. || 29 ||
It was characterized by hundreds of thousands of house-doors and courtyards occupied by countless throngs of guests who had arrived from various directions.
Description of the arrival of the charioteer:
In that hermitage, which was a temple of Śiva crowded with hosts of attendants propitiated by constant festivals,
and where fatigue was dispelled by the knowledge of reality— (31)
The high-souled sages, headed by Śaunaka, were firm in their vows;
they were constantly devoted to the knowledge of Śiva and immersed in the essence of devotion to Śiva. || 32 ||
They were solely devoted to the meditation on Śiva, intent upon the vows of Śiva,
regarding the worship of Śiva as their entire essence, and perceiving the majesty of Śiva.
Their sins were swept away by their intellects which contemplated the divine sports of Śiva;
they beheld Sūta, who had arrived there by chance with the desire to witness the sacrificial session.

To him who possessed knowledge of the three periods of time obtained through the grace of Vyāsa, and who experienced the meaning of all the Purāṇas as clearly as an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand. || 35 ||
His heart was one-pointedly fixed on Śiva, he was devoted to the initiation of Śiva,
and his inner being was permeated by the digit of consciousness through the contemplation of the non-duality of Śiva.
Constantly muttering the two-syllable mantra "Śiva-Śiva" again and again,
he turned his back on outsiders through his very sight, touch, and conversation.
Having realized the oneness of his own self with the life-force of the beloved Lord, he was a worshiper of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the moving deities;
his entire body was smeared with holy ashes, and a radiant Tripuṇḍra mark shone upon his forehead.
He wore necklaces, bracelets, a crown, armlets, and earrings made of rudrākṣa beads;
his physical characteristics from previous births had been eradicated by the moment of his initiation into the Śiva-dīkṣā.
Beholding him— who was rich in inexhaustible auspicious yoga, worthy of worship by the twice-born, and who fulfills all desires— those most excellent of great sages [were filled with wonder].
Rising from afar, they bowed and worshipped that guru;
they were honored by the blessings of the ash, rudrākṣa beads, and the favor granted by him.
Having seated him in the midst of the assembly upon a high seat of kuśa grass.
Adorned with woolen rugs and covered with a large tiger skin as an upper spread.
And all of them, individually, then diligently offered oblations such as fruits and flowers near his two feet.
Having prostrated themselves repeatedly on all sides like a staff out of devotion,
they placed their foreheads at his feet, thereby casting far away all evil words.
With their palms joined in reverence, they all stood and addressed the charioteer.
The sages said: O Blessed One, knower of all scriptures, expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas, O high-minded one, the Purāṇas are indeed the illuminators of the Vedas.
O ocean of compassion, you have narrated all of these to us.
Among them are the Śaiva, the future [Skānda], the Laiṅga, and the Vārāha. || 47 ||
The Skanda, Mātsya, Kaurma, Mārkaṇḍeya, Vāmana, and Brahmāṇḍa—these ten [Purāṇas] consist of three hundred thousand verses in number. (48)
Description of the Sages' Inquiry:
"The Śaiva Purāṇas, which are characterized by the quality of goodness (sāttvika), have been heard from the lotus of your mouth;
they are contained within that Purāṇa known as the Bhaviṣya, which is approved by Śiva. (49)
The life stories of the devotees of Śiva and of Śiva and Śivā themselves have been told;
[this occurs] when, in the sinful Tiṣya age, those intent on uprooting Dharma [prevail].
By many sinful heretics, such as the Buddhists, Cārvākas, and Kaulikas.
And by those devoted to other deities, who were intent on reviling Śiva. || 51 ||
By those born of the Brahmin lineage who had been cursed by Dadhīci and Gautama.
By the cruel followers of the Daityas, according to the various divisions such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others.
By those who had entered other paths, devotion to Śiva was neglected;
then, by the command of Śiva, incarnations of the lords of the Pramathas [appeared]. 53.
Likewise, he established those who had gained faith in him, as well as the suppression of the wicked and the perfect upliftment through the auspicious conduct of Vīraśaivism. (54)
According to the very sequence of the cycles of the ages, you have out of supreme compassion for us related everything as if it were already past, even though it was yet to come. (55)
In this account of the incarnation of Nandīśvara and the praise of his life,
[it concerns] the form of the Lord Maheśa in the great city named Kalyāṇa.
The arrival at the assembly hall of Nandīśa was described,
[the arrival] of the Lord of immeasurable splendor who was gratified by that propitiation.
O Sage, the instruction on the knowledge of Śiva has been described by you;
now we wish to hear [the teaching] of the omniscient Great Guru. (58)
The divine play of Maheśa, the embodiment of the Lord, which bestows bliss and possesses the skill to uplift those submerged in the impurities of the Kali age. (59)
How did this Mahādeva, who is untainted and possesses the form of the Lord, descend upon the earth? You should tell me of his majesty.
If we are worthy vessels for the compassion of the venerable Guru, then gladden us now with the streams of the nectar of his discourse. (61)
Thus entreated, the charioteer was pleased; his memory was awakened, and through the power of Śiva’s possession, there arose in him the emergence of supreme bliss and absorption.
For a long time his mind remained concentrated, finding bliss in the meditation upon the feet;
with his eyes slightly opened, he beheld the *liṅga* as if it were resting in the palm of his hand.

Meditating upon everything as consisting of Śiva through the equality of the external and internal, he became a treasury of knowledge of the three times and one who had directly realized the three worlds. (64)
Agitated by the questions concerning the stories of the venerable Guru uttered by him, he was completely filled with the sprouts of noble horripilation covering his entire body. (65)
With the corners of his eyes moistened by tears of joy,
he gazed upon all the sages with a face whose lotus was smiling.
Though desiring to speak, he restrained his words which were faltering with joy;
remaining silent for a moment, the fountain of his speech surged forth once more.
Having performed meditation upon his guru as prescribed by the Sūtra, and having described the greatness of the guru,
he remembered the sage Vyāsa with devotion, as well as his own guru and Gaṇanāyaka; then,
with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, he spoke these auspicious words.
Sūta said:
"Excellent, excellent, O high-souled sages of celebrated vows!
Since I have been made most fulfilled in this world by you."
This question of yours bestows joy upon the entire world.
By which very firm devotion toward the Guru, who is the Supreme Self, is produced. || 70 ||
Only those who possess supreme devotion toward the Divine, as well as toward the Guru,
are capable of posing this very question concerning the domain of Vedānta.
Oh, by whom on earth can the greatness of the company of the virtuous be described?
By whom I was urged in the narrative concerning the majesty of the glorious Guru. || 72 ||
Association with the virtuous and solitude, along with steady eyesight—by the absence of one of these he is called one-eyed, and by the absence of both he is declared blind. (73)

Those who are devoted to the auspicious and glorious Guru, who speak the truth, have conquered their senses, and are united with the Liṅga and the body—those pure ones are indeed proclaimed as saints (santaḥ). || 74 ||

Those who are disciplined by the use of ashes and rudrākṣa beads, devoted to the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara), and established in the knowledge of Śiva as superior to the universe, are proclaimed as true saints (santaḥ). || 75 ||

Those who are devoted to the auspicious Vedas, the Guru, and Brahmā, and who are attached to the nectar of their stories while remaining detached—they are the truly virtuous; indeed, association with them is difficult to attain.
"O sages, today a truly auspicious day has dawned for me, since I have been impelled by you to speak of the nectar-like story of the Lord, whose nature is truth, knowledge, and consciousness. (77)
He who is the Lord and creator of all beings who follow the path of the disciplined,
and who himself is the Guru who teaches the union of the body with the beloved Liṅga.
He who, for the sake of protecting his disciples, personally assumed a human form, having held his vital breath through the western path and awakened Kuṇḍalinī; (79)
Constantly offering his inner disposition with the exclusive water-pot (kumbha) unto the Liṅga.
He moves upon the earth according to his own will, like a yogi free from all limiting adjuncts.
Listen as I tell you of his incomparable majesty.
The entire majesty of the Lord—whatever has been, will be, and is now existing.
O Brahmins, it is not possible for me to describe [it] even in hundreds of years.
Just as Mahādeva, residing in the cave, causes me to be uttered here.
Likewise, let this discourse be regarded as being like an echo;
I do not speak, Śiva is the speaker, and Maheśvara is also the listener. (83)
This is a description of the greatness of the Lord’s incarnation and divine play;
O Brahmins, you are not mere mortals, nor is this a worldly tale.
This is the [teaching] of the Guru, who is the embodiment of the Great Liṅga of Guheśvara.
O believers, listen with faith to the majesty of the divine play-incarnations;
this is not merely for the purpose of passing the time, nor is it like listening to ordinary gossip. (85)
Those men who, with pure minds, constantly listen with devotion.
Śiva bestows grace upon them, removing the bondage of body, mind, and objects.
This is not a tale of war wrought by hatred toward one's kinsmen;
nor is it a tale of those greedy for and longing after the enjoyment of sensual pleasures with women. (87)
Nor is there even talk of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) for the sake of the happiness derived from sacred tradition;
rather, it is filled with the bliss produced by the yoga of Kuṇḍalinī.
The auspicious discourse that bestows the joy of oneness with the Self, which is the space of consciousness, is [the only one worthy of being told];
the talk of people and insects overcome by birth, death, and old age is not. 89.
This discourse is for those blinded by the darkness of karma who do not know the Śaiva dharma;
it is not for men who act according to their own whims and are blinded by arrogance.
Rather, [this applies] to those who possess bodies assumed for their sport (līlā) by their own will.
The story of those whose limbs consist of the ether of consciousness and who possess virtuous conduct.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, let this meritorious story be heard, which is like a ladder for the knowledge and devotion of Śiva’s Guru, and which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (92)
Having swallowed the stalks and leaves of the *ikṣu* plant, the goat is chewing the cud.
To such an extent is that person of meager intellect satisfied with only that much. || 93 ||
Likewise, a base person in this world, considering the highest happiness to be heaven and the like,
performs actions and encounters birth and death.
Just as an elephant becomes happy after tasting sugarcane juice,
so too does the wise man, having tasted the essence of devotion, partake of the nectar of immortality.
O lords of sages, you who possess devotion for the lotus feet of Śiva,
listen with reverence to the great divine play of the Lord’s Liṅga.
Just as an iron ornament in a body consisting of the element of touch becomes beautifully adorned when it turns into molten gold, so too [does the self]. || 97 ||
Likewise, even speech employed with extreme brevity shines all the more when addressed to the Omniscient One, who is a vessel for auspicious qualities—even by one who is unwise. (98)
Having bent forward and raised both arms to touch the sky, for what purpose would one stand upright? For that [space] is all-pervading and equal on all sides.

Thus, having failed to reach the glory of the all-pervading Lord— whether through his state of possessing qualities, his qualitylessness, or even his divine play— this speech of mine has come to rest.
What else could it rely upon? Without that, nothing exists;
a cow-calf does not abandon its mother cow to run after a female bear. (101)
Likewise, having abandoned Śiva, one should not resort to any other speech than mine;
for the majesty of the Lord Īśa was proclaimed of old by the Pramathas. (102)
Recalling how it will happen again and again through the cycles of the ages as if it had already occurred, I shall tell it today; listen, you who are faithful.
For time here is indeed beginningless; again and again in the Kali age, there are incarnations of the Lord and of the Pramathas, as well as their activities.
For the sake of establishing the Dharma, they should be known as the best among the believers;
the Lord is to be known as the holder of the machine, and indeed we are all the machines.
Just as he impels us, so do we act and not otherwise;
he is the Lord Siddhavīreśvara, the glorious Guru of the Śiva-yogins. 106.
One should apply the intellect that spans the three periods of time to the description of the Lord’s divine play,
for even the Vedas and other scriptures, along with the mind, turn back from it.
That which is empty of beginning, middle, and end, and which transcends sound, the point, and the digit—this very thing is utterly indefinable even by wise yogis. (108)
Śrī Śiva is existence-consciousness-bliss, devoid of name and form;
he is without attributes, the supreme reality, free from conceptual construction, and untainted. (109)
Bharga is the Lord, free from the association of creation and destruction;
he is the Supreme Lord, independent and having brought the great Māyā under his control. || 110 ||
Having dispelled the masses of the darkness of ignorance, he seized Nandīśvara and the other Pramathas, Brahmā and the other preeminent gods, and the celestial sages such as Sanaka and his brothers.
Bearing a desirable form, he carries the seal of supreme knowledge (*sujñānamudrā*) and a book, as well as a bell and a vessel of nectar, in order to bestow grace. (112)
He has a mass of matted hair shaped like a crescent moon, eyes extending as far as his ears,
long and lustrous ears hanging down, and a slightly prominent nose.
He has a neck like a conch shell and broad shoulders; he wears earrings of the lord of serpents, is adorned with a sacred thread of snakes, and is beautified by a yogic band.
He was glorious, with uplifted arms, endowed with a long line of body hair,
beautiful with a whorled navel, and graced by two thighs like those of an elephant.
Adorned with two feet reddened by a network of ruby-like radiance,
he shines forth, manifesting in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
The root of the banyan tree is indeed the temple of that Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
the water of that nyagrodha tree is known as the essence of tranquility (śāntarasa). || 117 ||
The description of the nature of the Supreme Self:
The virtuous assembly is its basin for irrigation, and the primordial syllable Om is its root;
the Vedas are its trunk, and the sciences are proclaimed to be its matted locks. (118)
In the same way, the Upanishads are said to be the branches and devotion is the fruit;
bliss is the essence of the fruit, and internal meditation is the means of attainment. (119)
"The abandonment of anxiety is to be known as the great path by the high-souled ones," [he said] at the foot of that banyan tree, which was surrounded by hosts of sages.
Seated upon the lion-throne of knowledge, that true Guru, though but a child, imparted wisdom through his silence to his aged disciples, O believers. (121)
Who indeed is capable of describing the majesty of that god?
He alone, the Lord of the gods of gods, has come to earth out of compassion for his devotees. (122)
Having cast aside the trident from his hand and the collection of serpent ornaments,
[he appeared] with many hosts of spirits and using a skull as his vessel.
With poison in his throat and an eye on his forehead, the Guru himself, his eyes moist with the essence of compassion and his speech as sweet as nectar, concealed [his true nature]. (124)
He was the personified essence of tranquility, radiant with beauty and self-restraint;
with a lotus-face graced by a gentle smile, he was as handsome as the god of love himself. || 125 ||
Adorned with garments that were slightly dyed saffron and beautifully washed,
he was the manifest bestower of liberation and the giver of joy to the people.
Renowned throughout all the worlds and the granter of the desired objects of his devotees, he has become manifest on earth by the name Siddhavīreśvara. 127.
Even Nandīśvara himself is not capable of praising the greatness of this great Lord of Yoga; how then could those like me possibly do so?
This very Siddhavīreśa, the crest-jewel of true teachers,
established the two traditions, namely the Sakala and the Niṣkala.
Having taught the Śaiva dharma to all, that ocean of imperishable knowledge, a treasury of compassion, protected the entire world. (130)
This is the birthplace of the entire succession of all auspicious qualities;
for the Self of all beings himself moves about here, assuming the form of a mobile linga.
He possesses the noble form of a jewel among living beings who are devotees of Śiva;
he is a poet, skilled in utterly destroying the blinding darkness of Māyā. (132)

He is like the fruit of a tree that is easily accessible to all, yet remains unapproachable by the vilest of men— the opponents such as the Buddhists, the Cārvākas, and the Jains— who are like insects.
Adorned with the binding of the turban of the conduct of ultimate auspiciousness, he is like a fragrant cow tied in the cowshed within the home of his devotees. 134.

He was marked by the title "Śūla" (the Trident) placed upon the head of the Jaina, possessing the insignia of the seed-syllable of evil pride, and displaying the audacity to crush that pride. || 135 ||
Purifying the earth with the graceful play of his soft footsteps,
Śiva, whose body is the dancing Liṅga, shines with the exquisite skill of his gait.
Whether saying that what is given to one who is initiated perishes or does not perish, he wanders the earth himself for the sake of protecting his disciples. (137)
This Guru, who removes the suffering of those who bow before him, bestows upon his devotees the merit of his own foot-water— a gracious gift that is the means to liberation.

He whose form is characterized by being the object of worship, who is a celestial wish-fulfilling tree for those who propitiate him, and who dwells everywhere throughout the three worlds—[he is present] far and wide. (139)
By worshipping the pair of syllables "Gu-ru," which dispels the inner darkness within the hearts of those who revere his feet, one triumphs spontaneously.
Endowed with the portion of pure being, though devoid of qualities, he is the locus of qualities; though one, he has attained manifoldness like the moon reflected in jars of water. || 141 ||

Due to differences in limiting adjuncts, and according to scripture as well as reasoning, the Brahman that is immediate, the teacher who is higher than the highest, does not [differ] in reality. (142)
The root of mantra is the word of the Guru; the root of worship is the feet of the Guru;
the root of meditation is the form of the Guru; the root of liberation is the grace of the Guru. 143.
The true Guru is subtler than the subtlest and greater than the greatest;
he is the path of life for the Praṇava and the one who reveals the meaning of the Praṇava.
He whose lineage of disciples has rendered the eight supernatural powers, such as *aṇimā*, as insignificant as blades of grass—
that yogi is a treasure-trove in the courtyard of his own home for those who have accomplished their life's purpose.
For those solely devoted to merit, it is like honey placed in gold;
it is a state of wakefulness devoid of the delusive conditions of dreaming and deep sleep. (146)
He is the witness of the three states, beautiful with innate bliss,
and he possesses a respectful knowledge of the reality of the connection between the body and the liṅga of the vital breath.
Having instructed his excellent disciples through the experience of blissful play, that great guru protects both enjoyment and liberation by means of his grace. (148)
To that venerable Guru, the great tree for the lords of the wise, whose nature is truth, who is his own self,
the meritorious one accorded by the Vedas, the ascetic, the infinite,
the Supreme Brahman; to Śrī Siddhavīreśvara, who is ever devoted solely to the protection of the multitude of his devotees— [I bow].
Salutations to you, the Lord Indra, who brings intense joy to the minds of all spiritual teachers. || 149 ||
Thus, filled with joy born from the hymn of praise to the most excellent Śiva-guru, and having subsequently attained the realization of all truths through his compassion,
Sūta, beholding the assembly of sages desiring to hear everywhere the divine play of the Lord Guru Śiva, spoke.
The Great-Souled One. || 150 ||
Listen, all you sages, with attentive minds;
this essence of the entire Vedānta has not been revealed to anyone. (151)
Without beginning, middle, or end; the first of all that is first; stainless; the goal indicated by the crest-ornaments of all the Vedas; peerless; and free from affliction.
That which is "this" is indefinable, beyond the reach of speech and mind; it is truth, knowledge, and infinite, the supreme mass of eternal bliss. (153)
It is free from conceptual construction, ineffable, without support, and undisturbed;
it is the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the Supreme Self, and the ultimate refuge.
Higher than the highest, the supreme light, transcending the path beyond the highest;
the self-luminous sky of consciousness, all-pervading and eternal. (155)
There the sun does not shine, nor do the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not flash there, so how could fire shine there? (156)
All this shines only by reflecting that which shines; it is through His light that everything becomes manifest.
For it is by His light that speech, along with the heart, turns back.

That by which this entire universe is pervaded, which is indeed the expresser even of speech, that which cannot be conceived by the mind, and that which, though thought of, remains unthought—[that is Brahman]. (158)
That which is considered immortal would be unknown to those who know, while it is known to those who do not know; it is one alone, without a second. (159)
That which is desired as the Liṅga of Brahman alone, known as the Changeless (nirvikāra), is itself the supreme reality, the wonderful substratum of all. || 160 ||
The immortal Brahman has three quarters; it is full, partless, and the cause of all.
It is signless, situated in the midst of signs, non-dual, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). || 161 ||
That reality known as the Unchanging (nirvikāra), which is the unsurpassed supreme syllable,
out of a desire to emit, favors Māyā in its sattvic form.
Therefore, that very Lord Sadāśiva has attained manifestation;
he alone is the supreme Śiva who has ascended to Mahākailāsa. || 163 ||
This very deity is the benefactor of all, transcending all principles (tattvas) one after another; his form is invisible, he is to be grasped through meditative absorption, and he consists of mind.
An exposition on the presentation of the sequence of creation through the five causes:
This Supreme Lord is formless and yet possesses form; He is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala);
though beyond the reach of speech and mind, He is accessible through devotion. 165.
The power of consciousness (cicchakti) born from Sadāśiva is that auspicious Ambikā;
non-different from Śiva, she is supreme bliss. She alone is considered Umā, the digit of consciousness (citkalā). 166.
Sadāśiva and the power of consciousness (cicchakti) entered into a state of wedlock by their own will;
from them Śiva was born, and he alone is called Īśvara. || 167 ||
He too resides in Kailāsa, the abode of causes, and is the concealer of all;
for the Lord consists of the principle of Miśra (the Mixed), being both with parts and without parts.
From that Śiva, the power of his own will (svecchā-śakti) was produced; from those two, having become united as a couple, the illustrious Rudra, the lord of the worlds, was born. (169)
He is the bearer of five faces because he consists of the five Brahmans;
he is the eight-formed one who effects the creation, preservation, and destruction of the world.
The Supreme Lord, known as Śrīkaṇṭha, who resides in Kāryakailāsa, sports at his own will with innumerable great attendants. || 171 ||
O lords of sages, from that Rudra the power of action (kriyā-śakti) was produced;
she alone is Gaurī, the daughter of the Mountain, the consort of Viṣṇu, and the daughter of Dakṣa.
The Goddess, whose nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas), is celebrated as Durgā and Kālī; she is the union of Rudra and his power of action (kriyā-śakti). || 173 ||
Viṣṇu, who is intent on protecting the world, has attained this state;
yet even he is possessed of the quality of tamas, such as sleep, laziness, and negligence.
Having attained the nature of being through the grace of Rudra, consisting of truth and bliss,
he dwells on Mount Meru in the city named Vaikuṇṭha and indeed protects the world.
From that Viṣṇu, she who is known as Mahālakṣmī was born;
she is the primordial Śakti produced from those two who had become a couple. (176)
Brahmā, the creator of the entire world, four-faced and endowed with the quality of rajas, was born from this King of Truth; indeed, from him the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti) emerged.
Through the states of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī,
as well as in its supreme (parā) form and its essential nature, that power called Speech becomes fourfold.
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded by her;
she is Brahmāṇī, born from the two, Brahmā and herself, who have become a couple. || 179 ||

All this, both moving and non-moving, is designated as the microcosm (piṇḍa) and the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa); since everything exists in the form of both the collective totality and the individual parts, it is entirely composed of Śiva.
Even Sadāśiva— the omniscient, the creator of all, and the Lord of the universe—
manifests through the expansion of his own power of will (icchā-śakti) in forms such as Maheśvara and others.
Having created this entire universe and having entered into it, the Lord became both the manifest and the unmanifest, existing in the form of both the universal aggregate and the individual.
All beings are one foot of Him; the three-footed immortal Brahman is in heaven.
He alone, O lords of sages, is this Mahādeva, the Lord of the Secret.
Free from the need for material causes, instruments, or purposes, he creates, maintains, and destroys everything by his mere will alone. (184)
Thus he covers [himself] and favors [her], yet through his blissful play,
desiring to sport with her who is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), he remains effortless.
In the act of creation, he appointed Brahmā; for both creation and maintenance, Mādhava;
and for creation, maintenance, and dissolution, the one Lord Rudra Paśupati.
Having consecrated them by his own command, he made them the lords over those respective domains;
therefore, Rudra, the Lord and Master of creatures (Paśupati), is superior to those two.
By virtue of his proximity to Śiva, he is equal to him in name, abode, and other attributes;
he was honored by the great architect Guheśa.
The omniscient Guheśvara, beautiful with existence, consciousness, and bliss, dwells upon the lofty peak of Kailāsa on Mount Meru, which is his abode of activity. || 189 ||
On the path beyond the great vessel of many millions of Brahmā-eggs,
he was accompanied by those eternally liberated in the stainless space of consciousness.
The Lord dwells upon the peak of Mahākailāsa together with Cidambā.
The sages said:
O Sūta, best among those well-versed in the Purāṇas, tell us in its entirety the majesty of Mahākailāsa, by knowing which one may attain liberation. (191)
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, with attentive minds;
what secret concerning the devotees of Śiva exists on earth that is [unknown] to those like me? (192)
This question concerning liberation is approved by you yogis;
but by whom can the greatness of Mahākailāsa be described? (193)
Having meditated upon the majesty of Mahākailāsa in all the places of meditation,
one should contemplate the Lord Sadāśiva on its highest peak.
Indeed, many millions of Brahmāṇḍas, guarded by innumerable great hosts,
are protected through the majesty of Maheśa.
Furthermore, above those infinite millions of cosmic eggs,
in the stainless great space that is free from conceptual construction and devoid of affliction— (196)
Description of Mahākailāsa:
By the command of Śaṅkara, this mountain Mahākailāsa exists as an object of knowledge for those who know the Vedānta, which is indefinable by space and time. 197.
Elevated by sixty koṭis of yojanas and extending for thirty koṭis, that abode of Ānanda is a treasury of splendors. (198)
O you of excellent vows, its summit, enriched with the nine gems, shines brilliantly above it.
There exists the city of Sadāśiva, which bestows liberation.
It was surrounded by walls of various jewels, gate-towers, and watchtowers;
in its center stood a divine palace beyond the reach of speech and mind.
In its center shines [the palace] enriched with thousands of jeweled pillars,
together with all the powers of concealment in the form of jeweled mechanical dolls.
Upon the most excellent lion-throne of the great wheel-king, brilliantly radiant, within the shimmering bindu-maṇḍala of the great machine of the sky of consciousness; || 202 ||
Seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana) was Mahāśambhu Sadāśiva, possessing twenty-five excellent faces that rose up with the twenty-five principles (tattvas). || 203 ||
Adorned with fifty arms raised aloft, wielding the weapons of the fifty Mātṛkās.
He is eager to embrace Jñānāmbā, who is seated upon the seat of his left lap.
He was adorned with a crown, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, bangles, and earrings,
as well as other ornaments inlaid with rubies.
He is the mass of truth, knowledge, and bliss; he possesses the radiance of a thousand suns;
he is the glorious one devoid of both the object of perception and its defining characteristics; he is the Great One with a non-material body.
From whom words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach Him—
He is this very one, the refuge of all powers, surrounded by many.
Endowed with all sovereign powers by the Rudras, Siddhas, and all the sages—who are eternally liberated, free from appearances, and devoted to the realization of oneness—[he shines]. || 208 ||
Constantly being worshipped, the eternal and all-pervading Supreme Self shines forth for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees. 209.
O best of the twice-born, around that Ratnaśṛṅga, eleven other peaks made of sunstone shine forth; oh, how wonderful!
Among them, O observers of noble vows, are five other forms of Śambhu; thus there are six forms in total, and there are yet other forms numbering twenty-five.
Likewise, fifty-one Mātṛkās reside there;
and surrounding them are peaks indeed composed of fire-gems.
In those [worlds], one thousand and one meditate upon Īśvara;
there dwell one hundred and eight forms of Tāṇḍaveśa.
Indeed, the deities of seventy million great mantras dwell there.
There are eleven thousand peaks extending all around it.
By the command of the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), great peaks possessing the luster of clear crystal shine forth;
upon them dwell Vighneśvara, Skanda, Mahāśāstṛ, and Bhairava.
The lords of the Gaṇas, headed by Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and Mahākāla; Dharma as a four-footed bull; and the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu, who grants all desires. (216)
By the command of Śiva, Durgā and the other Śaktis, as well as Caṇḍīśa and the other devotees, and the five weapon-forms of Śiva, dwell there perpetually. (217)
O Brahmins, their peaks, radiant with jewels on all sides, shine forth in a continuous array of one hundred and one thousand, truly enchanting to the mind. (218)
Those Viṣṇus situated on the western peak are intent on the worship of Śiva;
those Brahmās situated on the northern peak are intent on the worship of the Śivaliṅga;
and those guardians of the world (Lokapālas), headed by Indra, situated on the eastern peak, meditate upon Him.
The hosts of noble sages dwell in the southern regions, centered upon the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
On all sides, they have ten million peaks, each increasing by one;
these are made of gold, O Lord of Munis, and upon them dwell the lords of beings.
Furthermore, there were the ten weapons, the Śrī-rudras, the Siddhas, Garuḍas, and Gandharvas; the Vidyādharas, Surabhi, and the treasures Maṇi, Kalpa, Śaṅkha, and Padma.
The most excellent mountain Kailāsa, the delightful abode of Rudra,
possesses true majesty; even during the internal dissolutions, it remains visible atop the cosmic egg.
Those who rely on the nature of demons do not see this, for they are possessed by even a trace of evil. || 235 ||
On this great mountain Kailāsa, which is replete with existence, consciousness, and bliss,
resides the all-pervading Lord Sadāśiva, the bestower of grace upon all.
The Lord, who brings about the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all beings from Maheśvara down to Brahmā,
sports by means of his power of consciousness (cicchakti) for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees.
The Lord, having consecrated this very Rudra in the sovereignty over the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of all things, established him on Kailāsa.
On the northern peak of Meru, above the cities of Brahmā and Acyuta,
there is a mountain known as Rājatādri, the abode of Rudra and the refuge of the virtuous.
By the command of Sadāśiva, he too—who is of the nature of a mass of truth and knowledge—is as meritorious as Mahākailāsa and is worshipped by those of virtuous soul. (240)
It was as high and long as that [mountain], and endowed with peaks such as those;
there were the sons of Sadāśiva, his devotees, and great persons. || 241 ||
All those [beings] were likewise [manifested] through the very portions of Rudradeva himself;
O twice-born ones, the sovereignty of Rudra arose in that same manner through his grace.
Rudra possesses five faces, known by names such as Sadyojāta and others;
he has ten arms and is adorned with all the names beginning with Śiva.
He is eternally presided over by that power and likewise marked by its signs.
This entire universe is composed of illusion; the Person alone is partless and absolute.
He is the presiding lord of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the supreme cause of the universe;
his power, consisting of the three qualities, is praised as Māyā. || 245 ||
In reality, O twice-born ones, this Gaurī, daughter of the mountain king, the auspicious wife of Rudra, is Śivomā Pārvatī, whose essence is consciousness. (246)
Playing with her by the power of Maheśa’s grace, this Lord of the Universe, known as Śrīkaṇṭha, became one to be served by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other gods. || 247 ||
He personally occupies Kāryakailāsa, situated within Jambūdvīpa.
Thus, O lords of sages, I have indeed related to you this life-story of the Lord, which precedes creation and contains the essence of the meaning of all scriptures.
He who reads or hears it with supreme devotion shall, through the very compassion of the Guru, [attain liberation] within the three worlds.
One shall attain one's desired objects. || 249 ||
Thus, in the *Ārṣa-Śrī-Bhaviṣyat-Purāṇa-Kathā-Viśālā*,
which accords with the words of the *pramatha* hosts, whose nature is to uplift people submerged in the impurities of the Kali age,
and which concerns the divine play (*līlā*) of Lord Liṅga—

The First Chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Description of the Naimiṣa Forest, the Arrival of the Sūta, the Question posed by the Sages, the Sūta’s Meditation on his Preceptor, the Description of His Majesty, the Definition of the Nature of the Supreme Self, the Presentation of the Sequence of Creation through the Five Causes, and the Commencement of the Description of the Great Tale."
Description of Śrī Kailāsa.
[Now begins the second chapter.]
The sages said:
"Everything regarding the majesty of the Supreme Lord has been told by you;
now, please describe the divine play of the Great Mount Kailāsa."
Sūta said:
Those whose fear of worldly existence has been washed away by devotion to the lotus feet of the venerable Siddhavīra-guru, and who possess supreme spiritual power;
Let all the sages, whose nature is the bliss of sacred learning, listen to the divine play of the Lord Liṅga, which is pure in its meaning and pleasing to the ear. || 2 ||
Together with that power of Sarasvatī, by the command of Śambhu,
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, performed the creation of the cosmic egg.
From the earth up to the Satyaloka, and from the netherworlds (Pātāla) down to the lowest depths,
that Grandfather created the worlds according to the principle of the palace (prāsāda).

Having created [the world] according to the sequence of the creation of the elements, preceded by the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), and having established it within the macrocosm and the microcosm at the command of Giriśa; || 5 ||
Those three kinds of living beings who have gone to dissolution into primordial nature are recorded as:
Garuḍas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, sages, and gods.
Humans, serpents, Daityas, as well as the Moon, Sun, and Fire;
those known as female, male, and neuter, and whatever other multitudes of living beings there may be—(7).
Having created for those entities that are the enjoyers various objects of enjoyment as well as the aggregates that serve as the seats of experience, the Four-faced One [Brahmā] remained there.
O twice-born ones, that support which created this world in sixfold form— distinguished by name, form, and the divisions of time— was Mahāmeru.
Who can describe the great majesty of that mountain named Kailāsa, situated upon its peak, which is a vast treasury of wonders? (10)
Since that very Sadāśiva, the sole creator of the entire work of creation, having become the Lord Rudra, dwells upon the mountain; (11)
How could those like me, possessing only the physical eye, be able to describe it?
This very one, whose quality is pure sattva, has assumed the form of silver;
shining intensely with radiance, he brings delight to the eyes. (13)
By the command of Śiva, even though he was formless, Kailāsa became embodied;
there, the delightful Bhogapura was established, fashioned from the essence of bliss.
O Brahmins, the height of this rampart cannot be attained even by the Vedas,
and the depth of its moat is said to be unfathomable even by the Shastras.
Its great height is unsurpassed even by the scriptures;
its light, moreover, is extraordinary, shining without distinction day and night. (16)
The street of the Great King is pure devotion; therein shines that very egoism (so’haṃtā), which serves as the binding of a divine archway strung with jewels.
In that city, the subtle principles known as Sādākhyā are like delightful palaces;
there are also dwellings dense with the abundance of knowledge and dispassion—this is the description of the assembly hall of Śrī Rudra. (18)
This Kailāsa, the abode of Hara, possesses a greatness beyond counting;
there stands the temple of Maheśa, consisting of his own innate bliss.
In its center shines the pavilion of the abode, adorned with the door known as the mind free from mental fluctuations, which transcends sound, the point, and the digits.
There, the lofty celestial tree stands with its deep, unobstructed shade, its jeweled pavement struck by the rays of the eightfold sovereign powers.

There, upon the tip of the *praṇava* shimmering with the eight Mothers, on a divine throne adorned with the yoga of supreme knowledge, the Supreme Rudra ever dwells, delighting solely in the *bhadrāsana*, sporting in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the yoga of his own direct experience.
He is eternally real, free from limiting conditions, partless, the pure, awakened, and perfect conscious self;
stainless, incomparable, faultless, devoid of qualities, the singular object of the Vedas. (23)
The Goddess of Dharma presides over its gateway; the Goddess of the Vedas presides over its stables for the horses;
the Goddess of Peace presides over its personified form; and the Goddess of the Royal Treasury presides over its root-storehouse.
The Fortune of Liberation. || 24 ||
His two arms are the prāṇa and apāna breaths; his two feet are established as the beginningless and endless.
His form is the glorious resonance of the syllable Om (Oṃkāra), appearing as a streak of white light from countless rays.
Māyā, who possesses three qualities and rests upon the lap of that Rudra,
though she was brought under his control, nevertheless became the cause of the pride of him who desired to create the world.

She whose pair of feet are formed of conceptualization and discursive thought, who is graceful with the vine-like arms of attachment and delusion, whose hips are arrogant with pride, and whose breasts are desire and greed— she is Līlāvatī.

With knowledge and ignorance as her eyes, and with "mine-ness" (mamatā) as her face, she who deludes the virtuous shines forth, having undertaken the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the three worlds. (27)
The splendors of the glittering jeweled ornaments of this woman, who is a treasury of all beauty,
met on every side with the masses of light from the jewels on the hoods of the serpent coiled around her.

The side-glances of Maheśvara and the playful movements of the eyes of the shapely women, having met upon a path invisible to others, attain identity with them—oh, how marvelous! So it is with the lords of sages. (29)

The city woman, casting forth the god of love with her smiles that inspired shame in the lovely-smiling Purāri, quickly produced a mental agitation in him who was otherwise free from such agitation—how strange! (30)
There, that twofold form of hers shone forth like moonlight scented with camphor from the spotless moon, or like a streak of gold upon a fragrant stone.

Moreover, he is adorned by that [earth] which has as its bulb (kanda) the great seat (mahāpīṭha) where it meets the waves of the Gaṅgā surging from the basin at the roots of his matted locks hanging down to the soles of his feet;
and she is likewise adorned with petals in the form of rows of ornaments set with gems and flowers in the form of ivory.
Śambhu himself shines forth like a banyan tree, the root-cause of everything, from which all creepers [of creation] spring. || 32 ||
On Mount Kailāsa, with charmingly tinkling bracelets, shimmering chowries,
and other implements for fanning, as well as alms-bowls held in their hands,
and with collections of fine silk cloths rich with betel-rolls and beautiful water-jars;
The daughters of Śiva serve the god Paśupati, the husband of Mṛḍānī.

And other blessed Rudra-maidens [attained their state] through service to the two Śivas as prescribed by the sacred tradition (samaya), and by means of those palm-leaf fans and the preparation of mirrors suitable for beholding their beauty. || 34 ||
On both sides of Śiva and Śivā, who are seated upon a noble throne of nine gems,
Rudras and Rudra-kanyās, beyond all counting, worship them everywhere.
That Śakti, in order to constantly serve her husband with the three qualities of self-mastery, gave birth to innumerable sons who were humble through discipline. (36)

Among these three types [of Rudras], those who have attained greatness through their mother’s excessive affection are the Rudras themselves— possessing radiant bodies, endowed with tawny matted hair and an eye on the forehead,
with women joined as half of their bodies, bearing the celestial Gaṅgā, and wearing the crescent moon upon their crests.
Countless beings, filled with the intense emotion of wrath, attend upon Sāmba in the assembly hall.

Furthermore, millions of other sons of Acyuta— possessing Kaustubha gems on their chests, eager for the focused meditation on the feet of Śiva, lords of Lakṣmī, seated upon lotuses, fathers of the gods, with eyes as long as lotuses, and preeminent in goodness— serve him incessantly.
To Samba, the true Guru, and to the primordial speech of the Primordial One, [I bow] while stationed on His left side.
The Vedas, with their beautiful faces, arise with gentle smiles; bearing bodies like gold and holding lotuses in their left hands,
they take their place on the right side of the Lotus-born Lord and perform service to the All-pervading One.
The third group consists of the countless sons of Īśa who are endowed with the quality of passion (rajas). || 39 ||
To the west of that, hosts of Garuḍas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Sādhyas, and Vibudhas, along with the assemblies of the lords of the gods,
stand and worship the primordial sovereign Śrī Rudra from all sides with complete devotion.
The worlds are innumerable. || 40 ||

In front of them, all around, the bull— resplendent with a gentle smile like the moon shining from within a flower-cup, and having assumed the state of being the vehicle of Bhava— shone brilliantly as he stood facing the two Śivas.
There, Vīrabhadra, the lord of Bhadrakālī, whose strength of arm acted like a massive boulder upon the head of Dakṣa, attends upon Rudra.
The bliss of Śiva has its comparison in the rise of Śaṅkara;
the happiness of the Lord of Girijā is the stability, and it is the basin for the Mṛḍa.
The supreme lord’s mirror-like face, filled with loveliness and a treasury of true splendor, directly delighted his followers.
Bhṛṅgīśa, bestowing joy upon the heart of the Enemy of Aṅgaja (Kāma),
displays his mastery in the art of dance in the north-eastern direction of the Lord.
Whichever direction Śiva looks, those situated there bow their faces;
whatever he says, they all respond with "Oṃ-oṃ-ma-ma-oṃ."
"O Master, this is a great favor; this is a favor, this is a grace!"—having spoken thus, they quickly carry out those various tasks.
Just as Mahādeva speaks,
so do Gopati, Śrīpati, Brāhmīpati, and Gīṣpati bear it upon their heads incessantly.
He drank up the seven oceans, cast down the golden mountain,
and stirred the hollow interior of the vessel of the universe with his very hand.
Those of great strength, the Piśācas, Bhūtas, and Vetālas, who are capable of uprooting the fangs of Yama, stand with palms joined in reverence at all times.
Indeed, bearing the command of Śiva upon their heads,
Durgā, Vināyaka, the seven Mātṛkās, and Kālabhairava dwell there in service.
Turning back, those led by Helī,
endowed with steadfast devotion, attend upon him, having gathered together on both sides.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, as well as the two Aśvins;
Gautama, Atri, Bharadvāja, Kaṇva, Gālava, and Kauśika. (53)
By the command of Śiva, Mārkaṇḍeya, Vasiṣṭha, and others were present here and there,
eager for a vision of him, with their bodies bowed down on all sides.
The splendors of Gaurī’s ornaments, the luster of the earrings and other jewels worn by Śiva, the moonlight-like radiance of his gentle smile, the brilliant light of Bhṛṅgīśvara,
and the clear brilliance of the pearl necklaces of the celestial nymphs such as Raṃbhā— whose minds are moist with passion— all these [are surpassed].
The splendors of the crowns of the gods, Śakra and the others, shine with the light of the lamps of the radiant heavens.

Moreover, O Lord, in that assembly where the rising splendor of Your excellence causes the spectators to withdraw, all these people— each holding a hundred lamps in their raised hands, casting hundreds of shadows— mostly engage one another in hair-pulling quarrels.
Upon the peak of the king of silver mountains, she who consists of light shines resplendently. || 56 ||
Then Gaurī, whose pair of lotus-eyes were clearly manifested by the waves of beauty from her face of gentle smiles—
she who is Māyā herself, having brought even the Lord of All under her sway, being honored and bowing down, spoke with love:
The beloved one who grants freedom from fear and bestows liberation. || 57 ||
The Dialogue between Śrī Gaurī and Śaṅkara.
Gaurī said:
O Lord, in the assembly, those who serve you while contemplating the creation and destruction of existence [are present].
Are all these who are situated here composed of consciousness and identical with Your self? || 58 ||
"O Maheśa, why do they undergo birth and destruction again and again?
Please instruct me," she asked him out of compassion; being thus questioned, he smiled and spoke once more.
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim these words, the most secret of secrets.
Having heard which, a living being is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra. || 60 ||
Devotion toward me among men is twofold, distinguished as primary and secondary;
devotion free from desire is primary, while that joined with desire is secondary. (61)
Those devotees who, having abandoned the activities of name-and-form and being free from desire,
constantly take refuge in me, they indeed attain me alone.
But those devotees who are of dull intellect, undisciplined, and desirous of fruits,
O Goddess, indeed undergo the cycle of coming and going between the upper and lower worlds.
Having spoken thus, the moon-crested Lord quickly ceased;
and the Goddess, having heard this, was delighted, yet she fell into reflection once more.
This entire world, both moving and stationary, is composed of me;
while I am awake everywhere, who could transgress my command?
"That one who is free from desire attains liberation"—this word spoken by Śambhu is like a flower in the sky, because this son of mine possesses even greater desire. (66)
"Since even Śiva has fallen under the sway of desire, I shall take half of his body.
I alone am the supreme power (parā śakti), the primordial cause of everything. (67)
Alas, I am victorious, having brought about the two—name and form—which are beginningless, belonging to Śiva, the Supreme Self, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss! 68.
From Sadāśiva down to Brahmā, including Indra and the foremost of the immortals—all embodied beings are truly subject to my māyā. (69)
Those who are attached to the wine of a woman’s face, intent on meditating upon her form,
and devoted to embracing her limbs, truly live— of this there is no doubt.
All this, consisting of female and male, moving and unmoving, is my own form;
yet my self-identification with the female form is even greater therein. (71)
"Therefore, I alone am superior to all and face in every direction"—thus, that Māyā became excessively arrogant, her egoism difficult to restrain. (72)
The etymological derivation of the word *allama*:
Then, having understood her intention, the Lord remembered the Lord *Allama*—the all-pervading Īśāna, the Lord of Yoga, the mass of true consciousness. (73)
The sages said:
O Sūta, knower of the truth of all matters, ocean of the nectar of devotion to Śiva—who is this one called Allamaprabhu who is remembered by Rudra? (74)
O great sage, this term "Allama" is a designation for the Lord; whether by conventional usage (rūḍhi) or by etymological derivation (yoga), what is its derivation like? (75)
Whether it be an unestablished term, or one derived from the Vedas, or even a worldly word—O you of noble vows, we all wish to hear it; please speak.
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, with attentive minds, to the etymological derivation of the word Prabhāvallabha as it is sanctioned by the scriptures. (77)
The letter *A* is the primordial, eternal source of all phonemes;
it is also the first of the seed-syllable of all mantras, the *praṇava*.
Because it is immortal, formless, fearless, and unborn, the Self is indeed declared to be the letter 'A' by means of scripture, reasoning, and direct experience. (79)
The intellect, refined by the word "yat," becomes one whose very form is the word "yat."
Upon hearing the first letter of such a word, one would certainly remember the meaning of that word;
therefore, from hearing the syllable "A," the intellect [remembers] the Lord whose nature is the Unborn (aja) and so forth.
One should meditate upon the unmanifest object, the supreme Śiva, which is without beginning or end.
This letter "A" is the essence of all speech; it is manifest through the consonants (sparśa) and sibilants (ūṣman), yet it is transcendent.
The Śruti has proclaimed that he becomes manifold and exceedingly vast;
and the Smṛti declares that among all syllables, this [syllable] "A" is Śiva. (83)
The unsurpassed tradition thus comes to rest in the supreme syllable;
this very letter *a*, which is the nature of the *praṇava*, is proclaimed by the wise. (84)
In the same way, the entire alphabet arises again within the letter *a*; it dissolves back into and abides therein. Therefore, the letter *a* is the cause of all things.
O lords of sages, because the substratum of the manifold world of name and form is the conscious self,
that Brahman is indicated by the syllable *A*.
For, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the designator and the designated are indeed one;
since Brahman is eternal, characterized by existence, and is pure consciousness alone. (87)
Therefore, the best of scholars [assert] the identity of word and meaning due to parsimony;
for this being so, words are not merely manifesters of meanings. (88)
A novel power is postulated because the Supreme Self is luminosity;
it is one and the same, yet appears divided among cows and other things due to the differences in its relations to existence.
For that very genus (jāti) is the meaning of the word; words are established within it.
Indeed, this single word called "A" is of the nature of consciousness (cidātman). (90)
It itself becomes manifold according to the distinctions of its designations,
just as gold [appears differently] when its limiting conditions, such as earrings and the like, have dissolved.
Likewise, O believers, the entire web of sounds consists of the letter 'A';
that alone is determined in the Vedāntas to be the single-syllabled Brahman. (92)
Those who have attained the form of that [reality] through hearing, reflection, meditation, or even direct perception— these alone are proclaimed as such.

The suffix *kvip* is desired in the sense of "acting like" (*ācaranti iva*). When the augment *t* is applied, followed by the elision of *t* and the addition of the nasal augment *num*, they declare this to be the resulting form. (94)
And those Siddhas, highly fortunate, possess bodies consisting of nothing but the ether;
he who takes them up—that is, favors them—is the one who possesses "lā" (the act of taking/favoring), and thus he is Allama. 95.
That by which one is measured is *mā*; she is praised as the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
She alone is *vidyā*, the supreme bliss, capable of uprooting *māyā*. (96)
He always delights in knowledge and should discard illusion like a dog [discards] a bone;
by this very etymology, he is remembered as a Vīramāheśvara. || 97 ||
Because He is the Lord who transcends the universe, He is called the Supreme Lord (Aḷlamaprabhu).
This eternal Aḷlama is attained through both yoga and spiritual realization. 98.
Furthermore, those such as Akkā, Lāmbā, Ambikā, and others are proclaimed to have "Mother" (Amba) as their referent;
she is Māyā, the consort of Rudra, who is celebrated as the source (Alā) of all. (99)
Having addressed that proud woman in the assembly with the words "tatrāllamāllamā," she is called "Allamāprabhu" by the best of the Pramathas.
O best of sages, the manifestation of the Lord of divine name has been declared; now listen with reverence to His etymology and His divine play. 101.

Then the Lord, the Guru who transcends the universe, was remembered by Rudradeva, along with those perfected in supreme knowledge, the omniscient ones, the renowned ones, and the preeminent among the Siddhas. (102)
Being served, he bore a triple mark of white ashes rising upon his forehead;
his excellent body was radiant with a mass of splendor shining forth from within.
His arms reach down to his knees, his head is well-formed, and he is filled with the essence of bliss;
he is radiant, with the lines on the palms and soles of his feet proclaiming his greatness.
He is the most beautiful of all, possessing the auspicious sovereignty of the unique Rājayoga;
he is the shatterer of the intoxication of the great illusion of Māyā’s clamor. || 105 ||
He is the Vāḍava fire for the ocean of darkness that is the cotton-wool of ignorance;
he is the fierce sun for the gloom of nescience, and the goad for the elephant of primordial matter (pradhāna) as it rises up. || 106 ||

He is the one who has utterly uprooted the indeterminate, the natural snatcher of life-breath, the stone upon the head of the unmanifest, and the forest fire for the wilderness of the three qualities. || 107 ||
The arrival of the Lord at Śiva’s assembly:
Thus praised by the foremost of yogis with their own titles such as these, he was lauded by sages who stood with palms joined in reverence upon their heads. (108)
He was saluted here and there by perfected beings, vidyādharas, gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, who held their hands in añjali with flowers.
Having ascended his palanquin and adorned with garlands made of mandāra flowers,
this Lord Allama Prabhu arrived by way of the sky.
Quickly awakening the souls sealed in their natural state with the nectar-like words of consciousness,
that Lord, illuminating the quarters like Bhadrabhadra, attained the presence of Rudra.
Having perceived that the Lord had arrived, Śaṅkara, together with his consort Bhavānī, descended from his own lion-throne;
honoring him personally with a stream of nectar-like words, he worshipped him along with his attendants.

"Here is the *arghya*, here is the water for washing the feet, and here is the *madhuparka*,"— hearing these words spoken by Śambhu, the ocean of compassion honored Śiva with a glance and approached him swiftly. Even the Destroyer of Madana (Śiva) worshipped him within his heart as his own supreme teacher, conceived as the Supreme Self.
Sitting upon half of his own seat, he himself respectfully sat down, his face filled with emotion.
Then Śaṅkara, disregarding his own beloved who was possessed by the magic power (śāmbarī) concealed by that [deity’s] greatness, [proceeded].
He spent half a *ghaṭikā* discussing that discourse on the fully perfected reality and the ultimate truth.
Then, when the desired conversation had been concluded by Śambhu, the Lord— whose body was beyond the range of others,
self-luminous, faultless, stainless, untainted, and non-dual— departed in an instant by his own will alone.
O best of sages, such indeed is the majesty of the great ones who are attached to the stainless state;
though they themselves are unclad and dwell in the courtyard of the sky, they take refuge in a city for the protection of the world.
Then, the Lord vanished along with those noble-souled, peerless, and excellent yogis.
Having perceived him, O Gaurī, exclaiming "Alas! Who is this?", she spoke to her husband with a smile, out of sheer apprehension in her heart.
O Hara, God of gods, O great ocean of supreme weapons, you alone are remembered as the one Lord, our Guru;
you are the Great One, the mass of perfect reality, bliss, and consciousness, subtler than the subtlest even among the great, and all-pervading. (119)
You have been realized by me as my Lord, whose form is composed of all principles and who is a mass of undivided consciousness-essence;
yet I cast down all others—whether they be gods or sages—beneath my left lotus-foot.
Having understood this most wonderful dialogue between Śrī Gaurī and Śaṅkara— this very person, who has been honored by sages, gods, and asuras,
has ascended the divine throne of the Lord and, disregarding me with his titles of honor, has praised [the Lord] fearlessly.

Why have you been honored by me through a path stained with selfish motives, and why have you been treated with respect by my sweet words? O Maheśa, tell me, do you partake in fear or devotion during that worship, so that I may restrain my pride?
"Where indeed does this matted-haired ascetic dwell, free from fear on all sides; where will he go again, and where does he abide?
What business do you have with him, and what is this service to him? O Lord, tell me how he is desired by you here. (123)

Thus questioned by his noble wife, Śiva, whose lotus-face was smiling and who filled the horizons with the luster of his teeth, spoke these wondrous words to his beloved: iti pṛṣṭa eṣa nijabhāryayāryayā smayamānavaktrasarasīruhaḥ śivaḥ | nijadantakāntiparipūrṇadiktaṭo dayitāmuvāca sa camatkriyaṃ vacaḥ || 124 ||

O girl, listen: in ancient times, a sage who was a knower of the past, free from ignorance, egoism, and fear, performed most wonderful penance for a very long time together with his own wife, named Saṃpadbodha.
While I, possessing steadfast devotion, was performing penance for a long time out of a longing for a son who is the very form of the Supreme Self,
O beloved, there arose for them a son named Allama, whose body was radiant and free from all limitations, and who is my own imperishable self.
O young girl, I do not know his greatness, for without a mirror I cannot perceive his face;
even I, though possessed of noble qualities, have myself fallen into forgetfulness, like one who has lost the jewel around his own neck. (127)
That Guru is beyond the reach of the entire world, his form being irreproachable in its mastery of the meaning of the Vedas and Agamas;
he is the Lord Allama who generated self-awakening within me—how much more so for those whose awakening is not yet equal to his own! 128.
While Śaṅkara was speaking thus, she, filled with great pride, spoke again to the Lord: "Alas! What is this you say, O sir?
While I am awake, how can there be a Lord of All in the three worlds, or the production of the word 'consciousness'? (129)

I do not know him; for this entire world is ever shrouded by my *māyā* which pervades everywhere. Yet, if there is grace from me toward even a person who possesses nothing, he indeed knows the pure certainty of his own self.
Or rather, by your grace, may everyone become a knower of the true nature of my own Lord.
O Lord, what is this deception before me today? Where is your affection, and where is the realization of the conscious Self?
"The immortal is considered mortal; the unknown is known"—alas, this statement of the Vedas is full of contradictions!
How can knowledge arise from that which is not known? What further excellence do you attribute to this [Veda] here? 132.

If indeed all those who know the supreme reality were to prevail in the worlds, alas, then the tufts of hair from the Vedas would surely fall everywhere upon surfaces made of heaps of dried cow-dung! 133.

Having heard these words of the daughter of the lord of mountains, Giriśa, his face lit with a gentle smile, illuminating the earth on all sides with the splendor of his divine form and fame, spoke this to her:
"O Satī, I speak the truth: since I am here now, enough of your harsh speech."
If you were to speak without having properly investigated the matter in my presence, this moon would not remain here. (135)
He does not fear us, for we speak falsely; he does not even converse with those who chatter in vain.
Because of his firm resolve and steadfastness, this one—neither self- nor other-regarding—is indeed not overcome by deceit. Alas! 136.

Just as on earth, people—whether middling, superior, or inferior—respect it [the lotus] according to their own hearts, so too is this [the poem] esteemed by those who know its measure; for in lakes, a lotus is perceived only in proportion to the water. (137)

Having experienced the state of fullness, with minds that have swallowed the entire splendor of the world and have attained the nature of the universal self, where is there any coming or going for those who have found refuge? 138.
This entire world shines within the heart of the Supreme Refuge like a city in a mirror;
yet he, having attained the state of ultimate reality, perceives this as a mere magical illusion and not as truth. (139)
He is the refuge of all worlds, the refuge for those seeking shelter, the protector, and the one who wards off danger.
He is my refuge as well, the ornament upon my crown; for without him as my refuge, I have no other refuge at all.
O Girijā, for one who knows the supreme truth, there is no talk of distinctions created by name and form regarding this All-pervading Lord.
This great, imperishable Lord, whose body is like the sky, consists of all the Vedas.
While Śaṅkara was speaking thus, Girijā— having realized the supreme majesty of her lord—
nevertheless spoke to her husband with humility and a smile, in order to examine his heart.
O Lord of the World, Your word is not false; nevertheless, my heart does not yet reach certain conviction.
If He, the Lord, has not been moved by my *māyā*, then I understand this to be the ultimate truth.
For one whose mind is defiled by longing for fickle young women and wealth is indeed a beast;
but he who is intensely filled with detachment toward all such things is truly, beyond doubt, the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati). 144.
The three qualities (guṇas) dwell within me for the purpose of agitating the mind of the yogi, yet they are not known by you.
If my heart were to fall under the sway of their play, I would indeed consider them as my guru. 145.
Having heard the words of the young woman, Giriśa, adorned with a crescent moon of gentle laughter, spoke again:
"O passionate lady, alas, you do not know the extraordinary greatness of this All-pervading Lord."

Having disregarded many bold words in this assembly, you who are devoid of understanding, what indeed do you say here? Even before the Supreme Self, the witness, how could your wicked arrogance not vanish before that all-pervading Lord? 147.
Abandon this ill-conceived resolve if your heart inclines toward the desire for victory;
otherwise, you will meet with humiliation, like a creeper struck by an elephant's trunk, lashed by the whip of disillusionment.

Having heard the words of Giriśa, the queen spoke repeatedly: "O Lord, O All-pervading One with the eye on your forehead, enough of this today; let me take an oath, and by that single part [of my vow], may I be victorious. (149)
Then, observing Śāṃbarī standing bowed before him with a body shimmering with her own darkness,

and beholding her full of grace— having surpassed the Apsarases with her peerless splendor— he took up these words: "O Lalitāṅgī, in the assembly of the gods, I spoke with haste and declared it under oath."
It is known by you that she, experiencing great [power], is renowned for churning the minds of sages.
In this matter of upholding my greatness, you alone are truly victorious as the most skillful;
for with the burden of my task entrusted to you, I rest at ease upon the lap of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva). 152.

O lady of unfailing gait, by means of the great wonder of your gestures, expressions, playful arts, sweet songs, and dances, you shall bring the Lord under your control, making him a target for the arrows of the Flower-Bowed One.
Thus addressed by Ambikā with a mind overflowing with the nectar-like essence of her soft and sweet words,
Śāṃbarī, acting with great audacity, immediately joined her palms at her forehead and spoke.
O Mother of the Universe, O Goddess, for me, your handmaiden, there is nothing on earth that cannot be accomplished;
by your grace, which brings about even the creation of the Supreme Soul, I shall bring about even the impossible. || 155 ||
Having constantly caused Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and the other gods— who find their sole refuge in the abode of Madana—
to experience the expansion of Māyā and the descent upon the world of mortals through her dark sorcery (śāṃbarī),
how much more easily does she rend the heart of me, whose resolve is most exalted? (156)
"Is this sequence of soft and affectionate words toward your attendant something new to you?
O Mother, by your very command I have achieved my highest purpose; therefore, please show me your favor. (157)

Whether on earth, in the oceans, in heaven, in the caves of Mount Meru, or in the subterranean pits of the netherworld—whichever beloved of the virtuous exists within their hearts, may I swiftly bring him under your control through your supreme grace. 158.

If, by the extraordinary power of the siddhis such as *aṇimā*, it should dissolve anywhere whatsoever, then, having experienced my own true nature, I shall instantly withdraw it and thereafter bring it under my control. (159)
Having understood these words spoken by Māyā, and having favored Girijā for her departure to the earth, she,
full of compassion, even gave her a strip of cloth made from the leaves of the nāga-creeper that clung to the clusters of betel-nut trees.
Thereafter, that very Māyā, who was Tamasī, bearing the command of the Daughter of the Mountain upon her own head and firm in her self-vow,
descended from the peak of the Silver Mountain to the surface of the earth by way of the path of the sky-dwellers.
Desirous of conquering. || 161 ||
Whoever causes others to hear or listens themselves to this "Prabhu-Śubhaguṇa-līlā," spoken by Nigamaśikha, which bestows all desired objects—
having enjoyed all worldly pleasures here in this life, they shall thereafter attain the state of Śiva.
One does not undergo birth and death. || 163 ||

Thus, in the *Ārṣa-Śrī-Bhaviṣyat-Purāṇa-Kathā-Viśālā*, within the *Prabhu-Liṅga-Līlā*, this is the section concerning the description of Kailāsa, the manifestation of the majesty of the assembly of Śrī Rudra, the dialogue between Gaurī and Śaṃkara, the etymological derivation of the word "Aḷlama," the arrival of the Lord, the expansion of Māyā, and the dark sorcery (*tāmasa-śāṃbarī*) upon the world of mortals.
The second chapter, titled "The Path Leading to the Demonstration of Non-Origination."
Description of Various Foreign Lands.
Homage to the illustrious Nandikeśvara.
[Now begins the third chapter.]
Sūta said:
Those whose mental impurities have been washed away by the bliss of meditating upon the lotus feet of the venerable Siddheśvara Vīradeśika Mahārāja, and who are endowed with truth and purity;

May those devotees who are intent on pure daily duties and who have taken refuge at the root of the tree of liberation always listen to the virtuous pastimes of the jewel-like Lord Śrī Allāla. || 1 ||

O believers, that Karṇāṭaka country now shines upon the southern slope of that very mountain where, it is said, Hara made his bow and recited the Śāntimanu mantra for the sake of peace among the gods and serpents. || 2 ||

Therein lies the region called Biva(?), renowned by its ancient name; it shines as the very boundary of the earth's crown, frequented by all its people who delight in truthful speech and follow the paths of dharma through devotion to the feet of Śivaguru. || 3 ||
In this land, the Dharma—far removed from the arrogant and established by the noble ones, the ignoble-free, and all the stainless kings—abides through its four pillars. (4)
In the center of that region shines the wondrous pleasure-palace of the digits of the moon;
that city, known by the name Vanavāsī, is like a portrait painted upon the face of the Earth.
O lords of sages, only the one born from the lotus is capable of describing all the specific excellences of that city;
this city is a secret created by the variegated power of Maheśa’s Māyā.
The dense forests there were filled on all sides with trees marked by sprouts that had just begun to bud.
[It was] adorned with buds and flower-buds, endowed with fruit, and constantly frequented by the spring season. || 7 ||

With *jaṃbīra*, *jaṃbū* fruits, *pūra*, and *pūga*; with *kharjūra*, *mālūra*, *kapittha*, and *cūta*; with *aśoka*, *raṃbhā*, and *panasa* as foods; and with *punnāga*, *cāṃpeya*, and *nārikela* [fruits]. || 8 ||

Furthermore, it resounds constantly with the clear calls of cuckoos, śārikās, parrots, bees, and peacocks, as well as the warbling of royal cranes; it is adorned with *pāṭala*, jasmine, *jāji*, *mallikā*, *kuruṇṭaka* flowers, and budding *ketakas*;
and with *syāmanti*, *karavīra*, *nandyāvarta*, land-lotuses (*sthalābja*), and mountain-jasmine (*girimallikā*).
With spring-blooming flowers such as the *kāñcanakesara* and others, which are dense with blossoms at all times; || 10 ||
That city, adorned with thousands of flower gardens filled with fragrant scents, shines brilliantly, always inhabited by devotees of the Enemy of Mahāmāyī who are intent upon great enjoyments.
Description of the City of Banavasī:
In every street, it was vast and beautiful, with balconies smeared with musk;
it shone eternally with thousands of jeweled archways and festoons of blossoming foliage.
Moreover, they were wandering over cool grounds moistened with fragrant water,
and they gathered flowering clusters thick with the scent of shimmering sandalwood.
Having struck it and partaking of the flavor found therein from all sides,
they arrived by way of the row of blooming lotus ponds and departed.
Approaching the young women very slowly with the manifestation of honeyed sweetness, he said:
Having seized them and having torn open their hearts, || 15 ||
Having shaken their upper garments and made themselves subject to another's will.
