And having avoided the quarrels arising from their mutual affection. || 16 ||
Having touched the seats of the arts and stirred longing with their beloveds,
the young breezes from the Malaya mountains acted like tender sprouts within that city.
Possessing the entire essence of Maheśa’s māyā, they move at every step.
O best of the twice-born, among the sciences such as the Vedas, Śāstras, and Āgamas, here—
Through wisdom, they become seekers of victory over the pervasive delusion born from the lotus of worldly existence.
Without having harmed their own people, they are striving to subdue others. || 19 ||
Having attained victory there, the local rulers shine forth;
what kind of lord is he who possesses nine treasures by number? (20)
In this way, litigants who possess countless riches become arrogant;
even under Vikramāditya, these Bhaṭṭas were sent forth and they assailed him.
Out of shame, they make Balabhadra, the wielder of the plow, appear white.
There, women bring even Madana under their control in an instant.
There, the elephants and horses of Śakra make those two appear pale with shame;
even the donors there beg from them, for the suppliants do not seek out the lowly.
Seeing a petitioner, donors do not remain silent or simply walk past him;
nor does a woman devoid of devotion to her husband go there alone to seek him out. 24.
In that city, there was not even a fool who was unskilled in protecting his wife; moreover, the height of its ramparts and the depth of its moat were such that— (25)
A description of the king who creates illusions:
Without him, none of the gods, nor the tortoises, nor the serpents know [the truth].
But no one at all was able to measure the height of that row of palaces.
O Brahmins, even in heaven there is no beauty of houses that can compare to these, which resound with the trumpeting of intoxicated elephants and the tinkling of jeweled bells. (27)

The successions of verbal embellishments from the throngs of bards and panegyrists, the sounds of the neighing of celestial musicians, and the tones arising from delightful musical instruments; || 28 ||
The clamor of the people pervaded the ten directions in that delightful city, where a king named Mamakāra reigned. || 29 ||
This sovereign of the mandala is arrogant with great pride;
his retinue is bold and haughty, and he is devoted to the power of desire.
Oh, how much can his good fortune be described? He possesses the beauty and form of Rati’s husband (Kāma) and the wealth of enjoyments of the king of the gods (Indra). || 31 ||
In sovereignty, he would be the King of Kings; in honor, he himself would be the Lord of the Kurus.
Who is capable of praising that lord of the earth, the King of Aṅga, in his renunciation? || 32 ||
He is indeed the very source of the manifestation of the playful illusions of Mahāmāyā.
He who has crushed his enemies with his sword and pierced the orb of the sun.
And [he approached] his own maternal uncle’s daughter, who possessed beautiful limbs and lotus-like eyes.
He also married Mohinī by name, who was enchanting to the three worlds.
Those two, the husband and wife, overflowing with passion and prepared for the battle of love,
sported for a long time, nourishing the aesthetic sentiment of erotic love (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
Like Śacī and Indra, like Lakṣmī and the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
and like Rohiṇī and the Moon, they two shone like Rati and Smara.
Those two, the letters 'ma' and 'ka', are the deluding ones, suited for the action of naming.
Having united as a couple, they were joined by the very tender noose of desire.
Endowed with one-pointedness of mind yet entwined by the creeping vine of possessiveness, they spent their days in the grip of passion while established in youth. (38)
Without having attained the recovery of their life-force, both were overcome by anxiety.
Then, having ceased their play in private, the two of them engaged in deliberation.
What is the use of sovereignty or pleasure, what use is eloquence in love or valor,
or what use are these auspicious and exquisite ornaments shining with various new jewels? What use are elephants, chariots, tall horses, or the delights of palanquins?
Even with delicious foods and incomparable garments, he remains devoid of progeny. (40)
A description of the worship and other rites concerning the son of Mohinī and Mayaka:
"The wise who know the scriptures say that there is no destination for one who is childless;
even the Veda clearly declares that there is indeed no world for one without a son. (41)
Having reflected thus, he repeatedly questioned the astrologers,
and likewise listened to the words of the omens from those who were experts in them.

On the days of the sun and other planets, over the respective planetary deities of those castes as prescribed, the two heard the *upaśruti* mantras while scattering unbroken rice and other offerings. (43)
Placing their hands upon the hands of the palmists for the sake of obtaining a son, they both made this inquiry: "Tell us, is there a line or not? (44)
Standing before the female fortune-teller, [he offers] pearls, unbroken rice, and so forth.
Having given it and then taking the handle of that winnowing basket, he asked them about their welfare.
O twice-born ones, these two should observe all the vows in the manner prescribed by the Noble One, through the offering of gifts and other such means. (46)
Having spent much wealth with the desire for a son,
that couple, enveloped by great delusion, performed a sacrifice to Mohinī.
With substances such as oil-cakes and garlic, and with the dancing performed by Mātaṅgīs,
they worshipped the minor deities with liquor, meat, and other offerings.
Those two deluded souls indeed did not worship Śiva and the consort of Śiva, the lords of the world, who are filled with the essence of pure *sattva*. (49)
As the days passed in this manner, after some time, Mohinī herself conceived a child through the service of certain base, tamasic powers.
That Tāmasī Mahāmāyā was commissioned by the wife of Śiva—
the omniscient consort of the Lord— in order to reveal the true nature of the Lord.
Having immediately entered that womb, she, whose perception was free from delusion, experienced it instantly.
He brought about the fulfillment of the joy of those two, who were so well-suited to one another.
Having extracted the very essence of the beauty of illusion,
she who deludes people was born as the daughter of Mohinī, the destroyer of discernment.
Then, in that city, a succession of heart-stealing sounds from various musical instruments resounded,
as deep as auspicious rain clouds.
He, gathering together, gave with longing to all the twice-born who had extended the tips of their hands and were offering abundant sacrificial fees.
The description of mental transformations and the like of the Lord of Sages and others through the arising of illusion;
and [the description of] intentions, fields, wealth, horses, elephants, cattle, chariots, and herds of cows.
Whatever anyone desired, he gave that very thing to each of them.
To those who remain in their homes, having become coupled together through a desire for sense objects.
The Lord of the Deluder bestowed [these] upon the multitudes of those seeking desired objects and those facing misfortune.
In that wondrous great festival of the arising of Māyā for all living beings,
the seed of men and women flowed forth instantly, moment by moment.
A shameless woman [desires] a man, and a flat-bellied woman [desires] a man.
Having embraced him and tasted his lip, she touched the secret place.
But those who stand on the path to nirvāṇa, having abandoned villages, fields, houses, and the like, reach formidable forests and become ascetics who abstain from food. || 60 ||
On the banks of rivers such as the Gaṅgā, in the caves of mountains, in special places of the Siddhas, and likewise in groves of Bilva trees; || 61 ||
In the midst of the five fires, in the snow, and in the middle of water,
they likewise warded off the affliction of hunger day after day with fruits, water, and leaves.
With their mental fluctuations ceased and meditating within themselves upon the Supreme Lord,
they constantly perform austerity with an unwavering resolve that must not be abandoned.

The minds of those who were solely intent upon Śiva, having arisen and attained a similarity of state with mental modifications (*vṛtti-sārūpya*), became oriented toward external objects as they appeared. (64)
Even among the elderly ascetics, whose heads were trembling,
who were devoid of passion, and even those who were grey-haired, mutual delight shone forth.
Of trees, mountains, creepers, grass, and stones.
Then, through mutual affection between the males and females, a state of melting occurred.
Even having abandoned their consumption of grass, the multitudes of deer, birds,
and beasts constantly took delight in coupling together, both by day and by night.
For those whose bodies have become like wooden pillars through long-term meditative absorption, even after the passing of an eon, they remain thus, hidden within anthills.
Even the minds of the sages, who were like fire and whose semen had fallen below during meditation upon women, became filled with longing.
Emerging from that state, all the sages were astonished, wondering, "What is this?
Overcome with anxiety, they meditated for a long time and then once again turned their attention outward.
Alas, what misery! Oh, what great misery! What is this condition of ours?
By which we cast aside the knowledge of the Self and attain an orientation toward sense objects. || 71 ||
Thus, overcome by anxiety, all the sages gathered together;

and is both possessed of and devoid of qualities— having manifested within the hollow of the lotus-hearts of the divine couple, [remains] as the object of their contemplation.
As pure as crystal, he attained complete perfection.

Then, at the forefront of those two, the stainless splendors merged together externally; alas! that radiant being, whose form was quivering with life, appeared as if separate, and brought to their minds the thought, "It is our son," as they emerged from the end of their sleep.
Seeing that most wonderful splendor, Sujñānāmbā and Nirahaṃkāra attained the state of being sons; thus, they were immersed in the ocean of the nectar of supreme bliss.
By good fortune, the gods rained down a shower of blossoms born from the wish-fulfilling trees;
the celestial drums resounded, and the Gandharva maidens and Apsarases danced. (71)
The attendants, out of their great joy, recited prose compositions that were pleasing to the hearts of the perfected ones (siddhas);
and Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, and the others rejoiced through the direct experience of their own selves.
When the Lord had then descended upon the entire earth for the welfare of the world,
the groves of *sthāṇu* trees became leafy, barren cows gave milk, and cows that had never calved brought forth calves.
Opening his eyes, the sage named Nirahaṃkriya beheld Guheśa appearing as his son;
looking again within himself and observing them both, he realized their identity.
Then, perceiving within his own mind that [the Supreme] dwells entirely within his daughter and has become his very own life-breath;
Beholding her greatly astonished, he, with a concentrated mind, remained for a long time absorbed in his own bliss. || 75 ||
Is this the sun who, having abandoned his nature of fierce heat, has come to the palace as a friend to the lotuses?
Is it the moon, whose essence is nectar, having cast off its frost? Or is it fire, filled with bliss, that is without burning? (76)
Thus the sage, having reflected upon his own inner state, became certain that Śiva-nature resided within himself;
and that devoted wife, perceiving her son to be Śiva, became one whose breasts were flowing with milk.
Then, as his mother— her limbs bristling with joy, longing and approaching to embrace her son and tuck him under her arm— was looking on,
the child was seen moving most gracefully, as if clinging to the hands, feet, face, and every limb and member of his mother's body.
Possessing the splendor of ten million suns. || 78 ||
Thereafter, extending his pair of soft lotus-like hands with a joyful heart,
he began to describe the superhuman qualities of the child Līlābāla to his wife, who was free from egoism, so that she might take him from nearby.
Like the sky, he was not capable of being touched by anyone at all; how much less, then, could he be attained or firmly embraced?
"What is this? asked Sujñānā, questioning her husband; he, who had realized the truth, replied to her with a smiling face:
"Know that what shines before us like the Supreme Self’s light is not merely a son, but like a son."
Abiding within all. || 80 ||
O beloved, it is impossible to describe him as having form or as being formless;
he is self-luminous, partless yet possessed of all arts, beginningless, the primordial source, the ancient Puruṣa. || 8 ||

The Supreme Self is not perceived as "unborn," nor as "born," nor as being endowed with reasons and examples; He is neither devoid of qualities nor possessed of qualities, neither a child nor a non-child.
Neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor wind, nor sky is able to touch this ultimate reality;
nor can it be delimited by time, space, and the like, for it is the Self of the Self, the Lord.
Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, He who is himself both the cause and the effect;
likewise, though called the cause of causes, He cannot be understood by the intellect, yet He is not unknown. 84.
Although all his senses remain intact, the qualities of the sense-objects do not belong to him;
he is not brought under control by illusion, but having mastered illusion, he conquers it, remaining unattached.
He who knows all the vital points (marmas) is indeed the knower of those vital points, and no one else whatsoever.
The very essence of beauty, He is to be beheld by one’s own eyes; being like the sky, He cannot be touched.
He cannot be known by the various and complete Vedas nor by the scriptures, for He is not unknown to them.
O virtuous lady, He is unattainable even to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other gods; yet, precisely because He is unattainable, He is attained.

Among these lords of sages, who have conquered their senses and are constantly practicing austerities with discipline, the Lord of the Cave (Guheśa), though omnipresent, is perceived as if His mind were fixed within them, yet He Himself is not fixed. 88.
Those sons who suckle at the breast, who are bold and excrete dung, remain attached to the junction of the two openings of the womb.
There are hundreds in the world of animals bound by the six waves; may they bring happiness to you.
This son of ours is extraordinary, for he belongs neither to the past nor to the future of anyone else;
yet the Lord of Guha, our guru, becomes manifest before our very eyes for the sake of our fulfillment.
Thus the Lord explained the nature of his beloved, the Self-born;

then, having praised the Lord through an investigation of His names by means of the crest-jewels of the Vedas and Agamas, the two of them bowed down out of the power of the aesthetic sentiment of devotion. 91.
Then, having immersed themselves and emerged from the ocean of their own innate bliss, the virtuous couple,
with the permission of Kumāra Jiṣṇu, announced the festival for the birth of their son throughout the city.

Then, having bestowed upon all the beggars who had arrived a multitude of desired objects according to their wishes, his mother and father deliberated thus in their minds regarding the naming of their son: || 93 ||

Neither name nor physical form, nor even bodily action, belongs to this Lord; what name could there be for Him, the crown of the crowns of the Vedas, that would be suitable for worldly usage in the three worlds and yet be established by the Veda? (94)
When investigated, his state of being a transmigrating being does not exist, nor is he established by the term "non-transmigrator";
for he is eternally the refuge for those seeking refuge, being ever characterized by compassion toward those who seek shelter.
Nor is he a mortal, even though he is honored upon the earth, because he is not bound by the fetters of caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama).
Indeed, all phenomena must be set aside through hearing within this absolute, supreme Brahman alone. 96.
Therefore, enough with the purpose of negating words; and because of its connection with the word *alam*, let it be *alamā*.
May this name, *Alamāprabhūti*, which incessantly obstructs the ignorance of people, prevail forever.
Or rather, may this illustrious one, renowned in the assembly as Allama, be the grace bestowed upon those who possess the nature of the letter ‘A’,
the Great Lord Guheśvara who assumes the form of the venerable Guru through his union with Śrī. 98.

If one should recite with devotion these syllables of the name "Allama," which are unfailing by force, he shall shatter the mountain of this harsh saṃsāra and, rolling in the treasure-trove of his own bliss, become happy. (99)
Having reflected thus, the two gurus bestowed upon the Teacher of the Three Worlds the auspicious name "Allama.
Then the Lord Allama Maheśvara engaged in such play as a child.
Where does she dance, where does she sing, and where does she run about under the influence of her playful charms?
Where does she gaze intensely with eyes closed, and where does she perceive the entire universe as her own?
Where is he who is beheld by the foremost of the wise and honored with hymns out of exceeding reverence;
where is he who is experienced by those skilled in the arts, and where is he who is cherished by the ancestors and their leaders? 102.

Where else could he have gone, following after the wise, having studied for a moment the auspicious scriptures of the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Āgamas, along with the fine arts, and then himself reciting them with the appropriate accents while teaching multitudes of other young students? (103)
Having studied the entire collection of his master’s new and ancient compositions and having understood their meaning,
he followed the groups of scholars who had come to the city and attended upon them. (104)

Having deliberated whether there exists anything superior to this scripture in the world, or perhaps nothing at all, the Lord declared, "There is nothing else," while saying, "It is small. Thus, the father’s wonder was pacified.
Saying "Ahaha! The sight has been seen," the mother mimicked him as he swayed within the house;
she placed a mark of ink on his forehead and thrice smeared his limbs with sacred ash.
Then the All-pervading Lord Himself, following after the children and possessing incomparable play like a child,
demonstrated the meaning of the Vedas by His own self and at times attained a state that was beyond the reach of the senses.
Then, entering the city of the Lord of Serpents, that Lord momentarily seized the jewels from the tips of the serpent's hoods;
returning once more to play with his own children, he shone forth with those gems as if they were the very light of the sun.
Thereafter, entering the city of Indra, he instantly gathered flowers and other offerings from the forest near its outskirts.
Having experienced [these states] and bathed in the river of the winds (the subtle body), he returned once more through the powers of *aṇimā* and the other *guṇas*.
And where did this Lord dance, having taken up the pair of the sun and the moon as cymbals, with his neck graced by a shimmering pearl necklace set with round stars held upon his radiant chest? (110)

And where did he, possessed of such wondrous majesty, sport by tossing Mount Sumeru about with his two hands like a pot of butter, and engaging in the play of a ball with the great boundary mountains? (111)
And where, having taken up his two brilliantly radiant discs like flowers and uniting them, the Lord encircled the lord of serpents and engaged in the sport of a potter within its interior? (112)

"This is surely a mere child"—with such words, the Lord, whose play is a wonder to the three worlds, was addressed as the "Master," the "Cause of all causes," and the "Sovereign" by the multitude of people from every land who followed him. (113)

Meditate upon this light as the primordial one who bears the moon within his heart-lotus, whose long-fortuned root is the Veda, who resides in the hearts of the assembly of seers, who is the perfect whole, inseparable from the supreme consciousness, and who is the essence of the nada, bindu, and kala.
Having heard these words, so noble and sweet in meaning as uttered by the wise one, the parents were filled with joy.
Attaining a sense of fulfillment, they praised him within the lotus of their hearts, regarding him as their own good fortune.
[This concludes] the description of the praise offered by Sujñānāmā, who was free from egoism.

Victory, victory, victory to you, O Jigme Lingpa! You are the boat for crossing the ocean of existence; victory, victory, victory to you, O Jigme Lingpa! Always grant us the fulfillment of our purpose.
Victory, victory, victory to you, O Jigme Lingpa, whose fame is praised by the world! Victory, victory, victory to you, O Jigme Lingpa, the very embodiment of the nature of consciousness!
Victory, victory, victory to you, O Allama, the Supreme Lord, the Eternal Self! Victory, victory, victory to you, O Allama, higher than the highest, the Conscious Self!
Victory, victory, victory to you, O Allama, ocean of the nectar of supreme immortality! Victory, victory, victory to you, O Allama, who has attained the auspicious state of oneness! 117
Victory, victory, victory to you, O Allama, ocean for the jewel of true devotees! Victory, victory, victory to you, O Allama, kinsman of those who have renounced the world!
Victory, victory, victory to you, O Allama, moon in the firmament of consciousness! Victory, victory, victory to you, O Allama, who delights in the lotus of the heart!
O my father, O my son, O my heap of gold, O my heart, O my compassion, O my most excellent Guru!

O giver of my boons, O destroyer of my elephant-like pride, O you whose crown is my prostration; O source of my prosperity, O origin of my power, O ornament of my lord; O you who possess compassion for me, O creator of my senses, O sun to my lotus-heart; O abode of my face, O known by me, O son;
O mirror of my mind, O crest-jewel of my head, O enemy of the god of love within my heart; O you who take delight in me, O cleansing agent of my soul, O wise one spoken of by me. 119–120.
O Lord of men, O Master who is my guru, O bestower of my desires!
O you whose form is my *liṅga*, O glory of mine, O most excellent Lord, be gracious unto us! 121.
Having thus praised both their mother and father repeatedly,
and having bowed with a spirit of true devotion, they both entreated their son.
O ocean of compassion, having dispelled all the darkness of ignorance and shown us the path of true knowledge, protect us, O you who possess auspicious marks! 123.
Thus entreated with devotion by his parents, the Father of the World, the Lord who is dear to them, spoke these words out of compassion. (124)
O mother and father, having ascertained this secret of the true meaning through both scripture and reasoning, let it be heard with careful attention in your hearts. 125.
Fixing his steady gaze upon the chosen liṅga and remaining free from desire for anything else,
one of firm vows should cast off the delusion of this wicked saṃsāra.

The instruction of the parents regarding the worship of the threefold liṅga: One should diligently stabilize one’s firm devotion toward the prāṇaliṅga, constantly floating within the blissful sleep of prāṇāyāma. (127)
In the linga of existence, through complete satisfaction in the non-duality of Śiva, one becomes Unmanā;
this alone is the supreme limit in the realization of the ultimate reality.
Having thus lovingly taught this essence, the *Unmanīkīlaka*, to his parents, Mallameśa—
the teacher of all teachers— plunged into the ocean of the nectar of the awakening of supreme knowledge and proceeded on his way.
Thus Śaṅkara, having compassionately instructed the lotus-faced daughter of the mountain, gratified that blessed lady.
O auspicious one, understand in your mind all this that has been told by me here; it is a task not difficult for us to accomplish.
Having clearly heard these words of Vimalā, Māyā was tormented by the futility of her own efforts;
yet, enveloped by the illusion of Śambhu, she remained bound by the noose of hope to subdue this excellent sage once again.
It came to pass. || 131 ||
Those who, with firm devotion, even once read or recite this unfailing life-story of the Lord which I have narrated to you,
shall become the abode of all happiness in this world and, finally, attain the state of the Pramathas.
They indeed attain the perfected state. || 132 ||

[Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Account of the Manifestation of the Lord's Play," within the *Prabhu-liṅga-līlā*— the extensive narrative of the venerable *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa* composed in accordance with the words of the hosts of *Pramathas*, whose nature is to uplift people submerged in the impurities of the Kali age.]
The Beneficial Instruction on Illusion spoken by Vimala.
Homage to the illustrious Nandikeśvara.
[The Seventh Chapter]
Sūta said:
O best of sages, having attained the fulfillment of all goals through devotion to the priceless lotus feet of Siddhavīreśvara, listen now to the excellent narrative of the Lord.
Then Māyā, having understood through pure words the divine majesty of the Lord, spoke to Vimalā, who brings about the destruction of the three impurities.
O Vimalā, the Supreme Lord Śiva himself has been presented by you;
being worshipped, what desired object would he not grant us? (3)
Vimalā said to that Māyā: "Listen, O beauty of the three worlds, to the [exploits] of that high-souled Lord who desires to conquer through his power of illusion. (4)
For those who serve by following the will of the mind, what indeed is difficult to attain? Pure devotion to the Lord of Gods bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Just as the status of a village headman is inferior for one consecrated to a great kingdom,
so too, for one devoted to the lotus feet of the Lord, what is this worldly life?
Having heard that, Māyā said to her: "O Prabhā, tell me a means for making the Lord manifest; O friend Vimale, make me successful. (7)
Vimalā said to the slender-limbed woman: "By worshipping Śiva with devotion, one shall obtain through that merit such an assembly of noble-souled beings."
Therefore, you too should always worship with devotion the omniscient one, who has a blue throat and three eyes; by that, the Lord will be pleased.
O Vimalā, Madhukeśa spoke to Māyā: "Having worshipped him day and night, I did not obtain even the slightest fruit from that. (10)
To Māyā, who was saying, "From now on this story must not be told," Vimalā said: "Let there be no such stubborn persistence on your part."
"O evil-minded one, abandon that logic by which you yourself, having fallen through negligence, censured the earth; you now vainly censure Śaṅkara."
For those whose intellects are purified and who worship Śambhu as their own devotee,
the priceless Madhuśiva places his own gold in the palm of their hand.
In his courtyard was a treasure consisting of gold bound in covered cloth;
he was renowned as the wish-fulfilling cow, the wish-granting tree, and the thought-gem.
Having propitiated that Great God, what mortal indeed does not obtain a succession of their own desired objects? What wonder is there to be marveled at in this? (15)
Regarding Māyā, this is the exposition of the procedure for the worship of Lord Vimalokteśvara:
for those who perform the practice after having understood it, Śaṅkara grants fruit immediately;
however, an action performed without such knowledge certainly becomes fruitless. (16)
Therefore, O lotus-eyed one, I shall declare to you the secret of the scriptures, by hearing which and subsequently practicing it, one obtains the fruit from both sides. (17)
In the beginning, one should take refuge in a lordly guru endowed with excellent qualities;
for only the knowledge imparted by the guru will immediately bear the fruit of ultimate welfare. (18)
Devotion abandons one who has not served a guru and for whom the ritual of worship has not been instructed by him, just as a female elephant leaves the lion. 19.
Purifying the vessels and ritual substances according to the procedure taught in the scriptures,
and having understood the limbs, hands, face, and so forth, one should worship Śiva.
Through ignorance or negligence regarding the instructions of the scriptures and the teacher,
the deluded person attains fruitlessness in the worship of Tamas.
Just as one might place sound upon the tongue, or taste upon the ear, or form upon the nose, or touch upon the eye, or scent upon the skin; 22.
If one of deluded mind performs a semblance of worship through a lack of discernment, that act becomes fruitless for him; Śaṅkara does not become pleased with it. (23)
Therefore, having understood the faces of Mṛḍa, the Supreme Self, the wise man offers [the sacrifice] through discernment; such is the determination of the meaning of the scripture. (24)
If a man, having suddenly and forcibly cast leaves and other offerings before the Liṅga by means of common people, then offers low-quality cooked food; || 25 ||
If one devoid of faith performs the worship of the Lord, that Rājaśekhara does not accept his worship with affection. (26)

He who is averse to the practice of giving and virtue, who reviles wisdom and consciousness, and who, moreover, having abandoned the scriptural injunctions spoken by the venerable Guru, acts according to his own whims; (27)
If one performs a Tāmasī worship, Śaṅkara does not smell it.
Therefore, [one should study] the Śiva-jñāna-śāstras, Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Saṃhitās. || 28 ||

One should take refuge in that true guru who, having taught the meanings of those [scriptures], awakens one's understanding—a guru whose heart is moist with compassion, who knows the inner state of others, and who is wise. (29)
Having stabilized his devotion by His command, accompanied by a living image (jaṅgama),
and with his mind restrained, he should worship the Lord of All according to the prescribed rites.
The high-minded one who worships all the lords with a one-pointed mind attains liberation if he is free from desire, and enjoyment if he possesses desire. || 31 ||
The instruction for the worship of Śiva spoken by Vimalamāyā is as follows:
"That which grants enjoyment does not grant liberation, and that which grants liberation does not grant enjoyment;
however, this sattvic worship of Śiva bestows both enjoyment and liberation. (32)
Having worshipped Śaṅkara, all the gods, beginning with Hari and Brahmā,
attained their respective lordships over those worlds along with all splendors.
Just as a body with hands, feet, and other limbs, though complete in its characteristics, is devoid of life when lacking the compassion of the venerable Guru, so too is a base person.
Having ploughed four furrows with the plough and cleared away the weeds,
he leveled the ground with the harrow even as the rain-cloud was pouring down half its waters.
Even when the earth is moist and still damp, he who, resorting to indolence, does not sow the seed—how can his fertile field ever bear fruit? (36)
Having understood this and having duly performed the service for the Guru,
one whose heart is purified by initiation should worship the Supreme Lord.
If one should worship Śaṅkara, having abandoned all qualities of the elements, how could that great-souled person not attain the fulfillment of his desired aims? (38)
Just as a blind man does not see his own reflection even when a mirror is held in his hand, so too a worshipper who lacks instruction does not attain perfection. (39)
O Māyā, if Śambhu was worshipped by you according to the proper ritual, why would there not be the fruit of that worship? Or is it that the procedure for instruction was lacking? (40)
Was the mantra not properly received, or was the procedure for recitation not performed? Was it not understood according to the scriptures, or was devotion insufficient? (41)
Or perhaps you lack faith in this traditional mode of worship;
if the complete collection of requisites were present, how could your desire not be fulfilled? (42)
When Vimalā had thus spoken with sound reasoning, Madotkaṭā, out of pride in her illusory power and majesty, treated her with contempt and said this: || 43 ||
"O beautiful lady, let there be no such effort as providing instruction and the like;
the entire world should be accomplished by your own will alone, and not otherwise. (44)
Having heard these words, the virtuous Vimalā then abandoned such talk and became immersed in illusion within the ocean of miserable existence.
"By what sequence of means shall I deliver her from this peril?
Having thus reflected in his mind and deliberated upon a single expedient, [he proceeded]. (46)

Recalling that command of the Mother of the World, which is difficult to transgress, he addressed Māyā with words of affection, turning her toward him after remembering the secret dialogue between Māyā and Vimalā. 47.
This friendship between us two has been established from time immemorial; it is certainly not new.
You surely know this, yet I ask you one question, O fair-faced one.
"I ought not to be deceived; if you wish to deceive me, then listen! An order has been given to you by me, O Gaurī; do not feel ashamed. (49)
"Speak the truth as it is, O auspicious lady, for truth is indeed the highest vow.
Having thus encouraged her, Vimalā questioned her in private. (50)
O vain woman, this most excellent body of yours, like a delicate creeper, appears as if pierced by the arrows of the Mind-born God in its vital joints. (51)
"How may I show it to you, O auspicious lady? In what has your delight arisen?
Tell me that; I shall tell you the remedy for it," he said, and she replied: || 52 ||
O Vimalā, I shall tell you of a certain man who is like another Desire incarnate; he possesses praiseworthy qualities and is most excellent in his learning. (53)
Renowned by the name Allama, he possessed a profound and noble form;
he was skilled in all branches of knowledge and preeminent in the qualities of a wise and magnanimous hero.
Trapped within that cage of illusion, she fell under the sway of King Rati;
having abandoned her self-respect, her mind became wicked, overcome by anxiety, and her intellect was wavering. (55)
Deprived of her senses and lacking fortitude, with all her memory lost,
she lay like a tuft of cotton within the inner chamber of the house, resting upon a couch.
Covered along with my friends, yet pierced by the volleys of Māra’s arrows,
I have fallen into this wretched state and become diminished.
Then that Vimalā said to Māyā, "O moon-faced one, listen;
he who has captivated your heart is truly Allama himself."
The Lord, who is superior to the universe and its witness, has brought Māyā under his control;
there is no one else more worthy of honor than He, who is eternally liberated and stainless.
Do not consider him merely a drummer; his preeminence in knowledge is established by his very nature.
Indeed, the Śruti also declares this Lord of Guha to be Maheśāna, the sovereign of all branches of learning.
This very Lord is the director of the drama of illusion,
the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of these worlds;
who He is, from whence, where, when, and by what means He is— He is impossible for even the Vedas to fully know.
He whose forward-facing [consciousness] does not perceive the cultivation of form and formlessness—by what means or in what manner existing is he not defiled? (62)
Having heard that, Māyā said: "O Vimalā, what are you saying?
There is a meeting of Allama, Māyā, and Vimalā at the abode of Madhukeśa.
Do you know anything? Enough with these words of yours alone! (63)
He alone is declared to be the Supreme Self, the Lord known by the name Allama;
this Allama of mine is like a drummer to these actors and rogues. (64)
And do not compare him to that [other person], however slight the distance between them may be—
just as one would not compare the sun to charcoal, or the great ocean to a mere pool.
In this manner, there occurred a series of dialogues between Māyā and Vimalā;
and by virtue of that very association, [the Lord] went to the abode of Madhukeśa.
Having worshipped Maheśāna there and gone outside, that beautiful woman entered the middle of the arena with kingly grace.
The king also, seeing her intent on dancing with a pure smile,
was greeted with astonishment by the Vidyādharas present there who were superior in knowledge.
Thinking, "Today itself I shall conquer this Māyā through the science of instrumental music," he skillfully played the mṛdaṅga drum while she was dancing.
Seeing Māyā dancing with her mind fixed upon him, overwhelmed by passion, Vimalā then reflected in her heart: || 70 ||
Here there is dancing and there longing; here my-ness and there speech;
here the *rītis* and there respect; here vision and there delight. (71)
Oh, what a truly great marvel! Māyā makes all beings dance; yet this very Allama, appearing like a mere sprout, makes that Māyā itself dance.
Just as a red crystal appears so due to the proximity of a hibiscus flower, even so the Lord, though endowed with qualities, is perceived as such due to the proximity of Māyā. (73)
Just as a crystal appears pure when the flowers [placed near it] have been removed, so too,
having cast off illusion (māyā), that one devoid of qualities (aguṇa) is eternally stainless.
Having thus reflected and again scrutinized Māyā, Vimalā, after showing him Ālma with her gaze, revealed her own self.
Bringing about the union of the two while indicating her own separate standing from him, she signaled her act of salutation to him with her very glance. (76)
O believers, having successively honored the earth and the sky, that beautiful woman then spoke to her regarding her own duty by means of a sign alone.
When he stands silent there, having set his drum upon the ground, let him then be seized by us both under the pretext of clasping his feet. (78)
If, by describing my skill in dancing before the Lord,
it is understood that "this is not the Lord," and if this Lord should then be grasped as being empty like the sky, [then what is gained]? (79)
Thus instructed by Vimalā with a glance from her eyes, Māyā herself signaled to her in return, saying, "So be it. (80)
"Aha! Indeed, women first moisten men with their very glance;
yet, they bend them once more with the sweetness of that same look. (81)
By their very glance they bring delight, and in an instant they seize that wealth;
by their very glance they provide fuel for the fires of separation.
Ah! Women are indeed snares for men with fickle minds;
the very arrow of their glance is the instrument for the defeat of men. (83)
"The eyes are the primary wealth of women, and indeed their very support!
Thus the connoisseurs there spoke among themselves upon seeing her gestures. (84)
O brahmins, as Māyānartī’s mind was fixed upon her lord, all her limbs became emaciated as she was scorched by the fire of separation.
She lost her concentration, her mind wavered—oh wonder! Abandoning the rhythmic measure of the *tāla*, she danced with uneven steps.
In her dancing, the rhythmic clashing of her feet surpassed all else;
the song, touched by discordant notes, fell into unevenness. (87)
Then Allama, having understood all her actions, thought:
"This dancing of mine is in vain; what is the use of this? (88)
Leaving behind the great and wonderful mṛdaṅga drum in the midst of the arena,
the Lord quickly departed from the city and went wherever He pleased.
Then Māyā, as if having reached the tenth stage [of pregnancy], became deeply distressed;
with her heart's fortitude destroyed, she fell upon the ground in a swoon.
Then, somehow having recognized him, she lamented repeatedly within herself: "Alas, alas! O Lalla, having abandoned me here, where have you gone? (91)
She did not tie her loosening hair nor did she close her bodice;
her friends of even brows prepared the upper garment and other attire for her.
Then, O twice-born ones, Vimalā approached Māyā and consoled her:
"O girl, why do you distress yourself in vain? What is this persistence of yours now? (93)

"By the same path through which the Lord of All has gone, let us quickly follow our Master outside the city of Māyā, accompanied by Vimalā and all the other female friends, as well as by the two of us. 94.
Just as a thread follows a needle and thus glides along, so too,
O lady, shall we follow that path and proceed in like manner.
"O auspicious lady, having searched heaven and earth, we shall surely find that Allama wherever he may be; once we have seized him there, we will bring him under our control."
"I shall go, free from fear, until we behold the Lord;
meanwhile, O Māyā, take hold of Manojava and rise up at once! (97)

"Abandon your anxiety and quickly take heart," she was thus addressed by the noble lady; "So be it," she replied, and though she was intensely tormented by the longing for her illusory lover, she accepted the advice.
Then the beautiful woman, together with Vimalā and her other friends,
began to depart, concealing the hearts of the citizens.
"Alas! The daughter of the lord of men has gone following the mardala player"—such was the rumor that arose among the people. (100)
Thus conversing with one another, they were unable to restrain themselves; standing there as motionless as wooden posts, they all remained still, and as soon as she heard them, that Māyā departed.
"O faithful ones, thinking at every step, 'When shall I see Allama?', Māyā abandoned her slow pace and ran swiftly. (102)
As she ran with swift speed, her feet were covered in severe sores;
her body, parched by the heat of the sun, quickly became as radiant as a withered creeper.
In some places, the illusion took the form of a path leading astray, entwined with coils of creepers;
there, her toes were cut by stones and bled profusely.
O twice-born ones, on the ground scorched by the heat of the sun, the dust burned like glowing coals; her throat-pipe, parched by thirst, became motionless and withered.
As this Mohinī, the soul of all beings, proceeded with such agitation, some sages staying in that hermitage trembled upon seeing her. (106)
O twice-born ones, having beheld that moon-faced woman who was the very essence and entirety of beauty, those of firm vows fled like deer upon seeing a hunter approaching. (107)
"Kāma is indeed devouring us; what is our fate here?"—thus reflecting with anxious hearts, they fled in the ten directions.
In the forest, he was subjected to the reproach of the *lamas* who had been made his illusory companions;
likewise, he [offered] yoga-staves, yoga-bands, linga-cases, saffron robes, tiger skins, ashes, and fruits. (109)
With their hands clutching clusters of rudrākṣa rosaries, books, and water-pots,
they held their lips tightly together in fear.
Seeing them fleeing, the Lord, the Sovereign of All, the Supreme,
his heart moved by compassion, then resolved to protect the sages from the women.
Having steadied their minds, the Guru, assuming the guise of a sage,
appeared before them in person and rendered all of them one-pointed in mind.

Once again, having become a deceptive actor and assuming the guise of a libertine, the Lord of Yogis returned to the presence of the woman with his illusory power (māyā) in order to deceive her as before. (113)
Seeing him, all those women, like wretched creatures who had found a treasure, were delighted in their hearts and spoke out of affection and the onset of anger: || 114 ||
"O Lord, alas! What fruit have you obtained by tormenting our dear friend Māyā, who is under your protection, for the sake of a rogue? (115)
By causing this young princess, whose skin is as soft as a jasmine flower,
to suffer in Hasantikā, you have destroyed her very essence.
O rogue! How can she, who is worthy of sleep upon a bed of swan-down feathers, deserve to travel on foot like a grain of sugar that resembles a thorn? 117.
"How can my friend, who is to be served by her companions on a lion-throne, deserve to sit upon a mat of kuśa grass in the forest, O fair-faced one? (118)
How could she, who used to travel seated upon a golden couch while being fanned by her companions with fans, wander through the forest?
How can the daughter of a universal monarch, who sports with ease in a palace made of the nine precious gems, be worthy of staying in the bowers of forest thickets? (120)
O Lord, we alone are at fault here;
it is not your fault, since we gave you our hearts without knowing your inner mind. 121.
An action performed without deliberation leads to ridicule; those who have deceived themselves do not trust the Veda, which is the true cause for men, nor do they consider outward appearance. 122.
As if compassionate at heart, he has for this long time deluded the girl,
concealing his own crookedness while artfully producing pleasure.
How is it that today, following the manner of Kaṃsa, you have shattered my heart and entered this terrible forest?
Having abandoned gratitude, you have come to the state of a rogue.
The description of the words of distress from the illusory friends:
"Even a male bee or a child would be unable to enter so far;
yet out of love, you have entered the palace of this jewel among young women. (125)
Having surrendered his entire being to our friend, this master of our house now torments her at the end; oh, how small indeed is his fame! 126.
O Lord, this infamy has indeed been brought about by you;
in separation from you, how could her mind remain as steady as Kaṃsa?
Having heard these words of reproach, the Lord of Ālāla smiled;
looking at his illusory companions, he spoke these words: (128)
Enough with these useless, harsh words; go away, you fools! Or rather, do you think I have any desire for an alliance with Māyā? (129)
"Did I perhaps become intimate with her through the 'seven-step' rite?
Or did I leave your hermitage today after having started a quarrel? (130)
Seeing me standing with an indifferent disposition in the temple of Śiva, she herself, deluded and overwhelmed by passion, desired me. (131)
And since I had then abandoned all desire, being unaware of her feelings, for what purpose did she manifest her passion before her friends? (132)
Alas, that passionate woman herself, through her own futile passion and the behavior of a paramour, has brought infamy upon me, though I am free from desire! 133.
Let her desire change me as she wishes; for I shall not be changed by her. Indeed, a blazing firebrand is not extinguished by a mere insect.
To remain silent with the thought that "women are deceitful" is like a great offense; alas, what a perilous danger is association with the wicked! 135.
"O noble ladies, what is this? Why have you, out of delusion, falsely imputed an offense committed by me to Kapi and come to the forest by force? (136)

O assembly of women! In this entire circle of the earth, by what manner of brilliance or conduct has Caṇḍabhānu prepared his equipment? Is he one whose attire is charmingly adorned with fine ornaments, or one who wears saffron robes, or perhaps one adorned with clusters of gold and jewels—yet remains indifferent to all?
Or, adorned with rudrākṣa beads and free from the objects of the senses, I wander alone at my own will.
Everything has arisen in me alone; this entire world-process exists within me; finally, it dissolves back into me alone, while I, pervading all, am like the thread that runs through pearls.

Unaffected by any scent brought toward me by those who pursue it, I move about as if possessed of qualities, perceived by people as one who possesses grace for the sake of severing the bonds of those who are devoted. || 138 ||

In the forest, having attained the state of a yogi, I was subjected to contempt by those created through illusion; yet I am capable of manifesting in the world my supreme status as a *parahaṃsa*, my preeminence within the Śaiva tradition as praised by the Vedas, and also the initiation of Śambhu.

Having assumed his very form and being engaged in the creation of the world, how could I—who am independent, yet subject to Māyā, an enjoyer of diverse sense-objects, and a performer of deceptive acts—be anything other than he? (139)
While the Lord was speaking thus, Māyā, bewildered and lacking awareness of the truth, cast aside her shame under the sway of passion and spoke once more to him,
the sole teacher of the three worlds; for indeed, a person afflicted by lust has no discourse on discernment.
O rogue, having first entered my heart through lustful desire, you have manifested a state of affection for me, though I was previously unacquainted with passion.
Having produced confidence by saying "I am under your control," what will you say now after casting aside those words? Or rather, why do you remain hidden? 141.
I am not mad today, nor am I deceiving you; I do not abandon you, for I swear this by your feet.
Setting aside this talk of the Brahman as mere words, reflect first upon it and accept me, who am devoted to you.
In your one wife alone. || 142 ||
Deceit, the practices of the Śabaras, muttering spells, false dress and speech, the enchantment of women, dancing, singing, and instrumental music;
the suppression of youth, hypocrisy, fraudulent medicines, treacherous acts, boisterousness, wandering about, and despicable sorcery.
Gambling, sorcery, deceit, mockery, crookedness, fickleness, dexterity, and trickery—
whether these are the established characteristics of men or of women, everyone in the three worlds knows this. (144)
When Bhuvanaikarati had spoken thus, the Lord, laughing, ceased from his debate with her rival, saying, "What of mine is this? And that very Māyā, through a ruse, said to Allama: "She herself. (145)
"Aha! Having assumed a worldly state, you have offered yourself up to me; yet, disregarding me, you proclaim your own absolute independence. If that is so, then hear my power! (146)
I render the gods, such as Hari, Brahmā, and Hara, though they possess great power, devoid of self-control;
I cause the foremost of great sages to stumble, their ascetic vigor failing, and I make their bodies cling to the embrace of women.
Treading upon the chest of Hari, I dwell there; I take away the left half of Hara’s body.

In the forest, the Lord spoke thus to Māyā, who was exalting herself: "I shall impose a verbal fetter upon the Lotus-born Brahmā; as for Indra and the other gods, how insignificant they are to me! (148)
Having made the Ādityas, Daityas, Uragas, Siddhas, Sādhyas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and others my servants, I set them in motion; how insignificant you are that you seek to oppose me! 149.
"Therefore, you must not practice this deceitful conduct, especially in our presence;
act according to my word with propriety. Thus addressed, the Lord spoke thus with persistence: || 150 ||
O fool, why do you engage in useless disputes with such garrulity, like an old woman of Vārāṇasī with stories of the past? You do not even fear the censure of others. 151.
If you possess your own capability, or even if you rely on my power through the explanatory passages (arthavāda) concerning the experience of the true nature of the Self,
then first conquer my knowledge by means of statements and arguments based on the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious.

If you possess the power of unbroken scholarship, refute my arguments and accept me as your own; but if, out of the force of your ignorance, you merely desire pleasure, you will not even move the tip of my nail.
"I am capable of bringing about the defeat of even the gods, headed by Hara, Acyuta, and Brahmā"—I do not heed these words spoken with such stubborn persistence, for young women are reckless. (154)

If that Lord—who, awakened by you and established within you, himself impels you toward actions at all times—should possess compassion, then victory would belong to you over the enemy of existence through his honor. (155)
Having heard these words spoken by Allāma, she was unable to give a reply;
then Māyā, reflecting upon something within her deeply distressed self, spoke to her husband, who is the embodiment of truth: 156.
By whom was he awakened? Where indeed is he established? Or who impels him himself toward actions?
Who is the Lord? Whence would his compassion arise? How might I conquer [this ignorance]? Out of respect, I do not know. (157)

O Lord, how can this [speech] of mine become so harsh as to offer a rebuttal to Your hymn? If what I say should cause displeasure in Your heart, then let my desire be fulfilled in whatever way it may be. (158)
Having served food such as *puroḍāśa* and the like, is it right to steal away [the meal] from one who is tormented by hunger?
How much more shall I speak before you? Take me, whose lips are like tender sprouts. 159.

Having thus rejected her words with indifference by means of a gesture of his hand, the Lord spoke to Māyā—who was boasting of her own excellence in the forest. Then the sovereign teacher, who has transcended all illusion, addressed Māyā once more, preceded by a sound of "hum. 160.
O Māyā, what is it fitting for you to say to me in this manner—me, who am like a fan to the creeper of desire?
To speak of one who has reached delusion is like saying, "Wrap your head with a pestle"; therefore, follow my advice. || 161 ||
For sensual desires—such as those for garlands, sandalwood, and the like, which are like poison—are indeed sweet at first sight.
Alas! Having accepted them like foolish people, how will those who are solely intent on Śiva perish?
Who among those initiated into the Yoga-tantras are not unattached and ready to renounce these objects of sense that lead to miserable ends?
They say that what is preceded by experience is what is to be known; however, these views are not approved by me.
Just as when oblations are poured into a blazing fire, the clarified butter does not merely cease to burn but blazes up even more intensely;
so too, when an object of experience is enjoyed, desire does not subside but increases, and that hope then grows twofold.
Having eaten mustard seeds, a bull does not abandon his hunger;
rather, his belly withers from the heat caused by the provocation of the digestive fire. (165)
Therefore, for a person devoid of discernment—a fool—there exists not even a trace of happiness through attachment to sense objects, under any circumstances whatsoever. (166)
Having burned his home with passion, where could one arrogant with pride remain?
Having destroyed discernment through desire, how can a fool cross over illusion? (167)
Thus, disregarding the words of the Lord of All through lack of discernment, Māyā began to speak out of possession by a stubborn obsession. 168.
"O rogue, having displayed your eloquence before me, what do you say? Are you like one who considers himself to have accomplished his purpose merely through an outward display of detachment? (169)
The states of speech known as Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī—
all these have attained their manifestation through the stirring of the lotus-feet of my state.
Beneath my left foot, all the playful manifestations of speech abide;
casting aside the illusory web of words, enjoy the pleasures together with me.
Allama also said: "O Māyā, have you not heard this?
It is declared that enjoyment lasts only until the full moon of this [lunar day]. (172)
"O deluded one, why do you prattle in vain before me, casting aside all shame?
Abandoning the snare of false hope, go home together with your female companions. (173)
Then, having heard the words of Allama and perceiving his intent, that woman wept repeatedly, exclaiming "Alas!
Alas! Yet, regaining her composure with some effort, she spoke these words while censuring the Lord:
In front of Aḷlama. || 174 ||

The Lord’s words regarding Māyā in the forest were proven false when He said, "By whatever means the worship of the Supreme Lord is performed, it will bear fruit, fulfilling all desired objects," for by those very words I have indeed been worshipping Śiva alone for a month.
Having offered everything with devotion to Madhukeśvara and having prayed, she worshipped you, bound by her heart’s affection;
yet that divine teacher, alas, constantly casts away compassion from his heart and torments me— how could this be?
Having heard this, the Lord of Allāla laughed and said: "What is the use of censuring the mountain-bowed one who wears serpents as ornaments?
To those who worship him according to the rules and have conquered the host of their enemies, Giriśa grants [their desires]."
Complete happiness. || 177 ||

Those base people on earth who, with a mind full of darkness (*tāmasa*), worship Śiva solely according to their own whims and devoid of scriptural instruction, do not attain their desires through that limb-deficient form of worship; they instead revile the deity and the guru.
When a connoisseur says, "This is gold, unmarked [by a stamp]," what can one who engages in futile quarreling accomplish?
O Māyā, you too should likewise censure me, or else Maheśa; for what can be accomplished here by you, who have not realized the true nature of reality? 179.
Who are you, with your mind entangled in fallacious reasoning; what connection could you possibly have with me, a treasure-house of dispassion, fortune, and ultimate truth?
Go back to your own city in the forest! Or rather, what is this pride of yours, O you whose mind is so firmly resolved?
This one. || 180 ||
Having heard what was said, she was then deeply distressed in her mind; afflicted by passion and censuring the powerful Self-born One,
she sighed like a serpent whose strength is constantly checked, and, utterly agitated, she collapsed upon the heart of her own friend.
Seeing her friend— whose beauty was like that of a night-lotus scorched by the rays of the sun, and who was distressed by the feverish heat of the arrows of Love—
the pure Rasajñā spoke with words as sweet as nectar to the jewel among lords, Allama.
To the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow down. || 182 ||
O support of all worlds, O refuge for those who seek shelter, O omniscient one endowed with excellent qualities, far removed from the discourse of the six waves;
O essence of truth, destroyer of the three impurities, witness of all— out of compassion, I make this petition to you regarding me.
Protect this! || 183 ||
Having previously protected Māyā with compassion, you have now abandoned her; tell me, how indeed does she still live?
Whether your dwelling be a village or a forest, let your footstep be fixed right there.
May this [teaching] of ours be taken as a refuge. || 184 ||
The Lord’s address to Vimalā in the forest:
"Or rather, O noble one, having relied upon compassion, you shall return to the city that dwells within the forest, which is [in truth] Māyā."
Having clothed him and favored him in every way for some days, let the Blessed One then set out on his journey; what indeed would be the harm in that?
Thus, with palms joined in reverence and bowing with humility, she made her request preceded by a hymn of praise;
then the Lord of Lords, Tāmallama, who knows his own true nature, spoke to Vimalā with a smile upon his lips.
When it is said, "Make [the truth] real," who in this world would be able to conduct their affairs with these deceptive words?
When it is said, "Resort to illusion (māyā)," how could those like us, who are hostile to Śiva-yogins, resort to it?
Milk attains the state of curd only through churning; milk never attains that state through webs of deceitful speech.
"The ignorant man falls into restlessness regarding sense-objects, but not the wise man; having reflected thoroughly, desist from the awakening of darkness.
Hearing these words of Allama, Vimalā said to him again: "I have been accepted by you out of compassion.
By that very merit of yours, I am already worthy of you—just as iron, when pierced by the touch of [the philosopher's stone], becomes gold."
Then Tāmralipta accepted your words; yet, alas, even truth is not like gold to a clod of earth.
Having attained this human state, she who does not seek the supreme goal is indeed a fool.
Nor [should one go] with a clod of earth as the interval [between oneself and another]. || 190 ||

Having thus cast all this aside in her heart, she spoke; then, having ascertained his state of supreme dispassion, Vimalā addressed him again with humility, indicating to herself her fear of shattering her pride through her friend.
O faultless one, delighter of the minds of the wise sages, nourisher of devotees, ocean of wisdom, abode of compassion, noble Lord!
If you do not abandon Māyā, my dear friend, then the eloquent speech of Haimavatī will find no favor.
O Hemādri, why this loathing toward the void? Let even Lord Śiva enjoy blissful dalliance with Śivā.
This is no fault for one whose fame is like the stainless moon; for the primary duty of yours, O Śiva, is indeed the gratification of Śiva and Śivā.
"If there were a wager between a woman and a man regarding victory or defeat, the leader would surely consider the woman as the one achieving victory;
O learned one, do not perceive even the slightest inferiority in Śambhu because of this— reflect thus in your mind," he said, and then he looked at her.
He said: || 194 ||
In the forest, I heard Vimalā speak of the faults inherent in the quality of illusion;
today, O Vimalā, I have understood what you said within my heart— how previously, in her heart thick with passion, it was otherwise.
For she desired delight in illusion, being inclined toward sense objects due to a lack of discernment, rather than the path to eternal bliss.
Māyā is indeed a transformation of darkness (tamas), for she is of the nature of tamas; whatever seed is sown by her upon this earth becomes that very tree.
Even in a dream, she experiences only the pleasure of the body suited to her own nature through the latent impressions of sense-objects, which is the ultimate reality.
This one. || 196 ||
I speak the truth: the entire water of the ocean is a palace, the peaks of Meru are the surface of the earth, and all around they take on the appearance of creepers.
Even if all trees were wish-fulfilling kalpa-trees, one would still not attain the realization of one's own true self through illusion. (197)
Having drunk with her ears the nectar spoken by Ālambā, she then reflected upon the mind of the God and the power of the young bride’s fortune:
"Who among people like me knows whether you are indeed worthy vessels? Thus, again and again, we have not taken [the opportunity], yet we remain free from fear."
to speak || 198 ||

Having placed his forehead upon the pair of her lotus feet and bowed with devotion, the Lord, the conscious self, having observed that Māyā had become pure and ceased from activity, spoke these words— desiring to make her heart indifferent to her own influence.
Where is the blinding darkness and where is the sun? Where is the pride of desire and where is the contemplation of the supreme reality that makes the self perceptible?
Where is the surface of the earth situated below and where is the back of heaven? And where are you?
The functioning of stainless, non-dual consciousness of Śiva. || 200 ||
Addressed by Lavana, who said, "Go quickly to that place suitable for attaining him," the fair-toothed woman, burning in her heart, replied:

"Alas! Having met with you, who are known throughout the entire world, how many nights have passed? Where will you go? And she added, "Even in my dreams, you have sported with me many times during our amorous dalliances; [is this not so] in your own heart?"
"I have taken refuge [in you].
How will the pain of your having departed from me today ever pass away? This delusion will not cease," she said as he spoke thus.

In a dream, you were bitten by a venomous snake placed there; waking up in distress and weeping, you later weep even more if your desire is attained. If I move about out of delusion, it is not for me a cause for reproach.
"O you who are helpless under the snare of delusion, you have indeed fallen into misery through the illusion of sexual pleasure, having gone forth into the forest in vain without support"—
this is the Lord's speech directed toward Māyā as she speaks impetuously in the forest.

"Since I am free from attachment and desire, and remain unchanging, do you not perceive my state of being agitated by passion? Therefore, enough of your wicked gestures and words! Thus addressed by Āllama, the young woman approached him with her illusory power (*māyā*) and said this in wondrous words: "O you who have assumed a fabricated body, you appear like Kāma himself; from where indeed has this desire come?"
I shall not abandon you; I swear this by oath, or else I shall take you by force and go to the city, or death shall follow in the end.
Let the vow of the Daughter of the Mountain be renowned upon the earth, for I am certainly not a woman who fails to fulfill her promise.

Having heard these boastful words, the Lord laughed and said: "In your house long ago, when you were afflicted by passion, my body was grasped by you for an embrace; alas, you do not realize that it was not truly grasped."

Having long gazed at my limbs in union with yours, you— blinded by passion— have touched even my smallest member; yet how is it that you do not realize, alas, that my hand, foot, penis, or even my throat and lips have not been touched?
This is an error. || 208 ||
Having heard his words, "Go quickly home," Māyā, together with her circle of friends known as the Eyes,
desired out of folly to seize him who was the essence of all souls; however, the illustrious one departed for the invisible realm.
He is the God. || 209 ||
Thus, O lords of all sages, I have related to you in its entirety the life of the Lord, which is rich in uprooting ignorance and karma.
That person who recites this with supreme devotion becomes free from defects and attains the Supreme Reality.
The happiness of universal sovereignty. || 210 ||

[Thus, in the *Ārṣa-Śrī-Bhaviṣyat-Purāṇa-Kathā-Viśālā*, which accords with the words of the Pramatha hosts, whose nature it is to uplift people submerged in the impurities of the Kali age, and which concerns the divine play (*līlā*) of Lord Liṅga— ]

The Seventh Chapter, titled "The Path Demonstrating the Conquest of Māyā through the Description of the Lord’s Greatness as Revealed in the Vimalāgama and the Narration of His Divine Playful Incarnations."
The arrival of the parents near their daughter who was lamenting in the forest. || Salutations to Śrī Nandikeśvara ||
[The Eighth Chapter]

Sūta said: O sages, whose hearts are moistened by the essence of devotion to the Siddhas, Vīras, and Gurus, and who have conquered Māyā through the grace of Lord Allama— listen with reverence to the divine play of the Lord, which is guarded by his host of Pramathas.
When the Allama had vanished, Māyā sank deep into an ocean of grief;
beholding Vimalā, she spoke these words in a faltering voice, overcome with distress. (2)
How shall I go into the presence of the stainless Pārvatī?
And how can Śivā, having seen me frustrated, go into the presence of Śiva?
"Alas, what misery! Alas, what misery! My vow has been rendered futile. All the members of the assembly will laugh at me in their midst. (4)
Having spoken thus, lamenting in her own distress, sighing again and again, she fell to the ground unconscious in the presence of her friends.
Then the king, accompanied by his forces, came with the intent to see his daughter;
having searched the forest, he finally beheld her somewhere within it.
O twice-born ones, seeing their daughter then exhausted and overcome with anxiety along with her friends, her parents became distressed and approached her side.
Embracing her with both arms, the enchanting king said:
"O lotus-eyed one, cast away your anxiety; why this delusion of the mind?"
"O daughter, today the son of the lord of the mandala desires to marry you;
having followed him, how have you reached the forest, O daughter of the mṛdaṅga-player?"
"Alas, O lotus-petal-eyed one! How can that very Śiva, being so merciless, cause you to experience such a wretched state? (10)
"O slender-limbed one, how is it that you have not heard what your wise mother, having arrived at midnight, told you? (11)
"I am renowned as the husband of other consecrated kings;
having disregarded such a person as me, how have you come to such impudence? (12)
How could she be prepared to abandon the established traditions of her lineage? How could she be so reckless as to dare to transgress the command of her parents? (13)
"What indeed is the use of this? One should surely contemplate the course of events while still standing; for what is the point of building a dam once the water has already flowed away? (14)
In the forest, before the eyes of King Mohinī and Vimalāmāyā, [the two queens] ascended to heaven from the earth.
"I have forgiven this offense; rise quickly, O young girl!
Ascending the palanquin, let us go toward the palace. (15)
Having observed the king who had spoken thus, the fair-faced Vimalā spoke these words clearly with mature speech: || 16 ||
"O King, abandon this delusion regarding your son; this is the illusory power (māyā) of the Mountain’s daughter.
Indeed, she made a vow in the presence of the God of gods. (17)
"Having subdued Allama Prabhu, who is dear to me, by means of my own gestures, expressions, and other charms,
I shall carry him away," [she thought] together with the daughter of the Mountain King.
Although this Lord, who pervades the entire universe, has been deceived in many ways, he has conquered Māyā and departed; thus, her vow has been struck down by him.
"Let us two go to Kailāsa; there is no business for us on the surface of the earth.
O King, casting aside your despondency, go to the city without delay. (20)

Having thus consoled the king and his wife with these words, that Māyā departed from the path of the earth by the power of her own yogic discipline; and that beautiful woman also, having met her for a moment in the clear sky, vanished.
Śambhuśaila || 21 ||

Then the king, together with his wives, tormented by great agony and crying out, "Alas! Oh, alas!", fell upon the ground, drenching his head with dust; rolling about and weeping, he cried, "O daughter, where have you gone?"
Crying out, tormented, why was he withering away?
Becoming hunched, trembling within himself, stumbling, gasping, unable to stand—O brahmins, he suffered from the separation from his daughter.
"How could that beauty, that cleverness, and those graceful charms not be within our sight on this earth?
How indeed can we bear to forget them? Thus the king lamented along with his wife.
Then his illustrious preceptor, known as Ahaṃkāra, arrived there in haste.
Alas, he has attained the awakening of discernment; why then this vain self-affliction regarding what has already passed?
What living being here is capable of transgressing the command of Śiva, the beloved of all?
For what reason has Māyā, having dwelt in our house, departed once again? (26)
Her birth and her wondrous deeds are superhuman; they are manifest even to us.
Is it because she is not his daughter that he remains unenlightened even after hearing this much, which has been clearly proclaimed? (27)
In the forest, for the sake of "mine-ness," the royal policy taught by the weight of "I-ness" is required.
Therefore, O crest-jewel of kings, do not suffer; for you have not deviated from the path of policy.
Since you have gone to the forest today for the purpose of searching [for me], let the path of policy not fall away. (28)
Seeing the disappearance of her lord, Māyā might herself depart along with his body;
for this world would then become a source of doubt, thinking, "The king's daughter has been carried off by a libertine. (29)
For this reason as well, you must not deviate from policy; indeed, you must enter the capital.
For if you were not to go there again, there would surely be doubt in the minds of men.
For the king is everywhere father and mother to his subjects; the king is their teacher and their kinsman.
He who always punishes the wicked and remains vigilant to protect the virtuous is a king.
Or, he who is purposelessly addicted to vice and is unable to protect his subjects in accordance with dharma—
abandoning him, all people go to the kingdom of another king who is endowed with dharma and artha.
Therefore, our [people], preceded by the domestic priest and the ministers, have been separated from you.
"All shall go to another king, and the kingdom shall perish while you remain in distress. (33)
Having thus composed the king's mind, he who was called Ahaṅkāra led him to the city of Mohinī and settled him in his own abode.
O Brahmins, Mamakāra also, together with Mohinī,
sportively protected the entire kingdom and dwelt there in happiness.
There, Vimalā and Māyā went to Bhuvaneśvarī and,
with palms joined in reverence, placed their heads at her pair of lotus feet.
Then, seeing Māyā standing on the ground with her head bowed down while she was drawing the Daughter of the Mountain, he considered her efforts to have been rendered futile.

Realizing that the preceptor was invincible, Ambā too, devoid of joy and sighing in her heart, felt overcome with shame at the thought of going to her husband’s assembly; she could not endure even remaining within the house, as if she were hidden away.

Having heard this account, even the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva), assuming a playful form out of compassion, approached the inner chamber of Pārvatī’s dwelling and, while pleasing her with words of consolation,
proclaimed the greatness of Allama once more in order to loosen her sense of ego.
Thus he spoke this āryā verse to the Teacher of all the gods, who removes ignorance through wisdom.
In the inner apartments, Gaurī and Śaṅkara engage in this dialogue:
"Even a hundred thunderbolts could be shattered; even a terrible poison-bearer could be seized."
O Gaurī, even by you with your well-sharpened fangs, can this heart of Aḷlama, which cannot be shaken by Death, be torn open? 40.
Where is illusion, and where is the Lord’s fortitude? You have acted without reflection; nevertheless, O daughter of the Earth, abandon this anxiety in your mind. (41)
Having heard her husband’s words, Gaurī, the daughter of the mountain king, spoke with her face slightly bowed in modesty; out of her feminine nature, she spoke with words full of charm. (42)
O Lord, that illusory power consisting of my own essence which was sent by me to the surface of the earth, you have conquered it by standing firm in the spirit of a wrestler. (43)
"Your vow has been fulfilled; I have been conquered by you," she said.
To her who spoke thus, the Lord replied out of his sense of self-importance: ||| 44 ||
By you yourself, who sent your own woman of tamasic nature toward the earth,
you have been defeated through futile exertion.
Alas! Having perceived him as a mere mortal, she sent forth Māyā, though he was a treasury containing the very essence of the beauty of innate bliss.
How could this insentient illusion possibly stand before the Lord, the Stainless One? It is like the [illusion] of a human being who possesses only limited knowledge. (47)
The Great-Souled Omniscient One possesses no bodily qualities;
there is no connection with the objects of the senses, nor any activities such as volition and the like.
Not having realized the conscious Self, the witness of all, who is the wrestler of wrestlers, one forms through delusion the stubborn obsession: "I shall conquer," though doing nothing at all. (49)
When the Lord of Gods spoke thus, the Goddess, repeatedly feeling loathing, said this to the All-pervading One: "Why do you strike me with arrows of speech? (50)
Having cut off my nose, why indeed should a mirror be placed above it? Enough with counting my offenses; how small am I [compared to them]? 51.
"O Śambhu, ocean of compassion, protect me with patience!
Thus entreated, the God, with a pure smile, spoke to Ambā.
"Be firm, O auspicious lady; do not worry over this much.
By the word of Śiva, may that Lord—the incarnation of the sattvic portion sent by Pārvatī—somehow dispel your distress. (53)
Having heard that, the goddess Pārvatī prostrated herself like a staff and,
having prayed, "How may I be freed from this wretchedness?", he spoke.
That sattvic, stainless goddess, non-different from me, whose nature is consciousness—the very digit that resides within you—is to be meditated upon in the lotus-hearts of yogis. (55)
"Having rendered her devoid of karma and filled with devotion and dispassion, send her to the earth in female form; the Lord will become subject to her. (56)
Where there is devotion, there the Lord is; and where the being is pure, there is devotion.
Therefore, that Lord bestows His grace upon your sattvic quality.
Having graciously revealed His own true nature, the Great Lord will for a long time delight your sattvic aspect.
Having been addressed thus, that Great Goddess, thinking "this is a great favor," dispatched her own earthly, sattvic portion.
Then, out of an abundance of bliss, the Mother nourished her limbs intensely;
seeing her, Vṛṣabheśāna spoke to Īśāna at that moment.
"How is it that this Gaurī became so emaciated in her limbs?
And now, why has she nourished all her limbs with such a joyful soul? (61)
Having heard the words of the lordly bull and having fathomed their intent, and knowing that he was a great soul, he spoke in the presence of everyone: || 62 ||
O Great-Souled One, best of bulls, vessel of auspicious qualities!
With whom can you be compared, since you are the very refuge of equanimity? (63)
"You are capable of supporting the world, since you are more capable than I am"—
thus the god praised Vṛṣabheśvara like a reciter of sacred texts.
Having heard this, some members of the assembly censured him out of malice; having heard the words of reproach, Vṛṣa maintained an attitude of neutrality.
Then, his soul exceedingly delighted, the enemy of Smara— who is fond of virtuous qualities—
looked upon those who were worthy of great respect and spoke thus to those who were his detractors.
Even after hearing those disparaging words uttered by you who were overcome by envy, he remains as lofty as a hidden pearl; alas, why does he not say something to you out of pride? 67.
"Even for the great sages, this peace is not found; indeed, he alone is blessed.
Thus Śaṅkara spoke these words to Nandin regarding his descent upon the earth.
Having thus instructed them on the true nature of Dharma, the Lord summoned the bull-king and said: (68)
O Nandin, you are the bestower of great joy upon these gods and are worthy of their worship;
yet in the Kali age, men, due to their feeble spiritual capacity, abandon the state of being worshippers at my feet. (69)
Therefore, Paraśambhu himself, whose form is rooted in me, became even greater in order to uplift humanity;
he was born as the immeasurable son named Allama to Sujñānadevī, free from all egoism.

O you who are a mass of merit exalted by the purity of your being, having descended upon the surface of the earth into the lineage of devotees, remain there engaged solely in the assembly of spiritual experience, with immediate attentiveness and faultless devotion. (71)
