There, having approached you in person with devotion, let Allama show you the path of focused attention;
and by pleasing his heart, he will also settle your mind in the knowledge of the secret.
Then, having removed the sense of distinction between you and his own self, the Lord will soon fulfill your purpose;
and though your purpose is already fulfilled, he himself has commanded you: "Fulfill the entire world. (73)

At the command of Śiva, "So be it," Ṛṣabheśvara vanished; then, looking at his own attendants, Śambhu, the Lord, said: "There shall be a private conversation between Nandin and me, consisting solely of our own experience."

"You too, having grasped this with your intellect, must uproot those spikes of doubt in your minds; then, with the goal firmly determined by higher knowledge, practice that devotion which is renowned throughout the earth.
Having thus instructed the principal lords of the Gaṇas there with compassion, the Lord entered the inner apartments.
Seventy-seven leaders of the Pramatha hosts, together with seven hundred [attendants], descended to the earth from Gaurī; for the command of the Lord is indeed inviolable.

[Thus, in the extensive narrative of the venerable *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*, within the *Prabhuliṅgalīlā*, this is the section concerning the departure of Māyā, Śiva’s consolation of Gaurī, the play of the descent of the *citkalā*, the description of the greatness of Vṛṣabheśvara and his instigation of the descent, and the arrival of the Pramatha hosts upon the earth.]
The eighth chapter, titled "The Way of Transcendence."
[Thus the first part is completed.]
Salutations to Śrī Nandikeśvara.
[In the Śrī Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, within the Prabhuliṅgalīlā, begins the second part.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Sūta said:
O lords of sages, those who delight in worshipping the feet of Vīreśvara have heard the essence within this collection of narratives:
the descent of the Pramatha.
Taking as my subject that which was taught by Vyāsa, may you, who are connoisseurs of devotion, listen to the divine play of Lord Liṅga. || 1 ||
Then, by the command of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain and by his supreme wisdom, the lords of the Pramathas [acted].
Born among the Vīraśaiva-Vimalātmans, they have ascended to various heights upon this earth. || 2 ||
It triumphs, as radiant as the crest-jewel of the Earth-bride, lofty and possessed of beautiful branches.
The city of Uḍutaṭī was adorned with buildings and golden palaces that rivaled the splendor of celestial cities.
In that city there was a man named Vimala, whose nature was pure, and who was like the Rohaṇa mountain for the growth of excellent jewels of innumerable virtues.
And his wife was Sumati, foremost among those who regard their husband as a deity, of great majesty, and worthy of high honor;
she was a virtuous woman sent by Girijā after considering this Kali age and her own auspicious conduct suited for its prosperity.
Then, enclosed within the pearl-oyster shell that was her womb, she was born as if liberated,
being intensely devoted to Maheśvara, the bestower of liberation.
Beholding her, who was as worthy of being gazed upon as a spark of consciousness, the host of her kinsmen cried out, "Surely she is the Daughter of the Mountain herself in person!"
Having assumed a body on this earth, he appeared as an infant; thus, all rejoiced on every side.

Fashioning a white line of sacred ash upon his forehead like the forehead-plate appropriate for the occasion of initiation and consecration, his father then bound a *liṅga* around the base of his neck; furthermore, having placed in his hand and upon his head that which was to be worshipped, [he said: 7. [He fashioned] a white line of sacred ash on his forehead like a forehead-plate suitable for the time of initiation and consecration; then he bound the *liṅga* around the surface of the base of his neck, after having placed in his hand and upon his head that which was to be worshipped.

Having whispered the five-syllabled mantra, supremely purifying, into his ear with reverence along with the blessing, "May you become one whose mind is filled with pure knowledge and devotion," the high-souled Maheshvara attended upon him.
"This is the Sāttvika Kalā of Maheśa’s consort," she herself [declared].
The best of the gods bestowed upon her the name Mahādevī.
The noble state appropriate to her name was heart-stealing, like sacred knowledge accompanied by disciplined conduct.
Having ascended to devotion, she shone like a female rider alongside the male practitioners of the lineage.
Those other lords of the Pramathas were stationed here and there at various places.
The account of the descent of the venerable Siddha and Rāma Ācāryas:
They were born into lineages of devotees and remained firmly established in devotion. (11)
Free from passion, pure in conduct, fearless, and free from affliction.
Bestowing upon living beings the wealth acquired through righteous means, || 12 ||
The great city named Svarṇalā on the surface of the earth is worthy of description.
It shines, surpassing the city of gold, filled with all forms of prosperity.
There was one named Mugdha, a devotee of the Deluded One, who was with a woman named Mugdhā.
Undertaking the worship of the Linga and the Jangama without sloth, he should remain diligent.
His son was Pramatha, who was awakened and renowned by the name Śrī Siddharāma.
He became mature through devotion, detachment, and awakening, and was full of faith, striving in the Śiva-yoga-tantra.
In the city named Parimalikā, there was a great scholar who was the foremost among the family of devotees of Hara.
The attendant known as Maṇivālamācaya is one who knows the higher and the lower. || 16 ||
Renowned for the title of Great Lion, who is a formidable elephant-tamer against the pride of opposing disputants.
Victorious is he, renowned as the supreme sovereign of the Varamāheśvara-paṭṭa. || 17 ||
He who bestows devotion to Śiva upon living beings through his most pure vision.
Having purified the hearts of devotees and descended [to earth], what wonder is there in this world? || 18 ||
Constantly engaged in the deliberation of the Śiva scriptures together with the hosts of Śiva’s devotees.
That Śiva-yogin shone upon the earth like a very Mācaka among the wise. || 19 ||
In the land of Karṇāṭa, there is a city like a choice vine upon a cow-horned tree, a garden of the Bhāgavata.
In that city resided a famous lord of the earth, a leader among devotees named Mādanamantrin.
His daughter-in-law was named Mādāmbikā, who possessed excellent conduct and was devoted to her husband.
As the two of them were propitiating [the deity] for the sake of a son, Nandīśvara became their gratified offspring;
that child Kakudman remained in her womb for three years while she maintained meditative absorption.
Then he was born for the protection of the three worlds, amidst the sounds of celestial kettledrums and showers of flowers.
Opening his eyes while his limbs remained folded like a bud, the child did not experience even the slightest restlessness.
Then, at that very moment, Saṅgameśa approached and placed his innate, beloved Liṅga upon her body.
In his heart, he was performing the ceremonial enthronement for the sovereign empire of his own devotion.
Having applied the brilliantly shining sacred ash upon his forehead, the Lord named him Basava;
then, placing the palm of his hand upon his head and casting away all illusion (māyā), he instructed him in his ear.

Then Maheśa [expounded] the five-syllabled mantra, together with the *praṇava*, along with its *tattvas*, its *kīlaka*, and its meaning, to Śrī Basavarāja at the time of his initiation for the wearing of the *liṅga*.
Then the Lord of Love vanished from the hearts of the women present there.
Having remained as if opened and then closed, they became utterly astonished. || 26 ||
Śaṅkara himself, the ocean of compassion, having come in person for the sake of his most wonderful son.
Immediately upon his birth, he bore a mark on his throat that had never been seen anywhere before.
While those women were thus speaking to one another, in an instant this child became possessed of a hump.
He shook his limbs, beginning with his hands and feet, and then his eyes were opened.
The father also, having performed the funeral rites for his son, [consoled him] with offerings of food and nets of light during the meal following the departure.
At the very time prescribed for each respective ritual act, he regarded Nandin alone as his son.
Having heard that Basava was the name given by Maheśa, his father also did exactly the same.
Day by day, he too grew, like the young moon, the lord of stars, increasing in its digits.
Having approached the assembly of teachers and students, the child hears it but once.
He effortlessly grasped the entire web of the Vedas, Āgamas, and Śāstras, along with their essential meanings.
Furthermore, by means of the certainty derived from the treatises, the scriptures, the mass of the Vedas, and even the collection of the Upanishads;
With the desire to understand the essential meaning through its underlying intent, he meditated upon supreme devotion toward Maheśa.
Then, at the time of the eighth month of pregnancy, the husband and wife were joyful in their hearts.
The two of them became desirous of performing the initiation ceremony for Basava. || 33 ||
Having understood that, Basava then consulted with his father and became free from worldly desire.
She spoke to her own sister Nāgāmbikā, who was devoted to her.
He is my preceptor, my guru, my master, my teacher, and my guide.
For the Lord alone is supreme; He indeed shall lead me [to Him]. || 35 ||
There is no other bringer of me [to him] except for the Lord, the Sovereign of All.
For us, whose nature is auspicious, it is fitting to depart from our homes at once.
Having spoken thus, that Basava, who was like Śiva himself, [remained] together with her.
Having departed quickly from the palace, he went to the meeting place of the mendicants.
There, he was intent upon the propitiation of Śrī Saṅgameśa.
He dwelt there for several days together with a few devotees.
O Great Goddess, he dispatches the lordly bull toward the earth.
Those who, out of enmity, spoke words there devoid of trust. || 39 ||
Then, in the regions surrounding that place, all those opponents [were subdued].
Born into lineages such as the Buddhists and others, they were even there intent on quarreling.
Among them, the chief was a rogue king named Bījalo.
He ruled over Kalyāṇapura, the cause of all auspiciousness; [now follows] the account of Basavarāja’s journey toward Kalyāṇapura.
There, in that abode of Maheśa, stands a lofty stone edict.
It was established by someone unknown; its script is marvelous and cannot be recognized.
Seeing that seed-syllable script, he was unable to decipher it.
Having summoned all those on earth who were knowledgeable in scripts, he showed it to them as well. || 43 ||
They too did not know that King Bījal was there on that stone slab covered with dust.
He made a further vow, preceded by the sounding of a drum. || 44 ||
Whoever on earth reads this marvelous inscription, whoever it may be;
"May he become the sovereign lord of his own kingdom, the foremost leader among the chief ministers. || 45 ||
Then Baladeva, his minister and the best among the lineage of Vīraśaivas, [spoke].
Having heard of Basava’s superior wisdom from a multitude of guests, [he was filled with wonder].
Having informed the king, the chief minister went to the meeting place of the beggar (karpaṭin) and,
after persuading him in many ways, brought him back toward the city.
The king arrived accompanied by the splendor of songs, instrumental music, dance, and other such festivities.
He went out to meet Basava, who was surrounded by the attendants of Maheśvara.
Having brought him to his own city, the king [placed him] in a temple.
Having shown him the teaching, he requested, "Please recite it. || 49 ||
The Vasus quickly recited the divine instruction as if it were already mastered.
Having fathomed its essential meaning, the king obtained a great treasure.
Having satisfied the king with the gain of ten crores of wealth, he [departed].
Having entreated Basava, he made him the chief leader of the council of ministers.
By the king’s command, Baladeva, the lord of punishment, was well-pleased with him.
He gave his daughter Gaṅgāmbikā to him after she had made a formal request.
Having married according to the path taught in the Vīraśaiva tradition, Basaveśvara...
At the request of the king, he remained protecting the entire earth. || 53 ||
By mere sight, he creates, protects, and destroys the entire world.
O twice-born ones, how great was the burden for that carrier when carrying the portion of the earth?
Always practicing meditative absorption with equanimity toward both the external and the internal.
He protected the earth with his own glances, which were graced by side-long looks.
He constantly performed the worship of Śiva with countless devotees of Maheśvara.
Eating food offered with devotion, he caused the Vīraśaiva tradition to flourish.
His sister was Nāgāmbā, the daughter of Basava, who possessed a most excellent disposition.
Following the path thus instructed, he protected the dharma of Śiva.
The narration of the glorious rise of Cannabasava;
she who was devoted to the vow of celibacy and filled with supreme dispassion.
Knowing the distinction between the higher and the lower, they took refuge in the supreme Śaiva [tradition]. || 58 ||
Once, the illustrious Basava, together with the foremost among the Jaṅgamas, [proceeded].
Having propitiated the Great Lord with devotion, he partook of the food granted as his grace.
At the time of his meal, five or six morsels of prasāda indeed fell from Basava’s mouth.
Seeing that the two eyes had moved on the earth by fate, Nāgāmbikā, who was steadfast in unwavering devotion,
herself took them up by the will of Śiva and touched the two eyes with her joined palms.
With devotion and attentiveness, her mind composed, the slender-limbed woman partook of it with a spirit of serene faith.
By that very merit, the slender lady conceived a child, and then Śiva appeared before her in person.
She gave birth to a son whose name was concealed as was fitting, a term that resolved all doubt.
He, whose nature is the wonder of the world, bore upon his body the marks of the Lord of Bāla.
He vanished for the sake of protecting the world, and thereafter he became renowned as Tachchhanna. || 63 ||
Through the arising of virtues such as conduct, devotion, and knowledge, he was equal to Basava.
He was renowned by the name Channabasava, the most excellent among the devotees of Maheśvara.
Having studied all the śāstras as well as all the Vedas and Āgamas.
Basavādeva, his disciple, became the commander-in-chief (daṇḍanāyaka) in disguise.
One who possesses knowledge of the sequence of the six stages and is conversant with the procedure for the rite of surrender.
He was diligent, possessed true devotion, and was a knower of the secrets of all mantras.
He had reached the further shore of the knowledge of the established tenets and the meaning of all the Śaiva tantras without exception.
Praised by the learned, he clearly expounded the Vedānta scriptures.
Having studied, understood, and practiced the extensive scriptures, [he should impart them] to his devotees.
Having extracted the essence from everything, he taught this in brief.
For the sake of protecting his devotees, Basava-yogin’s devotee stands as a guarantor.
And he, Channabasava, shone here as the concealed Ṣaṇmukha.
There appeared for Basava a jewel of a son, a crest-jewel of supreme devotion to the Lord who wields the bow of the Mountain of Jewels.
Gangāmikā, endowed with auspicious qualities, nourished him— who was renowned as Saṅgameśvara— just as Ambikā nourishes Guha.
The Great Lord Basava attained renown in the world for the sake of removing from him the state of being a stone, a tree, or a beast.

The wish-fulfilling gem (*ciṃtāmaṇi*) is in his mind, the celestial tree (*kalpataru*) is in his lotus-hand, and the wish-granting cow (*surabhi*) is in the courtyard of his home; thus, preceded by the etymological definition of the word "Vasava," there is a description of the wonderful manner of his bestowing gifts.
By the name "Vasu," he is the eight Vasus—the lords of the eightfold prosperity—and on earth, he is gold and divine jewels.
They are well-known.

He is called Vasu because he blows (vāti), causes fragrance (gandhayati), and goes (gacchati); this name is significant according to its etymology, as there is no distinction between the letters *va* and *ba*.

Therefore, for one who possesses vast riches and all manner of jewels that come under his control by mere thought— just as the eight Vasus appear like servants upon the sight of a treasure— what burden indeed could there be in granting the desired fruit to a supplicant? || 73 ||
Śambhu, at the very moment of dispatching him toward the earth for the sake of uplifting the entire world, [entrusted] his own [task] to him.

The Blessed One bestowed upon him the entire sixfold set of sovereignty, heroism, innate wisdom, detachment, fame, and glory, as well as the complete kingdom; yet, though the jewel among kings was under his total control, he remained like a servant.
Therefore, this donor of all that is sought performed, with uninterrupted devotion, the worship of his gurus and the mobile and immobile liṅgas.

Devoted to the daily worship of the Lord, established in his own yoga, intent on the path of liberation, and steadfast in his observances and vows, he constantly bestowed upon the rows of learned men, poets, brahmins, warriors, and beggars whatever they desired— be it a multitude of gold, jewels, garments, elephants, horses, cattle, land, grain, beds, seats, houses, maidens, palanquins, and so forth.
Filled with unattached devotion, a knower of the Upaniṣads, and possessing a heart free from illusion, Basava shone resplendent.
He alone, Basava, who was devoted and detached, is renowned throughout the earth surrounded by the oceans.
Having heard his fame, the best among the Śiva-yogins, desiring to see him, approached him.
With the understanding that vessels touched by outsiders are unfit to be accepted, [he should avoid them].
Some who were established in their vows arrived, endowed with specific restrictive observances.
They have turned away from cooking food with the wealth of houses belonging to those who are uninitiated.
Some believers, who were devoted to the practice of the primary vows, arrived there.
With firm vows, they did not touch food cooked by others with their hands.
Devoted to cooking with their own hands, they gathered together and approached him. || 81 ||
Those who are devoted to the offering of fullness, who possess auspicious character, and are most exalted.
Desirous of seeing the great minister Basava with devotion, they arrived.
Some delight in covering only the neck, while others cover all the limbs.
Those who are devoted to the vow of the wooden sandals, and those whose vow is to cover their noses; || 83 ||
They turned their backs on outsiders, avoiding looking at them, touching them, or conversing with them.
Others, however, were intent on worshiping with waters defiled by the rays of the sun.
The narration of the arrival of many heroic devotees of Maheśvara residing in various regions;
those who delight in food that ripens without being ploughed and are averse to food that ripens through cultivation.
Others were devoted to the worship of Śiva with flowers and other offerings gathered by themselves.
They turned their backs on the artificial trees that had produced leaves and flowers.
Without performing the worship of the mobile liṅga, they observed vows of fasting unto death. || 86 ||
Thus, having observed fasts and other such disciplines, they were devoted to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Some subsist on milk, some on measured food, while others eat only eight mouthfuls.
Others, devoted to the vow of celibacy, remained dedicated to sleeping on the ground.
Others are averse to swallowing water with their tongues protruding for the sake of worship.
Elsewhere, others are averse to even water, lacking the constituent parts of worship.
Others are averse to betel, sandalwood paste, garlands, and the like.
Others, devoid of the topknot, sacred thread, and so forth, are solely devoted to the *liṅga*.
Some worship at the three times of day, while others worship at the four times.
Others are devoted to worship performed six times a day, while still others are averse to fixed images.
They constantly observe the vow of smearing their entire bodies with ashes.
Some were endowed with all their own vows and the conduct of the virtuous.
Those who are devoted to the chosen liṅga and the mind, and who worship in the sixteen-fold manner twice or thrice [a day].
And others were devoted to the great vows (mahāvrata) as taught in the Śiva scriptures.
They all came to see the temple of Basaveśa. || 93 ||
Beholding them one by one, Vasava, the dweller in wealth, was well-pleased.
He honored them with due respect, according to the proper sequence and in accordance with what was appropriate for each.
With joyful hearts, they ministered to one another through services performed for that purpose.
Praising Basavādhiśa with words of benediction, they [spoke]. || 95 ||
Having spent several days devoted to the study of the scriptures, they remained intent upon hearing the sacred texts.
Immersed in the ocean of the nectar of Śivānanda, they remain established right there.
Having informed [the king] of their respective tasks, some were intent on making requests.
Having taken that immeasurable wealth given by him, they departed for their own directions. || 97 ||
Those shameless, fearless, and deceitful men who are wandering lechers there;
They beg for many kinds of goods; their number is beyond reckoning. || 98 ||
Many opponents who had gone there for the sake of debate—
Having settled them all in dwellings with food, drink, and other necessities, he— || 99 ||
Every day, in the hall of debate, he challenged [his opponent] to sit upon the appropriate seat.
Having recounted the account of Basaveśa’s refutation of the opposing disputants,
he had them debated by his own scholars, treating them with great honor.
Either adopting a position of neutrality oneself, or [employing] other distinct methods directed toward that end.
O believers, he employed only sound reasoning and not a web of mere words.
Then, when a dialogue with the Vaidikas had begun, he, who was an expert in the essential points of the occasion, [spoke].
At one time, he himself indeed held a great festival of debate.
Having brought about the defeat of the opponents' arguments at the end by means of logic, he effects their discomfiture.
Let it be today, tomorrow, or the day after; having deliberated, let a reply be given.
Having said this, he should cause food, drink, and other provisions to be given to them.
When he was told, "We have been conquered by the initiation," he made those [enemies] his devotees.
Having bestowed the desired objects upon the wise whose souls are devoted to Śiva.

however, the perfection of dress does not belong to one who possesses complete wisdom. || 91 ||

Therefore, in this matter, outward appearance, speech, and the like are certainly not the cause; rather, it is that supreme awakening alone which has become firmly rooted in the junction of the heart.
Since another's heart cannot indeed be known because it transcends the senses, one should not find fault with anyone; for that very act is itself the acquisition of a fault.
Having first corrupted one [quality] and then indeed exalting another, this practice of partiality is not worthy of a refuge-seeker.

Yet, with but a single fraction of her glance, she always pervades everything; therefore, she who views all with equanimity is indeed worthy of bestowing blessings for the protection of cows and Brahmins. May there be constant auspiciousness, and may the worlds likewise remain forever happy.
"Indeed, all virtuous people utter such a blessing; have you not heard this, O Siddharāma? (94)
Having heard the words of Allama, Rāma spoke with humility: "O Lord, alas, throughout these past days of mine..."

The vision of awakening, obtained through the merit of beholding the lotus-feet of Your Honor, has never been worn away by anxieties concerning the distinctions between mediocre, inferior, or great folk; thus, my own wisdom also perceives the equality of all beings.
"O ocean of compassion, instruct me as to how I, being such as I am, may not waver further from this state of mind. (96)
To him who was thus making his request, the Lord said to Rāma, "O dear one, day by day, rely upon the fortune of dispassion."
For one who maintains firmness through practice and gradually focuses the mind, the mind becomes steady by means of cultivating sattvic qualities.
When the mind becomes steady, there arises peace that brings about boundless bliss; for one who possesses tranquility, there is no perception of duality.
Then, when the delusion of duality has become slackened, the supreme light, which dwells within all, arises spontaneously and equally in every direction.
He attained uniformity toward enemy and friend alike, indifference to women, and a lack of distinction between his own home and the forest;

regarding his own and others as equal to a clod of earth or a stone, and indifferent to the low and the high, he found peace in his heart, intent solely on the state of a sovereign through his own bliss. || 99 ||
Until then, a person should not abandon Haṭhayoga or Rājayoga, nor should he hasten prematurely toward the attainment of yoga within himself;

even if distracted or indolent, he should not become despondent, but should increase his practice with moderation and maintain equanimity until the description of the greatness of Lord Siddharāma is completed for the sake of his own liberation.

Thus, he who, devoid of dispassion, abandons effort and desires the attainment of yoga with haste becomes fallen and ruined in intellect; therefore, his fulfillment shall come through approaching a venerable Guru. || 101 ||
Without the instruction of the guru, there is neither yoga, nor the powers of awakening, dispassion, and austerity.
Without the instruction of the guru, nothing at all should be heard; therefore, first [seek] the venerable Guru-nātha.
Having heard the words of the Lord, which are the essence of all that has been heard, Rāma bowed to him and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
O most compassionate one, the supreme among gurus, you alone, O Śrī Gurunātha, must instruct me. 103.
O Lord of Yogis, in this world there is no teacher superior to you, nor one equal to you in the abundance of knowledge.
The discernment of the *liṅga* is easily obtained through instruction; you alone are its fulfiller, and no other. || 104 ||
O Guru, the very sight of you constitutes for me all the unfailing, divine perfections of yoga.
O Lord, let the mere touch of Your feet now be my equanimity; accept me quickly.
O Master, liberation is indeed the glance of Your compassionate and moist side-long look; come to my monastery to grant me my heart's desire.
O sovereign of the circle of gurus, having beheld Malleśvara with compassion, quickly deliver me from this state! 106.
Having heard this, the all-pervading Lord Allama spoke again to Rāma: "Indeed, there is no distinction for the Lord of Yogins who is omnipresent."
Whether in a village, a forest, an excellent house, or a mountain cave; whether on a bed of lotus stalks and cotton, or upon a stone slab.

Rāma, delightful in his humility, addressed him: "O Lord, how could this man possibly offer a reply before you?"

Alas, those multitudes of sentient beings on earth, composed of eighty-four lakhs of enumerated varieties!

Rāma, with palms joined in reverence, said: "The four senses follow after their respective objects as they arise."
"O Lord, abode of compassion, how can his victory be like that of dogs against hares? Please instruct me properly. (122)
O mind, listen! You are the king of all the senses; therefore, restrain their inclination toward their respective objects.
For the senses follow after that which is directed toward the self, just as female bees follow a preeminent male bee. || 123 ||
Rāma said to the venerable Guru: "O Lord, if that mind of mine does not turn away from its own worldly activities, then, having accumulated wealth, I shall [provide for] my wife and children."

Nourishing those who seek his aid and bestowing what they desire, while practicing virtues such as sacrifices, austerities, and charity—is it not for one's own ultimate welfare to perform meritorious deeds by constructing temples, guest-houses, and ponds? 124.
Having heard this, he said: "This is indeed the common path of worldly men;

But alas, those laborers who cause distress are like farmers; they enjoy the fruit—which is comparable to a crop—of their actions whose nature is that of sowing seeds. || 125 ||

Temples, gardens, ponds, and the like—all such activities are obstacles to meditation. (126)
Action that serves as the cause for the attainment of fame is not the cause for the experience of eternal happiness.

Just so, the individual soul, from Brahmā downwards, due to its longing for sense objects, undergoes the suffering of birth and death.
Therefore, having abandoned all actions, one whose mind is dissolved in the indivisible light of consciousness [should remain].
One who possesses the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of constant contemplation upon Śiva shall attain the singular bliss that is free from all objective referents. || 129 ||
If one who is absorbed in meditation performs external rites, he may attain some slight increase by recollecting them.
For one should cover over the portion of the object of meditation, just as one covers over a field of grain and medicinal herbs when weeds have grown up.
The direct perception of the Cilligama-liṅga form, which is established solely through one's own personal experience.
Abandoning action, he who practices for the sake of its fruit is like one who, having covered his eyes, would fall into a well.
Even the meditator, when engaged in the performance of ritual action, will not achieve firm meditation due to the absence of a steadfast mind.

I do not know how that yogi, struck by death in the midst of his practice, will fare when he has fallen away. Then, having heard this, O learned Gurunātha, Rāma asked: "How does a mortal in this world transcend death?"
"Tell me, if there exists even a subtle path by which he might live, speak of it to me," he said. (133)
And the Lord said: "It is like sowing seeds of grass in a well-tilled field during a time of moisture."
When the mind is steady, having abandoned attachment to ritual action, one whose vision is fixed solely on reality cannot be harmed even by fate.

This instruction on reality composed by the illustrious Siddharāma is firmly established;
even Brahmā and the other gods, though they may be celestial beings, are never at any time capable of causing it to waver. (135)
Moreover, it is the established conclusion of the scriptures that no ritual system on earth, if even slightly deficient in its constituent parts, yields any fruit whatsoever.
Furthermore, an image that has been consecrated according to the prescribed rites becomes devoid of enjoyment for the deity due to defects of deficiency or excess. (136)
Having understood this, who that seeks liberation would cling here to the ritualistic portion (karmakāṇḍa) of the Veda, once they have discerned the nature of its merits and defects?
If one who is entangled by pride in the Vedas remains fixed in ritual action, there can be no attainment of the Supreme Reality for him anywhere.
For every living being, there is this duality of "internal" and "external"; yet the internal state of all is to be known solely through universal experience.
The wick of the lamp of consciousness shines forth unerringly, while the entire external world of false proliferation is seen [as mere appearance];
therefore, having shattered the outward-flowing movement of the heart, let the mind be directed solely toward the wick of the lamp of consciousness.
O Siddharāma, listen, O Siddharāma! A treasury of wisdom should always be intent on the practice cultivated within the path.

Indeed, the movement of the heart-wind is twofold—external and internal; here, that which pertains to the external is called *recaka* (exhalation), while that which pertains to the internal is called *pūraka* (inhalation). These two reside in the abode of the heart-lotus.
One should perform [the rite] when [the breath] has dissolved. || 140 ||
Having reached the peak of Mount Meru by means of the central channel, through which the two winds have been obstructed by practice, the yogi—
He who beholds here the supreme light, the divine Liṅga in person, is indeed the most fulfilled one, the Great Lord himself. || 141 ||
Just as one smeared with poison does not meet death even though it has reached the exterior, so too [the soul] does not die despite its attachment to the contact of external sense-objects.
Just as one who has drunk poison cannot be protected by a snake-charmer, even by a Brahmin, so too is one who experiences the objects of the senses.
O Rāma, who indeed has not become a means of accomplishment here by failing, out of delusion, to abandon objects that lead to endless suffering?
Having achieved [their goal] as if it were a fault, those of evil intent fall from both sides, like those who have lost the radiance of a yoga-gem.
Those who, being tormented in the midst of the fierce forest fire of saṃsāra, have come for refuge;
For those who have attained the state of supreme bliss through yoga, the craving for wicked sense-objects is no longer appropriate. || 144 ||
And who, indeed, do not assume the guise of a yogi—wearing saffron robes, carrying water-pots, and so forth—merely to fill their own bellies?

Indeed, they deceive others by means of mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like; nor is it even proper to converse with them, for their senses toward sense-objects are poisonous, yet they have abandoned them of their own accord, even though those objects were not to be relinquished.
The Śiva-yogins, having accomplished their purpose and being absorbed in their own bliss, do not fall into a state of deficiency. || 146 ||
The Instruction on Reality composed by Śrī Siddharāma-yogin:
Like a lordly elephant fallen into the mud, one must rely firmly upon one's own strength alone.
One who has risen by himself may take refuge on the bank; who else could be able to rescue him? || 147 ||
O Rāma, although your delusion of passion and darkness has been destroyed by Śiva-initiation, you remain [as such].
Alas! Having abandoned your own inner path, you have instead set out upon the external path of ritual action.
Having reached the culmination of the Nigamas and Agamas, you here renounce the systems of ritual action.
O noble Rāma, attain liberation immediately by conquering the enemy that is the cause of humiliation. 149.
In this world, knowledge and ignorance are the two causes of liberation and bondage respectively.
Devotion is knowledge, while action is ignorance; indeed, liberation is said to be non-action. || 150 ||
When karma is destroyed by knowledge, liberation is indeed already realized as spontaneously established.
Like gold upon the neck, let there be no doubt whatsoever regarding this matter. || 151 ||
If a man of knowledge, while attached to action, gives cooked food to a dog;
The fool, due to a lack of discernment, indulges in the foul-smelling excrement of a sow. || 152 ||

O Rāma, he who offers the entire collection of objects to the face of the Liṅga, partakes of them while intent on offering their essence, and attains freedom from action through that grace within his heart—he alone is known as the Lord of Māyā; what more need be said here? 153.
When all the senses are strong, one should then set one's mind upon conquering death, free from delusion.

O Rāma, one who is devoted to meditation and concentration, having cast aside the external world, abandons delusion regarding worldly powers, relinquishes all ritual action, becomes free from artifice, and— through constant practice of dhāraṇā— attains transformation into the Self which is Being, Consciousness, and Bliss, remaining firmly established in the Self.
Having realized the unity of the two aspects of Śiva and the individual soul, become one who is supremely stainless in form, O Siddharāma!

Having made this mind, which was crowded with thousands of fluctuations, the resort of a single fluctuation, and having firmly established it upon that pure liṅga of the vital breath (prāṇaliṅga) which is devoted to the Desired One; |||

From the understanding of the categories of the relationship between the sign and the body, and from the union with the oneness of the words denoting that relationship between the sign and the body.

He alone is the yogi, not merely a teacher among teachers; this is the well-ascertained meaning of all the scriptures. || 159 ||
Siddharāma is fully [qualified] by his mastery over the crookedness of the chapters on the systems of the Vedas, Agamas, and Shastras.

Having spoken thus, the preeminent guru, out of compassion, fashioned there a curtain of consciousness.
Having seated him upon a seat, he initiated him in secret and made him one who had fulfilled his purpose.
Then, having wiped away what was written on the plow-blade with his own foot, he drew lines with ashes.
Placing his hand upon the head, he purified his body with a glance.
Having instructed Rāma in the divine Śrīśāmbhavī mudrā and having fashioned his body of consciousness through piercing (vedha), [he departed].
Having awakened him— who was devoid of body, senses, and so forth— by uniting [him] with the Liṅga, the Compassionate One made his heart immersed therein;

thus the Lord gave him this beneficial instruction on the ultimate unity of the individual soul and the Supreme, which in an instant attained a state of firm stability within his heart, like the essence of light itself, consisting of his own pure consciousness, as if it were an image enshrined in worship.
Then, the swan [the mind] quickly took delight in that mental lake; sporting there, he attained complete satisfaction.
O Rāma, having transcended the path of the newly blossoming cakravākī birds at the limit of the suṣumṇā, he obtained the bliss of the sky of consciousness.
Then, having attained internal meditative absorption and tasted the incomparable bliss within his heart— the state of abiding in oneness with Śiva—
Siddharāma [proceeded].
Forgetting everything external, he spent some time by the grace of the Lord in the supreme ocean of nectar.
Furthermore, having gone outside to his own cherished *liṅga* resting in the palm of his hand, he attained the *asuliṅga* from that abode of true being (*sadbhāva*).
Having contemplated the vision and the bliss of abiding experience, he fell with joy at the feet of the Lord in the form of the Liṅga.
With eyes filled with tears of joy and his limbs covered in horripilation, he beheld this entire world as being of the very nature of Śiva.
Then, bowing with devotion and trembling with impetuosity, Rāma spoke to the Lord with his palms joined in reverence: || 168 ||
Through the power of serving the nectar of the lotus-like feet of Your Honor, the perfection of the yoga of Śiva has been attained.
The entire dense darkness of ignorance has been destroyed; here, the flame of the lamp of wisdom shines within my mind.
O Lord, Sovereign of Teachers, I am purified by your supreme compassion; indeed, today the fulfillment of my heart’s desire has been attained.
O sole kinsman of the three worlds, I have been brought under your power; O Kinsman, this bondage of mine is not caused by my lack of understanding of my own innate arts.
The auspicious benedictory verse composed by Śrī Siddharāma-yogīndra:
The Siddhas have arrived to witness the dialogue between the Lord Siddharāma and the ascetic (Yamī).
Having vanished at that time, they all thought thus in their minds.
O Siddharāma, where indeed has all that arrogance gone from within the matted-haired ascetic?
By what path has pride departed—pride that grinds everything down and is so unbending? || 172 ||
Where indeed has the desire for action been subsumed, and likewise the longing for fame?
Where was she previously withdrawn, and where now is she impatient? And how, in an instant, has she become relaxed? Oh, what a marvel! 173.
Or rather, the greatness of association with the virtuous is the cause of all accomplishments for men.
For the virtuous indeed regard association as medicine, since this person has accomplished his purpose through association with the Lord.
Then the Lord, having affectionately embraced Vinaya, who stood with palms joined in reverence, said:
He himself graciously bestowed boons with sweet words and a compassionate heart.

May purity of mind, steadfast devotion to Śaṅkara, stability in knowledge, complete perfection in yoga, the fulfillment of all desires, physical perfection, and the attainment of the compassion of the gurus be yours, O Siddharāma!
Thus, having bowed his head before the supreme Lord Allālaman, Rāma commanded him to grant his desired success;
then, thinking "So be it, my purpose is fulfilled," his mind became immersed in the ocean of the nectar of bliss, its state of being one with Śiva fully realized. || 177 ||
Thus, O lords of all sages, the wondrous life-story of Siddharāma, which bestows the desired objects upon the ears, has been narrated to you.
In this world, those who recite and remember [this] with joyful minds, the Lord bestows upon them an abundance of their desired success and happiness. || 178 ||

Salutations to Śrī Nandikeśvara.
In the Śrī Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, within the *Prabhu-liṅga-līlā*,
here begins the fourteenth chapter.

Those whose lotus-hearts are intent on meditating upon the lotus feet of the venerable Vīreśvara Siddha, the Great Emperor of Teachers, are devoted to the worship of the venerable Liṅga, their wandering gurus.

May the virtuous hosts of devotees—free from the wicked transformations of their senses being bitten by passions, seeking true enjoyment and liberation, and devoid of negligence—hear the divine play of the Lord. || 1 ||
Having repeatedly heard from wise men about the true devotion of the lord Basava, the Master,
his inner mind filled with the density of contemplated majesty, was deeply satisfied and longed to see him.
Then, having departed from the city of Svarṇalikā accompanied by Rāma, who was filled with faith in his own abode, he went to that city known by the name Kalyāṇa.
Along the way, there were groves of *nāra* trees whose inner sanctuaries could not be reached by the unrestrained rays of the sun,
and groves of *panasa*, *āmra*, *pūga*, *kadalī*, *jambīra*, *jambū*, and *vaṭa* trees.

Beholding at every step ponds, wells, and lakes with surfaces like palmyra, aśoka, kapittha, and pāṭala flowers— some resembling others and some beyond compare— as well as irrigation canals, he proceeded on his way.
He has separately laid out pleasure gardens, ponds with lotuses, rivers, rows of sugarcanes and plantains, and groves of jasmine, kunda, kurantaka, and other beautiful flowers.
Furthermore, beholding groves of rudrākṣa, agaru, coconut, badarī, and kharjūra trees, he proceeded, attended by masses of breezes from the mountains of cool sandalwood. || 4 ||
On every path, amidst the flower gardens, the breezes blow from all sides, dispelling the fatigue of travelers.
They served their master with the very slow, sweet fragrance of sandalwood from Mount Candanādri,
and with fragrant, cooling *uśīra* roots prepared and fashioned into the surface of the altar smeared with musk.
There, on the path, there would be beautiful and wonderful sights that bestow joy upon the hearts of travelers.
At intervals along the way, there were spacious Dharma-halls and settlements situated at various points on the road.

The sacrificial halls and water-stations, filled with food and the six flavors fit for consumption, shone wondrously; likewise, the play-pens and rooms for children, filled with jars of fresh butter and milk and hundreds of swings, nourished the infants and made them happy, and then [the mothers] themselves remained there.
Having eaten the pure food of their desired elixirs and having tasted that water, the travelers rested comfortably, reclining upon couches in the great forests.
For those who cherish sincere friendship, there are always sounds of affectionate greetings for groups of guests at the times of dawn, midday, afternoon, and evening, as well as during the nights.

In every forest, at every step, were heard the sounds of those who were satisfied with whatever food they desired for their sustenance, protected by the kingdom established by the Lord Basava; the sweetness of their polite speech cannot be described.

Or is he the very embodiment of dharma, having himself become the greatness of the fortune of Śrī-Bhāvasa’s form upon the surface of the earth, dispelling the Kali age and establishing the primordial Satya Yuga?
The virtuous soul himself immediately bestows the attainment of happiness in both worlds upon all those whose natures have been cleansed of defects through the worship of his own lotus feet. || 10 ||

Thus hearing that incomparable river of the guest’s speech, the all-pervading Lord beheld the splendor of the religious tradition of that Basava-clad man and contemplated it as a festival for the eyes.
Excellently describing her auspicious qualities with a voice full of bliss, he praised Śrī Basaveśa with great reverence, exclaiming, "Alas, alas! Such is the divine majesty! || 11 ||
Out of joy, the Lord sang his incomparable fame while shaking his head;
as if speaking from direct experience, he performed a dance and offered praise on all sides.
Presenting [the gift] to Rāma step by step, he praised him from within, saying, "O crest-jewel of the devotees of Lord Śiva, you are more devoted than I," and so forth. || 12 ||

The greatness of devotees cannot be described even by the mouths of the Grandfathers (the gods); there is not the slightest difference between the devotee and Śiva—the devotee is indeed superior to Śiva.

Since he himself is the bestower of liberation even upon his devotees, this very one is the essence of existence, consciousness, and bliss; he is Dharma, Śrī Basaveśvara, the teacher of all, and the wish-fulfilling tree of Vedānta. || 13 ||
Thus instructing Rāma in his incomparable devotion to Basava,
the Lord returned to the city known by the name Kalyāṇa, the abode of auspiciousness.
Within two krośas of the area outside that wall,
the Lord saw there, on all sides, dense and beautiful flower gardens.
The Lord beheld those floors paved with emerald gems, radiant with the flowers falling from the Aśoka trees, which resembled rows of pearls and jewels strewn about.
Furthermore, Arjuna beheld a multitude of noble trees, foremost among them the *mandāra*, as well as the *anaṅga*, *niṣaṅga*, *raṅgada*, *tulasī*, *snigdha*, *āmra*, and *mālūra*. || 15 ||

The Lord of the teachers of the glory of the three worlds went clearly to that wonderful Kalyāṇa grove, which was filled with birds such as parrots who had mastered the conclusions of all the scriptures.
O Lord Śrī Śambhu, O Śiva, O Śaṅkara! He heard from all sides the constant and loud chanting of those proclaiming the supreme Brahman as Sound (Nāda): "Śiva! Śiva! || 16 ||
They brought joy to the swarms of bees with their humming sounds, as if reproaching them by saying, "Is it not your skill in attracting fragrance that makes you the 'bearers of scent'?"

In that city of Kalyāṇa, children of the desert wandered about, their hearts longing for the sight of it after their journey's fatigue; they were like dense clouds of fragrance drawn from all flowers, as if from groves of camphor and plantain trees.
At every step there were yoga-monasteries for those seeking the path of *haṭha*, and in every monastery were groups of disciples preeminent in virtue;
with every virtue they contemplated the scriptures of Śambhu, causing great joy in the heart of their Lord.
The Teacher of the World himself favored with his very eyes such a treasury of all that is auspicious.
That Lord [reached] the city of Kalyāṇapura, which puts even Indra to shame and possesses lofty golden gate-towers.
The preeminent chariots, horses, and elephants of the sun-like king proclaim his lofty height of vast *śāla* trees; others do not.
The gate known as the Blazing Tiger’s Mouth acts as a source of terror for herds of hostile wild beasts. (20)
Since the mountain of the gods (Meru) yearns for the sight of Śiva, his city acts as a dwelling-house for Hara.
He stands gathered there under the guise of the lofty arches of a palace with golden, shimmering door-panels.
Having entered through that gate and passed beyond that host, he enters with circles of well-bent streams, free from fear.
Alas, the people, though accustomed to going out, are as if new to entering back in! 22.
Even Bṛhaspati would not be able to describe the fortune and splendor of that multitude of market streets.
When its rising heaps of jewels that scrape the heavens laugh at Mount Meru, which was bent down by the Lord of the Mountains.
By him the Kali age was made to be called Kṛta, and that city was protected for a long time by Vasu.
Oh, it is impossible to describe the form of that lord of the earth; it is clearly manifest as if it were the very pinnacle of sublime devotion.
For it is not possible for opponents or adversaries to enter, since that moat is difficult to cross.

O you of faultless fame, they say that the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence is *śravaṇa* (hearing), the establishment of the reasoning for that meaning is *manana* (reflection), and that which concerns the *liṅga* of Prāṇa and is primarily focused on the qualified (*saguṇa*) aspect is called *dhyāna* (meditation).
This indeed was the previous yoga concerning the realm of phenomenal expansion; now I shall tell you the supreme Uttara-yoga-tantra.
O Basavārya, listen to this sacred teaching regarding its practice: they call the fourth state "reflection," while the seal of silence is "listening. (22)
But meditation is a state free from qualities, stainless, and changeless; it is eternally borne as fruit within the symbol of the Supreme Self.
The junction is firm, the intellect is steady—oh, this sacrifice of recitation has been performed; such as I am, worship that alone, the singular, perfect samādhi. (23)
Having made this triad of speech, body, and mind completely one-pointed through intense concentration upon the form of the dense *liṅga*,
and knowing that this is the secret sanctuary for meditation, the devoted person who meditates therein attains the Supreme.
Independent. || 24 ||

For one who is devoted to the worship of the *liṅga* that is his own Self and intent upon its adoration, the three principles—the Guru, the *Caryā*, and the *Iṣṭa-pada*—reside within his own interior. Furthermore, all the means of accomplishment (*sādhanas*) are present right here, characterized by the practice of the water from the feet of the Lord’s grace which shines forth.
Having fully worshipped the *Paramātma-liṅga* through the multitudes of means consisting of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), he [attains the goal].
Having cast aside the triple-city of the battlefield of the senses,
for one who enjoys only bliss through the state of identity with Śiva— the supreme reality arising from the union of the Liṅga and the Aṅga— what need is there for external tantras? (26)
O Basavārya, he who does not know the divine *liṅga*—which is situated within, consisting of consciousness, higher than the highest, and supreme—does not know me.

Having established external actions within the Supreme Self, one should seek the inner purification free from desire; for the *liṅga*, the *jaṅgama*, the Guru, the most excellent, His grace, and the water from His feet are present in their fullness within the inner self.
One who desires the state of ultimate reality should worship [the Lord] as long as his own cherished Liṅga does not shine within the hollow of the hand. 28.
One who has understood the meaning of the categories as correctly taught by the Holy One, who has cast off disease and other afflictions, who is equanimous toward himself in both praise and blame,
and who remains unchanging in both suffering and happiness— such a devotee, possessing this equanimity, O Vasava, should worship Him for liberation from the bondage of worldly existence.

The five senses are the gateways for the mind’s wandering among sense objects; having restrained them by the power of dispassion and withdrawn [the mind] from those [objects], this devotee fixes his heart upon the mark of the Supreme Self and remains in unwavering samādhi. || 30 ||
As long as the movement of the mind does not cease, one does not realize the nature of the Self; therefore, devotion is for the sake of attaining Śiva.
The instruction on the reality of the Prāṇaliṅga was given by the Lord [for this purpose].
One devoid of devotion does not go to Giriśa, nor can one see Him without being eager to behold Him; indeed, without that, one does not attain liberation.
Just as a horse attains steadiness through the restraint of the reins, so the mind attains steadiness through the restraint of the vital air (vāyu).
By means of that restraint of the vital air, the hero among Śaivas, with his mind restrained, reaches the primary cause residing within the body on this earth.
That which is called *māyā* is the mind, or rather the transformation (*pariṇati*) of the mind; that wind became the supreme body, and it itself constantly afflicts the body.
Nowhere does it tolerate the sprouting of the tender shoot of devotion, nor its gradual progression.
If there were a conqueror of that [state] here on earth, it would be Basava; he is the foremost among devotees.
The mind is said to be the variegated bird; one's own two eyes are its feet, and the pair of winds situated in the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels constitute its three wings.
When the gaze is fixed on the two eyes, these are called *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
By means of immobility, the mind does not undergo fluctuation; therefore, it becomes steady. || 34 ||
When the mind has attained immobility, the incomparable jewel of consciousness (*cidbindu*) flashes forth;
once this [consciousness] has become perfectly stable, it triumphs over time, karma, and the like.
And its effect—this *māyā*, which is its root cause—is utterly uprooted.
O noble Basava, trust may perish; therefore, take full recourse in steadfastness within yourself. 35.
Having sown the seed that shines as food upon the site of the *liṅga*— the locus of the limbs— and having sprinkled it constantly with water along with the seven constituent elements (*dhātus*),
one causes the fruit of the tree born from that potent seed to grow until it abides in the form of the *bindu*.
He who, having given [his body] for the sake of its qualities, brought the Liṅga here—he indeed was one whose wealth was solely the Liṅga.

Having pierced the six cakras shining forth, beginning with the *ādhāra*, and having sequentially known the six locations (*ṣaṭsthala*) where the mind vibrates therein, the self-yogi [perceives] earth,
water, fire, wind, ether, and the mind through this practice.
Even after knowing these six, he whose mind is unmodified, who is full of devotion, and who remains detached; || 37 ||
O Sage Basava, there are six elements with the mind as the sixth, and a group of six deities;
likewise, there are six syllables of the pure, great Śiva-mantra, which are to be kept secret.
He who, having awakened within these six cakras, is capable of proceeding beyond them, has achieved his life's purpose.
Thus, he would have reached the further shore of devotion to the pure knowledge and liberation of the supreme Śiva. 38.
O wise one, I shall tell you the truth regarding the places associated with the Guru-Linga: the anus, the private parts, and the navel;
then above the navel, the heart, and the lotus of the throat—these three constitute the temple of the mobile Linga (cara-liṅga).
The very center between the eyebrows is known as Avimukta, and beyond that is the Brahma-aperture; these two together [form the immobile Linga].
Knowing that place to be the site of the Maheśa-liṅga, O Basavārya, the devoted one shall become a possessor of its grace. (40)
Having received the instruction on the reality of the *prāṇaliṅga* from the illustrious Basava Līlāśuka,
the noble disciple, having ripened that which consists of the *bindu* in the fire of the Guru’s radiant mouth,
should then offer it to the Great Lord’s *liṅga* in the presence of the mobile *liṅga* (the Guru) who has realized its true nature. || 41 ||

Having personally tasted and assimilated the remaining nectar of that [Supreme Being], casting aside all external flavors, the devoted Basavārya remained for a long time with his mind immersed in his own bliss, established in samādhi. (42)

The meritorious one who understands this state—endowed with earth, water, fire, Jupiter, Saturn, lightning, wind, and space; filled with the arrangement of the glorious moving world; possessing the union of mind and self; and endowed with the noble devotion to the oneness of the Śrī-liṅga—is truly fortunate.
This leader of the Śrīvaishnavas, who is devoted in the three ways, shall not exist at present. || 43 ||

One who abides in earth, water, and land is burdened by karma; one who abides in fire, wind, and space is a devotee; and one whose mind is endowed with the state of ether possesses excellent knowledge—enough of this!
Having understood this, and having ascended to the station of the Great Lord (Maheśvara) and other such states, one crosses over to the Supreme.
O Basava, he who attains the stainless state is to be known as the teacher of teachers. || 44 ||
Having understood that the place of power (*śaktisthāna*) is the pair of the secret parts and the *apāna*, the place of devotion (*bhaktisthala*) is the pair of the navel and the heart,
and the place of the digit of liberation (*muktikalāsthala*) is indeed the pair of the throat and the space between the eyebrows;
having thus known this, and having abandoned even the quality of power while embracing firm devotion—
The noble Basava, who knows the true nature of reality, shall himself attain incomparable liberation after that. 45.
If one knows the Self by oneself through the Self alone, then the power residing in the Self,
devotion to the Self, and liberation— which has that as its cause—
shine forth within the Self; for that [Self] is the very Self which exists by means of the Self alone.
O Basavārya, may the bearer of the liṅga, the foremost among devotees, be honored in my heart. || 46 ||

Thus, having bestowed the incomparable instruction on yoga— which was perfected through the secret rites of the eastern and western traditions, and which is suited to the practice of mudrās and the visualization of the peerless seat— the Guru Allama Prabhu spoke further to the lord Basava.
Constantly cultivating within yourself an uninterrupted devotion, never separating from those who know the Self and are endowed with reason, perpetually enjoy incomparable discourse;
do not cast your mind, which sustains your livelihood, into the downward stream, but direct it along the upward path.
Having quickly gathered [them], bring this stainless place with firm stability. || 48 ||
Abandon all anxiety regarding the divine liṅga; stabilize your vision within your own self alone, and enjoy the sovereign splendor of the wave of oneness with supreme nectar.
Now, do not forget the reality taught by our words, which you have already ascended to.
Now I shall declare to you its incomparable essence, the great reality of the oneness of the Liṅga.
Where those filled with devotion for the lotus feet of the Lord dwell, always engaged in conversations that calculate His incomparable majesty and yearning for His shore—
having gone there, through the core instruction on the path of devotion to Him, [cross] existence...
O noble Basava, I shall go playfully to wipe away [your sins] so that you may attain liberation. || 50 ||
Thus, while all the hosts of Gaṇas were listening in the assembly, the Lord of the Gaṇas, overflowing with compassion,
said to Basavanātha: "O most excellent sages, worship the union of the Prāṇaliṅga and the body."
And you are steadfast in meditation upon the lotus feet of the Lord. || 51 ||

He who recites with supreme devotion this true life-story of the Lord— which is the essence skilled in revealing the union of the soul with the *prāṇaliṅga*— or who, being firm-minded, retains it even after hearing it from the mouth of a wise man, for him [liberation] becomes exceedingly easy to attain.
The bliss of the unity of the vital breath and the *liṅga*. || 52 ||
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Path of Contemplation upon the Prāṇaliṅga," within the *Prabhuliṅgalīlā*, which is the extensive narrative of the venerable *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*.
Salutations to the venerable Nandikeśvara.
[The Nineteenth Chapter] Sūta said:
Those who worship the lotus feet of the Siddha Śrī Guruvīranātha are free from worldly desire.

May those who have attained perfection, whose natures are freed from the defects bound to the increased elements, who are blocked from the burden of the qualities of passion and darkness (rajas and tamas), who have realized the reality of the Self as Consciousness, who have placed their faith in the discourses on liberation, and who are connoisseurs of devotion— may they listen to the divine play of the Lord. || 1 ||
Then the Lord, having favored both the lineage of devotees and Basaveṃdra with his compassionate glances,
spoke these beneficial and concise words, desiring to depart.
"O leaders of the Gaṇas headed by Basava, a desire to go to the earth has arisen in me;
therefore, you too should fix your minds firmly upon the contemplation of the Self as described by me. (3)

O best among those who know the Self, spend your time with the heart fixed on the realization of the state of supreme reality, through the constant sequence of worshiping the Guru and the Liṅga, and through festivals consisting of the company of the virtuous.

Thus, making them experience [this truth] through the surging waves of the ocean of nectar-like words, the Lord was saluted by the Gaṇas, whose eyes were filled with tears of joy and who were marked by the sprouts of horripilation. || 5 ||

At the time of his departure, the Lord of Amanaska bestowed a blessing upon Allama, Basava, and the others: "O best of practitioners, having instructed Siddharāma and Sanmuni—who are endowed with humility—go to the city of Suvarṇalā; depart! Thus he spoke, and in an instant he departed.
Having followed his followers who had come with him and were now devoid of any desire to return,
the Lord stood for a long time on the path and, out of compassion, spoke to those who had taken refuge at his feet.
In order to protect the hosts of devotees on earth without exception by means of our timely grace, we have descended;
where do we not dwell, like the lord of day?
This slight effort on my part is for your sake, for I am unborn and stainless;
indeed, in the practice of contemplation, there is no agitation regarding external union or separation of the mind.
For I alone am the moving form; there is no difference between the moving and the stationary sign.
Therefore, having entered my moving form, worship it, and very soon you shall attain union with me.
Thus contemplating the minds of his devotees, which were perfectly composed, the Lord thought:
"May your devotion to Bhava be exceedingly powerful; may this be my blessing for you. || 11 ||

And having approached [them], the Lord uttered words of blessing: "May you, having attained eternal truth and constant service as attendants of the mobile Liṅga, become those who have fulfilled their highest purpose. (12)
Having turned back the lords of the Gaṇas, Basava, and others of equal majesty, the victorious Guru, whose sole intent was to protect his devotees, proceeded toward the northern direction. 13.

And the Basava ascetics, having shaken off the quality of passion (rajas) through the remembrance of the True Guru, returned to their homes and once again became intent upon the worship of the mobile liṅga, even more so than before. 14.
Constantly composed in their expectation of the Lord’s return, the Gaṇas remain, passing their days with the utmost longing for the Master. 15.
Thereafter, as the Lord King proceeded along the path, he beheld with his keen vision the mountains;
these were like the Golden Mountain (Meru), possessing divine wish-fulfilling trees, creepers, and shrubs.

The oceans were filled with nectar, the lakes were excellent in their touch, the lands were mines of jewels, and the sons of the earth (trees) bore fruit of their own accord; thus the world itself manifested a wonder of supreme qualities. || 17 ||
Then, having heard that their lord had arrived, those residing in the region, filled with deep devotion,
came forth together with the sound of musical instruments, carrying sacred ashes, fruits, and betel leaves.
The Description of Śrīśaila: The ocean of compassion, bowing at their feet and experiencing the identity of the Liṅga within his heart,
graced them with his favor and departed for Śiva’s assembly, engaging in conversations that were exactly as they should be.
Wherever the Lord stayed on the road together with the devotees of Śiva,
there he was greatly filled with the sound of celestial kettledrums along with a rain of flowers.

Having sipped the waters of that lake, which were as essential as nectar, they remained there for one day; indeed, that plot of land became a sacred field for those who dwell upon it with self-restraint.
Traveling along the path with the sound of his excellent bell, the Lord Prabhudeva clearly beheld the renowned Śrīgirirāja, the abode of the Supreme Lord, which bestows all spiritual perfections.
Indeed, even the Lord of Serpents is unable to praise his immeasurable virtues;
yet Parvateśvara himself shone forth, his sovereignty manifested through his ascetic penance.

In that [science] where the alchemy of mercury, the suppression of sexual emission, the attracting of the world, and medicinal collyrium are found—whereby invisibility, subjugation, and all such powers are accomplished—for the practitioners of mantras, [that is the supreme science]. (24)

Indeed, there exist therein the root of all wonders in the world, the action that restores life through nectar, the foremost of medicines, and jars of the essence of ambrosia for the perfect accomplishment of all goals. (25)

Bestowing the foremost of perfections—the celestial cow, the treasure-vessel, the wish-fulfilling tree, and the thought-gem—it is the glorious mountain alone that reigns supreme on this earth by virtue of its incomparable status in the Śiva-āgama. (26)
Indeed, the trees dance like creepers at the majesty of the Lord of Mountains;
the rocks laugh, and oh, the trees speak, saying, "We are exceedingly nourished and bear fruit quickly! (27)

The great lakes situated upon mountain peaks bestow physical perfection upon men through the drinking of their waters; furthermore, by bathing in them, one especially attains the recollection of past lives on this earth.
Abandoning mutual enmity, he who causes wonder among herds of variegated deer moves constantly upon the peaks of the immovable king of mountains, manifesting joy to the eyes of those who behold him.

There are also the various peaks of the king of mountains which he ascended with the thought that they were horses; those peaks quickly carry one to whatever radiant place is envisioned by the mind. (30)

O wonder! Upon the king of mountains, there shine everywhere countless divine caverns that reveal the paths to the netherworlds beginning with Atala, through which multitudes of living beings enter without even blinking. 31.
The meeting of Allama Prabhu and Gorakṣa and their exchange of inquiries regarding welfare:
O supreme practitioners, what need is there for much? Are you perhaps prepared to achieve [your goal] on this earth?
By approaching the King of Mountains and practicing with steadfastness, you shall obtain your desired object.
Then, thinking that there on that mountain dwelt one who had attained all perfections and was indeed a master of every yoga,
the Lord arrived there, reflecting upon the sage Gorakṣa in his heart.
Like nectar to one afflicted by disease, like the life-restoring creeper (saṃjīvanī) to the presence of the dead, so was the presence of the Primordial Lord.
The Lord, whose mass of merit was strengthened by the arising of the wealth of excellent knowledge, quickly reached the presence of Gorakṣanātha. || 34 ||
Seeing that deity arrived, this sage Gorakṣanātha, filled with agitation and reflecting upon his own welfare,
rose with palms joined in reverence and prostrated himself, performing worship with the offering of water for the feet (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), and other honors.
He smoothed it over with the essence of his words on discipline. || 35 ||
Having seated him upon a grand throne, [the king], bowed low with great devotion, asked: "O Lord, from where have you come, or to where must you go today?
What might be the reason for your arrival? Please tell me, O abode of compassion, for your coming today is due to my good fortune"—having heard these words, which were consistent with propriety.
Having swiftly cast aside his illusion and desiring to favor him, the Lord, the God, spoke to him with words preeminent in their abundance.

O Gorakṣa, we here on earth, terrified by birth and death, wander incessantly according to the methods prescribed in the Vedas and Āgamas, in order to establish those most excellent practitioners— whose limbs are composed of dense consciousness— by means of the nectar of the teaching on the realization of the identity of the Liṅga.

Reflecting thus upon these words of the Prabhuliṅga-mūrti, which expressed the ultimate truth through worldly speech, he thought within his heart: "Or perhaps this is the Guru Gorakṣanātha, who recognized me long ago. (39)
And he asked the Lord: "O Sinless One, I do not clearly recognize your form as it was seen before;
for you appear otherwise, neither in your ancient dress nor in your speech. I do not specifically know your natural appearance."
The commentary. || 40 ||
"Let the discussion regarding internal discernment rest for now; rather, having somehow understood the external, one is indeed fit to worship.
For in this world, people call him 'Allama'. Having realized this about him, Gorakṣa suddenly spoke with a lotus-face full of laughter.
How could he who, due to a burden of darkness, does not even know his own self, know the heart of another?
How could he who wanders from house to house on earth, oppressed by hunger, ever give food consisting of crushed herbs? (42)
The Lord’s symbolic words to Gorakṣa:
"What can be accomplished by a blind man even with a mirror held in his hand? Likewise, what can be achieved when the pair of eyes remains fixed on the external world?"
O friend, for one devoid of the eye of discernment, what common fruit is there other than the mere wandering among sense objects like a beast? 43.
For those rogues are solely intent on displaying their verbal cleverness; how could the weight of their awakening ever arise?

Like the doctrine of the body being the self, they appear to think that the body alone is to be cultivated. With a deluded mind, they hold that as long as the body of these beasts remains stable, liberation is most easily achieved; for when the body is ever weakened, it certainly is not.
The means to liberation is the attainment of that [divine] body; because this attainment is superior, those who know the truth declare that the contemplation for its sake is the Kāpālika doctrine.
This [body], drenched in filth and urine, is filled with skin, flesh, marrow, blood, bones, veins, and fat, and is loathsome to behold.
How could there be a sense of devotion to one's own teacher in a Kāpālika who has formed the conceit "this body is mine"? (46)
Having heard the exceedingly noble words spoken by Allama, Gorakṣanātha spoke again to the Lord:
"O Great-souled One, listen to the rule of the Siddhānta, by which practitioners attain the bliss of perfection."
For one whose body becomes steadfast through the power of perfected practice, even illusion would not dare to touch him; Death himself stands before such a person of sublime power, struck with fear.
His body attains the state of imperishability at will, yet we do not know how to speak of this web of words.
"We shall show you the accomplishment of that body; look!"—being thus addressed, the Lord spoke again.
"O Gorakṣa, what do you say regarding the stability of the body? Can there be permanence when only residual power remains?
How can that Māyā be conquered? Or how can liberation be anything other than the absence of death?
Indeed, all created beings are perishable; it is declared that only the Immutable (Akṣara) is the Unchanging (Kūṭastha)."
The Lord of the perishable and the imperishable, denoted by the word Hara, will bring the goddess of liberation to that person who possesses devotion to Him.
"Therefore, do not believe that your body is indestructible; through delusion, you think your body will not perish.
Seeing the Lord who had spoken thus, Gorakṣanātha suddenly said to him: || 52 ||
Abandoning this discourse of many kinds, quickly take up your sharpened sword;
exerting all your strength, plunge its blade into my body here.
In the examination of the attainment of yoga, the dialogue between the Lord and Gorakṣa:
"If even a single hair on my body were to break off, then there would be no perfection of the body;
nor would I be a perfected one in this world. I speak the truth—behold a sign immediately! (54)
Observing Gorakṣa speaking thus, the Lord said: "Indeed, they declare that testing [the disciple] by means of cutting, piercing, and so forth, is demonic; that doctrine is not approved by our Guru."
If this limb of yours were to be severed, then who on earth would possess spiritual accomplishment?
Is such speech born of true discernment, or is it the path of the True Dharma, or perhaps the state of death? (56)
"If it is said that the self is not touched by such states as death because of its association [with the body], this should not be spoken thus in the presence of those like us.
Thus addressed, the Lord Gorakṣanātha spoke again:
Having immediately dispelled my doubt, strike this vajra-body of mine!
There is not even a trace of destruction for me by your sword; reveal my own spiritual accomplishment.
"Please fulfill this desire of mine; my heart will not be satisfied except by the stroke of a sword's edge"—thus was he pressed by the forceful yogin. (59)
"Let his mind not be impaired; I shall firmly plant my sword in his body.
If he should die, pierced by my blade, I shall release another lord of the Gorkhas."
Thus the Lord, having accepted the sword offered by him and seeing that it was sharp, made it keen;
then, firmly grasping its hilt and blade with his fist and brandishing the edge, he struck him on the body.
From the terrible sound of that blow’s thundering resonance, the earth shook and the multitude of mountains trembled.
Not even a single hair on his body was severed; it remained as unharmed as a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
The Lord said to the ascetic: "This is not true accomplishment; it is merely an illusion that causes your body to become entangled in the manifold world."
Indeed, it was accomplished in vain that this word "rarāṇa" exists, for here death is truly as its name implies. || 63 ||
"What is the use of a thousand words? To claim that perfection of the body is achieved by conquering death—that is a false rumor.
Thus saying, Allama let go of the sword-hilt held in his palm and struck him down.
Laughing upon the earth. || 64 ||

Alas, how can these supernatural powers (siddhis) result in the calamity of universal dissolution? Time exists for everyone through the various methods of valid cognition. Listen, I shall tell you that reality which is designated by the term "attainment of the body" (kāyasiddhi); it is the secret essence of the crest of the Vedas.
The account of Gorakṣa’s sword-strike upon the Allama:
He who is unafflicted even by wind, heat, fire, thunderbolt, rain, or frost; whose divine body is free from disease, old age, and death;
and who, through the intellect that abandons all attachment, has ascended to the perfect *samādhi* of the Self as Lord—he alone is a true yogi.
He who has conquered the elements and their qualities, whose heart is unattached to external objects of touch, for whom a lump of gold and a clod of earth are equal,
and who— though seen by the physical attributes of the body— is not affected in his heart by them; he alone is truly filled with the perfection of the body.
The yogi. || 67 ||

Seeing his Guru, the Lord Gorakṣanātha, speaking thus, the sage reflected: "This is some unique channel of speech for him; today, having tested the firmness of his resolve, I shall honor him for his greatness."

Seizing that well-sharpened sword and expert at brandishing its rising blade, he swiftly pierced the form everywhere with dexterity of hand, moving left and right like the all-pervading Lord whose movement is in the sky.
Struck by that [arrow], the Lord’s body became as beautiful as the sky, its form remaining unaffected even by slight injury;
seeing it silent, peerless in luster, and devoid of any sign of agitation, Yama wandered about again in many ways. (70)
Leaping up, falling upon his head, and even upon both his feet, he stood by his side,
and with his arms and the pair of his hips,
moving with a variegated gait everywhere while wielding his brandished sword, he struck at the joints of [the demon's] body hairs.
The extension of the hand. || 71 ||

Like a bird previously unable to remain motionless in the expanse of the sky due to its pair of wings trembling violently, he leapt into the air, then descended again, and after leaping once more, moving sideways, he finally attained steadiness. (72)
Realizing that this was a great marvel and perceiving his immense majesty, the best of ascetics, bowed down with fear and devotion,
cast aside the sword held in his hand, struck his own pair of cheeks, and spoke: || 73 ||
If you, our guru and master, were not to grant such incomparable perfection to this body, for what ascetic in this world would it take on such a form?
And yet, this greatness— which creates wonder throughout the universe— is not merely this much.
It bears the fruit of the supreme non-duality proclaimed in the Vedānta. || 74 ||
This body of mine has been swiftly shattered by the sword; with a thunderous *khaṇiti* sound, it has crushed the very walls of the cosmic egg.
This is Gorakṣa’s repeated plea to Allama:
"O Lord, this body of yours shines like the sky; why is it now so silent? Tell me! (75)
The King of Gurus said to Gorakṣa: "Listen attentively! When the body becomes solid, that Māyā also becomes solid.
