When both of these have become thoroughly solidified, the shadow of phenomenal proliferation (prapañca) becomes stable; how then can this perfection of the body ever occur?"

Therefore, when one casts [the body] out from the heart and the shadow of the body perishes, then indeed this accomplishment, characterized by absolute liberation (kaivalya), becomes manifest; thus it is said. Having bowed once more, the yogi spoke again to Allama:
"O Ādinātha, O sovereign lord of my causal instructors, grant me this incomparable secret of accomplishment."
I was not aware at all that you had arrived, having favored me with your graceful speech and attire out of such great regard.
"O Lord, forgive my transgression today out of compassion; I am your servant," he said, and fell at his feet.
Raising him up, the Master made his heart unshakeable and filled with the experience of Śiva, and then spoke: || 79 ||
Just as iron shines forth through the process of smelting in a crucible, so too does the attainment of the fruit occur through the ripening of dispassion.
When he beheld Gorakṣanātha with eyes of grace and benevolence, O Lord, his passion vanished;
and along with that very passion, all its other manifestations fled from him.

At that moment, the great afflictions headed by stinginess, hypocrisy, and pride vanished through conversation; his ignorance and arrogance departed, and illusion fled at the touch of his hand upon his head.
Supplicating the Lord, that ocean of boundless compassion, the supreme ascetic Gorakṣa said:
"O sole kinsman of the world, I am blessed by even a mere touch of the pollen from Your lotus feet; yet today I ask for something more.
O friend of devotees, command me toward the highest goal, for true bondage is the attainment of the state of a Siddha through the perfection of the body. (82)
Thus favoring him who was making such a request, he, appearing in the guise of one seeking the welfare of others, nourished his satisfaction with a stream of nectar-like words.

O Gorakṣa, good man, listen! What is the use of much speaking? As long as the self does not abandon attachment to this illusory body, physical perfection will not arise; for a living being, knowledge alone is indeed no means at all [to achieve that]. (84) If the heart has the resolve to attain both physical perfection and liberation, these two true means must be acquired together.
In the examination of the perfection of yoga, there is a dialogue between the Lord and Gorakṣaka:
"Therefore, having abandoned the paths of both [worldly life and asceticism], worship with devotion the lotus-feet of the illustrious Guheśvara;
just as a devotee intent on the story of cooking [firewood] obtains relief from the cold, so too may you obtain all perfections at the feet of Guheśvara."
"By serving him as instructed by my guru, I have attained perfection; having reached this state within my heart, the yogi said to his guru:
'O Master! O Lord of Guha! Who is this unprecedented being you have mentioned? Where does he dwell, what does he sport, and of what nature is he?'"
"By what method here should I worship him? Tell me," he said to him with humility; and he replied to him: || 87 ||

O Gorakṣa, listen: there is certainly no one else in the three worlds who is denoted by the word Guheśvara other than I. Be free from doubt; let your mind follow the stainless path, and meditate on me alone, for you are ever absorbed in the Self.

He conceals His name; indeed, I, the Lord, always dwell within that place which is the abode of the Supreme Self. This name of Mine is "Ku-hana-nṛ-mūrti" (the one who dwells in the heart of all beings in the form of a deceptive human). For the sake of the welfare of the wise, I move everywhere as a virtuous being; therefore, those who worship Me with devotion know that I abide within the hearts of all creatures as their Beloved.
Between me and those of pure intellect there is no distinction; always contemplate me as being thus within your heart. (90)

All this conceptual proliferation of illusion is "this-ness" (idantā), while the individual consciousness (jīvaciti) conditioned by association with that is "I-ness" (ahantā). Having dissolved this duality through that [higher] I-ness into the state of Śiva, which consists of the perfect I-ness (pūrṇāhantā)—
"Stability" refers to meditative worship. || 91 ||

Thus, those on earth who are devoted solely to bhakti and remain constantly engaged in worship attain liberation while living (jīvanmukti). Therefore, worship Guheśvara with the realization that he is your own self, and you shall attain absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Addressed as "O Budha," he replied: || 92 ||
O Noble Lord of Guha, if you are indeed fully saturated with the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the inner spiritual sciences (*adhyātma-śāstra*), why then is this *liṅga* upon your body?
Is there any real distinction for you, who are the stainless, attributeless light of consciousness (*cij-jyotis*), other than that created by delusion— a distinction which serves only the base?
To Gorakṣa, the Guru said: "I am the non-dual One, who has assumed a physical form out of a compassionate gaze toward my devotees;
I carry the Liṅga of Consciousness and Vital Breath (cit-prāṇa-liṅga) in the palm of my hand.
While this is practiced by the most excellent ones, let other people here practice what is appropriate for them."
For the sake of benefiting the world, I wander about wearing an external, desired emblem; yet by that much, no duality exists for me.
This is the dialogue between the Lord and Gorakṣaka regarding the examination of yogic perfection.
They joyfully proclaim the union with the unity of the *liṅga* of the supreme divine light, which flashes forth both within and without, through their own [spiritual] attire.

For the sake of the world's welfare, I previously composed ten million verses for those who possess supreme detachment from consciousness and devotion [to worldly things], which sever all bonds of doubt; these have been clearly elucidated as a compendium of the essential meaning of the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and auspicious Āgamas.
Those who hear this here attain liberation through the gradations of their practice, their minds cleansed of sin; for he,
bearing various kinds of weapons, has indeed arisen on the earth from the training-ground as a practitioner of means for the sake of helping others.
In the same way, O Yogins, these [worldly things] do not serve my purpose for the sake of breaking through the immobility of dress, speech, and conduct appropriate to the occasion.
Just as the mental disposition of each person is, so do I swiftly prescribe the path of liberation for them;
likewise, although I possess dress and speech appropriate to the occasion, in reality these do not belong to me, who am stainless.

O Gorakṣa, I assume the yogic mudrā appropriate for seeking refuge in order to sow the rows of excellent seeds of devotion and the awakening of Śiva within the field of the hearts of all my devotees, both those attached and those detached; therefore, how could there be any talk of difference between me and you? (100)
If one harbors conceptual constructions in one's own mind, such as "Who has come?", "Where?", "How?", or "What?", how can there be devotion for Him?
Realizing that "everything is in Me," one who is immersed in the nectar-ocean of the bliss of Śiva should practice supreme devotion.
Devoid of the fragrance of virtues. || 101 ||

O Yogin, just as the notions "I am that" or "this is that," and likewise the sense of "I" and "mine," do not arise even in the slightest degree of egoism, so do I abide in the manner of a lotus leaf amidst water, experiencing perpetual stainlessness.
I am indeed considered by those who are established in the realization of the union of the *aṅga* and *liṅga*, through their discernment of the six planes (*ṣaṭsthala*).
Having abandoned all attachment and attained the state of oneness with the perfect Śiva, I become that very Consciousness, for they are composed of consciousness.
Of them. || 103 ||
"This is my majesty; there is no doubt in this matter. If you have any [doubt] today, examine it and then enter into meditative absorption.
Having spoken thus, his heart dissolved into the Linga that shone like lightning within a dark blue cloud, and he then became absorbed in concentration.
Then Gorakṣayoginī desired to take the *prabhu*-hand-liṅga; seizing it forcibly with her hand, she imparted the instruction on the reality of Allama to Gorakṣa.
It became something that could not be touched nor even seen, appearing like the sky itself. With a mind filled with wonder, she said to the Lord:
Afraid. || 105 ||
O Lord, Your greatness is unknowable even by the Vedas; who then, possessing such meager intellect as I, could fathom it through study?
Who would seek to find parity with You by examining the teeth of an elephant? Therefore, O Master, favor me with beneficial instruction;
for a disciple is to be tested by an excellent and true Guru, but never a Guru by a mere young disciple.
"You must be examined.

Therefore, O Lord and Guru, protect me with the Śiva-initiation. Thus praised by Gorakṣanātha, the Lord of the Imperishable (Akṣareśa) then, out of compassion, granted him initiation in order to bestow internal grace, employing a hundred thousandfold methods of instruction.
Having examined him,
he instructed him— who was now free from the dullness born of the fetters of supernatural powers— in the reality that is devoid of attributes, which bestows liberation.
O Brahmins, Gorakṣaka shone like fragrant gold by the mere instruction of his lord and guru;
moreover, satiated by drinking the nectar of the compassion of the ocean-like [guru], he immediately rendered all supernatural powers (siddhis) insignificant.
Having destroyed illusion and conquered the qualities of his own body, and having gradually swallowed both the gross and the subtle,
he then remained in the causal body and cast off the delusion of a vajra-body, his form now being a cloud of pure consciousness.
He is the yogi. || 110 ||
Gorakṣaka, having immediately acquired knowledge from his lordly guru through compassion according to the analogy of the bee-insect,
shone as one liberated by the attainment of the non-dual realization of the Supreme Śiva; though still living, he had turned back from the false phenomenal world.
Having cast off attachment and being liberated from the bonds of worldly existence by those still in the world, and having taken upon his body the emblems prescribed by Śiva,
this supreme ascetic Gorakṣa remains even today, taking refuge in the subterranean realm (Rasātala).
Endowed with devotion to Śiva. || 112 ||

Thus, O foremost sons of Bhṛgu, you who are firm in your vows, the conduct of Gorakṣa—which was rendered capable by the Lord through the initiation of Śiva at the glorious Girīndra—has been drunk in by the hollows of your ears; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Therefore, maintain a fervent longing for it.
Listen! 113.

[Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Account of the Bestowal of Grace upon Gorakṣa," within the *Prabhuliṅgalīlā*, which is the extensive narrative of the *Śrībhaviṣyatpurāṇa* according to the Ṛṣis.
Salutations to the illustrious Nandikeśvara.
[Now the twentieth chapter.
Sūta said:
Those who have taken refuge in the glorious Siddhas and Vīras, and who possess bodies that are both Liṅgas and Jaṅgamas...
May the hosts of sages who seek liberation listen to the divine play of the True Lord. || 1 ||
Thus, by imparting the instruction on the essence-knowledge of Gorakṣanātha,
he brought [him] to the state of having accomplished all that was to be done and bestowed upon him the rank of Siddhanātha.
Then, having been honored with hospitable offerings by that man endowed with faith,
he departed from that hermitage and went elsewhere, O brahmins.
The Lord beheld upon the lap of Śrīgiri the Pātālagaṅgā, the sole purifier of the world, with its restless waves, the bestower of auspiciousness.
On its bank, he beheld before him a great hermitage of sages, most venerable due to its blessed inhabitants, resplendent with rising leaf-huts.
It was exceedingly beautiful with various trees, foremost among them the mango, breadfruit, jackfruit, dates, arjuna, kesara, and kimshuka.
In that meritorious hermitage, tigers play together with deer;
mice kiss the faces of mongooses, and they in turn are kissed by them.
There, the elephants constantly form friendships with lions,
and the young parrots engage in playful jesting with cats.
Peacocks and serpents dwell together here;
others of opposing natures live as if they were of the same kind.
Seeing the Lord arrived by that path,
the Brahmins went out to meet him and felt in their hearts, "We have achieved our purpose."
The sages, having worshipped him with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and other honors, seated him upon a lofty throne,
and having praised that one worthy of praise with hundreds of hymns, spoke to him.
O Lord, O Omniscient One, it is indeed by our good fortune that we have obtained the sight of you;
may we all be protected by you, who perceive the ultimate goal.
Having examined Gorakṣa and having bestowed initiation upon him, they have made him well-protected;
knowing this to be so, they are now eager to see you. 13.
O true Guru, we have been dwelling here constantly awaiting your arrival; from that time on, our hearts have remained filled with longing.
This auspicious arrival of yours here is a favor to us;
indeed, our ascetic penance has borne fruit this very day—please show us your grace.
O ocean of compassion, having instructed us in the secret meaning of reality, please favor us sages, who are tormented by worldly existence, by accepting us as your disciples. (16)
"Let there be a conversation with Ālamba together with all the sages.
Thus entreated by all the munis, the Lord, his curiosity aroused, became gracious of heart, desiring to show them favor. (17)
For those who pray with self-restraint, the Lord takes the divine jewel of the mind situated within the ocean of the body, brings it to the state above [the head] called the *liṅga*,
and having polished it well upon the whetstone there, produces the supreme light of knowledge.
With the piercing of the vajra-needle called Sanniṣṭhā, he made an opening in its [the mountain's] side. || 18 ||
Having here aligned the stainless thread of the intellect, warding off its flickering instability,
and having transcended the distinctions followed by "I," "this," and "you," he established that [thread]—
previously unknown among the clusters of objects— flowing westward toward the ultimate goal.
Having caused the lords of sages, who were blissful through their contemplation of the Praṇava, to become silent, Allama spoke.
Without understanding this action called "neither white nor black" within the heart, one does not obtain the grace of Śambhu, the Lord who is the dancer in the sky of consciousness. (20)
Without the grace of Maheśvara, the inner self is not purified;
O lords of sages, without internal purity, delusion does not perish. (21)
Without abandoning the delusion of the mind, one does not deserve the knowledge of Śiva;
for without that, there is no liberation, as established by scripture, reasoning, and direct experience. (22)
Having heard that, he was requested by those best of sages for initiation into Śiva;
having rendered them all fulfilled, he spoke these words again.

O lords of sages, the kīlaka appropriate for the practitioner for the sake of liberation through isolation (kaivalya) is the constant state of remaining with focused attention on the unity of the individual soul with the Liṅga within the heart. 24.
Having thus given his command, the Guru Allama, honored with devotion by them,
saw before him as he proceeded a great forest ahead.
Its interior was impenetrable even to a mere fraction of the sun’s radiance,
for it was a dense circle of trees woven together by thickets of creepers.
Its groves have become the pleasure-residences for herds of elephants;
therein roam lions, tigers, rhinoceroses, and other wild beasts. (27)
While traveling on the road, being attended even by those animals, the god saw ahead a hunter who was cruel and harsh in appearance.
He prepared wooden hollow-traps, tiger-carts,
and strings knotted with cords, as well as packs of hawks, brown herons, and dogs.
Likewise, [he saw] rabbit-traps, nets, and Yavanīpa cloths; [this was] Allama’s instruction for the hunter as he, possessed of great strength, was bringing various other implements for the hunt. (30)
With a single feathered arrow, this hunter swiftly struck down hosts of deer whose eyes, ears, thighs, and limbs were like vessels, and who moved along variegated paths.
Like a lion [slaying] elephants, and likewise like a śarabha [slaying] lions,
he killed them in many ways with his arrows, just as a predator kills deer.
Like a hunter who is Time and Death itself, he effortlessly struck other living beings one by one with a single arrow in the forest.
Beholding that form of a rākṣasa, Mallama thought to himself:
"By him, this multitude of living beings has been slain; he is now a guest of Death. (34)
"Having observed and then disregarded [him], how could we possibly proceed with this task?
He must be restrained and favored; such is his cruelty," he then said. (35)
"Alas! Why is it that, having abandoned this internal pleasure of the hunt, you have gone out to pursue external game and are thus needlessly afflicted in many ways? (36)
Merely by hearing the words of the Lord, his sins were destroyed by that very sight;
an exalted thought arose within him, for such is the power of association with the great.
Endowed with supreme devotion, having cast aside his weapons and joined his palms in reverence, he bowed at the lotus feet of the Lord and spoke out of joy.
"O Ocean of Compassion, having instructed me in the bliss of internal hunting, please fulfill my purpose"—thus entreated, the Lord spoke to him who had prostrated before him. (39)
The body stands here as a forest; the deer named "ego" flees from it, while the mind, intent solely on devouring that deer, binds the senses with its fetters.
Then, with the eye of sublime knowledge, one leads that deer into the circular snare of breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having taken up the bow of fortitude, one should become a hunter of discernment, skilled in piercing its target. || 40 ||
Having fixed that arrow of "I-am-ness" upon the string of the bow, he discharged it;
having thoroughly cooked that wealth of knowledge in the fire of Dhanañjaya (the Conqueror), he offered it to Śiva.
Having instructed him, saying, "Eat this," that most excellent true Guru caused him to do so.
In an instant, he turned Kirāta’s heart into a whirlpool submerged in the ocean of the nectar of bliss.
Having thus shown grace to the Kirāta, the Lord then descended from Śrīparvata and, proceeding on the path toward the region north of it,
purified all those whose prior impurities had been diminished by the sight of his own lotus feet. (42)
Those who were servants of Kāma— proud women whose playful glances were fixed upon the weight of their breasts and who were greedy for the pleasure of passion—
even they, upon beholding that Lord, became inclined toward discernment and attained a happy rebirth through true honor.
They indeed made their request. || 43 ||
He gave various instructions to people from many different regions who had come to him;
and Allama, too, by virtue of awakening the power of the inner Kuṇḍalinī, [bestowed grace] upon that fortunate young woman.
He instructed them thus: "O you who are filled with detachment from social circles, whose hearts are immersed in the bliss of blossoming spiritual play,
and who wander wonderfully upon the earth seeking the perfection of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)— restraining that divine nectar consisting of your own *bindu*,
cultivate within yourselves that firm bliss of accomplishment."
The Blessed One is the inner self of all without exception.
Requested by others for the mastery of the alchemical elixir (rasaghuṭī), the Lord, with a smiling face, declared: "The elixir itself is the drop;
the breath that has ceased its movement is the peerless medicine; one's own mind is the crucible; and the fire is indeed the state of Maṇipūra—let them understand this!"
Through steadfastness alone, by the power of its maturation, that very *unmanī*— the elixir of nectar—
has clearly become self-realized. Having attained it, the very acquisition of the station above Hara, Maheśa, and Sadāśiva is indeed this innate perfection (*nijasiddhi*).
Eternal. || 47 ||
Having thus instructed the people of the earth in the essential truth and protected them, Allama then departed;
proceeding further, he beheld elsewhere an excellent hermitage of sages, fully supplied with wild fruits and flowers.
For those who have taken refuge in the one who wards off fatigue. || 48 ||
Dense with all kinds of trees— such as the mango, sandalwood, wood-apple, rasāla, sāla, mālūra, and campaka—
and surrounded on all sides by those who observe the vow of truth and have performed their daily, occasional, and other prescribed rites,
there the cuckoos sing sweetly from the mango trees, calling out to guests as it were with their warbling.
Come from all sides and drink, you who possess unbroken happiness, my essence-filled juices of excellent bulbs, roots, and fruits. (50)

"Restrain your thirst with floods of pure water; come here! thus do the flocks of swans, ruddy geese, rathāṅgas, krauñcas, and other birds appear in the lakes, summoning one another with their charming cries. (51)
As those aged and eminent ascetics proceed toward the rivers and streams, holding onto the hands of monkeys for support,
the parrots follow behind them, their own wings dense with blossoming plumage, seeking only shade.

In that place, herds of rutting elephants dispel from all sides the sweat of the swarms of hissing serpents— fatigued by being struck by the masses of matted locks of the lords of sages emaciated by asceticism—
by fanning them with the deceptive fans of their own ears.
A description of the forest-dwelling beasts serving the sages:
Having seen those established in most formidable vows, such as month-long fasts, who were rendered motionless by their steadfastness in posture,
tigers would approach from behind and stand at their backs for the sake of strength.
The great ones, whose bodies were carried upon their own backs. || 54 ||
Beholding the sages performing austerities amidst the five fires, the multitude of stars,
bowing with humility, brings water filled in their hands and sprinkles it all around them daily in his presence.
Then, where aged sages who have restrained their speech stand with hands raised in the desire to tie the girdle of munja grass,
the clear-sighted bears approach them, tear apart the darbha grass they hold as it is being used, and place it directly into their palms.
And there, the swans, having divided the clusters of lotus stalks with their beaks,

pull out the exceedingly fine fibers and offer them for the purpose of making sacrificial threads (*yajñasūtra*) consecrated by the Lord of Sages, imbued at that time with the sentiment of awakened devotion.

Where, among the students who are lazy about gathering sacrificial fuel, the sacred fire might go out, even the flock of old monkeys brings fuel there and personally places it upon the fire, making it blaze with the scattering of their own fine grass.
In that place, where sages who have severed the bonds of karma attain the yogic sleep of Śiva through their skill in concentration,
the lions dwell constantly near his leaf-hut solely for the sake of protection.
Being vigilant. || 59 ||
Where he recites the three Vedas, clearly practices the comprehension of their meaning, and articulates them with his speech; there,
amidst the assembly of learned men gathered for the study of logic and other sciences, the flock of parrots repeats after him on all sides.

It shone with the chanting of the *Sāmaveda* raised by those who delight in the meaning of the *mantra-āgamas*, with the tantric proclamations beginning with *śrauṣaṭ* and *vaṣaṭ*, and with loud cries such as "Anoint!", "Perform!", "Adorn the creeper of the auspicious occasion!", and "Prepare the purification of the *arghya* and other offerings!"
Furthermore, having honored those guests who have arrived at the time of the midday heat, you should devoutly offer them pure, delicious food; and saying,
"Offer what is desired to those observing vows," you should honor the monks— let this be heard here by the young students with great respect.
Speech. || 62 ||

Deer draw away the limbs of those sages whose bodies shine with Rudrākṣas and ashes and who are absorbed in most wonderful internal austerities; and female and male parrots drink the tears from their eyes of joy. (63)
Upon seeing the sages, a reflection arose in Allama’s own mind:
"Beholding such a beautiful forest of sages, Allama felt compassion for them and thought:
'Alas! These people perform actions that involve great effort yet yield little fruit; they act in vain, like those wearing ornaments made of iron.'"

Having abandoned villages and houses and dwelt even in great forests, yet failing to perform meditation upon the lotus feet of the Lord, those devoid of awakening— though subsisting on grass and leaves— should practice the abundant rituals of sacrifice and the like.
They proceed. || 65 ||

Or is it that in these terrible forests they have no pleasant dwellings for their beds, seats, and food; that they have no lovely silken garments for clothing, but only most coarse bark—alas, this is a hardship!
And that they do not wear radiant ornaments studded with jewels, but only rosaries of rudrākṣa seeds and lotus seeds?
They shall possess the fragrances of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and other primary scents, brought about by the prosperity resulting from their lifelong performance of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
What indeed can be accomplished by these through terrible asceticism, resorting to trees, lakes, and the like, merely to allay hunger and thirst?
Having experienced the happiness of the celestial realm, they have returned once more to earth; will they not fall again?
Illusion. || 68 ||
Indeed, one who knows the reality of the self as illusion must first conquer that [illusion], for without understanding the divine arts (kalās) that serve as its means,
a person of delusion will only further tighten his own bondage through the extremely formidable fetters of dull and excessive karma.
What is their [nature]? || 69 ||

If bathing three times a day were the cause of liberation on this earth, would fish and other aquatic creatures possess liberation? If worldly existence could be destroyed simply by bowing one's head, then what is the difference between such a person and a piece of lac?
Released from bondage. || 70 ||
Is it by mere silence that illusion is conquered here? Does not the heron remain silent to catch fish?
Has one studied all the scriptures in vain? Do parrots not recite everything they have learned, yet without following what has been uttered [by the wise]? (71)
Or does one who is intent on subsisting on air alone attain liberation on this earth? Do serpents not indeed devour air as well?
If that were so, then this Māyā would never depart from one burdened by the dullness of karma; for without that [air], there is no awakening.
Indeed, without knowledge, there is no liberation even through hundreds of ritual acts; and without the removal of *māyā*, there is not even a trace of awakening.
For *māyā* is indeed action (*kriyā*); thus, failing to understand this due to haste, one wanders in delusion.
Those who lack discernment follow after ritual action, being inclined toward it. || 73 ||
The instruction on reality for the sages was as follows:

"Just as a child standing on the bank of a pond must be taken up by one filled with compassion, so too these sages who desire liberation must be led by me and favored through the method of instruction on reality. Having observed them, the Lord spoke thus to them.
O sages, why this distress? There is no end to ritual action despite its great effort yielding fruit.
I shall tell you an easy means for the attainment of liberation; listen with faith.
By the power of fortune, that which was spoken by me [has been heard]. || 75 ||
Having heard the words of the Lord, those sages, filled with longing and desiring auspiciousness, then entreated him:
"O Noble One, command that which is for our own benefit, for we are your disciples; [teach] the sole means to liberation. Thus the Lord spoke.
Furthermore: || 76 ||
By whatever method one may practice non-violence (ahiṃsā), which the wise declare to be the primary means for attaining liberation—
that very act of violence inherent in ritual action must indeed always be abandoned by you, O best of Śiva-yogins. (77)
Those who currently harm the multitude of living beings in this world—Yama truly destroys them thereafter;
therefore, by casting off this dullness born of such karma within your inner self, I shall declare to you the unfailing core of the practice of wisdom and action.

The ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is declared to be the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) prescribed for the internal sacrifice; the filling of the vital breaths (*marutpūraṇa*) is said to be the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); this mind, which is consciousness (*vijñāna*), is the fire (*agni*) and the nectar (*sudhā*);
the lunar juice of the *soma* plant is the host of cups (*grahagaṇa*); and these are the wheels of the *suṣumṇā*.
That very self, being the sacrificer, shall attain the desired fruit, which is the singular accomplishment of liberation. || 79 ||

Having thus eradicated their karmas— which were composed of the realization of being pervaded by the Inner Space (Antarmakha)— they further received initiation from the Lord Guru through his compassion; with the doubts in their hearts shaken off, they became firmly established in the sacrifice known as knowledge, which is filled with the stainless yoga of Śiva.
Having transcended the snare of illusion, they rejoiced in the eternal ocean of supreme bliss.

Having fulfilled all rites— the twilight prayers, recitation, study of the scriptures, deliberation on the teachings, steadfastness in yoga, the fire-sacrifice, Vedic study, and the worship of the Noble Ones— within the Supreme Śiva, those sages are perfected, their minds fixed solely upon internal inquiry.
They became. || 81 ||
Beheld by the side-long glances of the Lord’s compassion, they were instantly freed from their bonds and became solely devoted to the tradition;
having realized that the deity is indeed Paraśiva, those wise ones performed worship once more and spoke to him.
The lords of sages. || 82 ||
O best of gurus, at the time of the manifestation of Māyā on earth, when all the duties of the sages according to the Vedas had been undertaken, you alone— dwelling within the cavern of our hearts—
protected us from the praise of the Lord offered by the sages;
this too is well known to us as being exactly like Durvāsas.
"O Supreme Person, by serving you, liberation in non-duality is held in the palm of one's hand; fortune is not the cause here.
Thus being praised on all sides by the sages, the Lord then gave his consent.
He became hidden within himself. || 84 ||

Then once again, in order to protect his devotees, the venerable Guru himself appeared here and there, constrained by the singular devotion of the virtuous; at every step, he instructed practitioners in the worship of the mobile guru and the Śiva-liṅga.
He moved about. || 85 ||
Those hosts who, with the approval of Tripurabhid, were thoroughly acquainted with all affairs on earth and possessed of ancient wisdom,
obtained birth here in the lineages of Brāhmaṇas and others; having received the authorized Śiva-initiation, they [sought] their Lord.
Having attained [it], they were joyful. || 86 ||
"This family of ours, the Pramatthas, is purifying and maintains the Śiva-initiation that protects the world; there is no difference whatsoever in this regard.
Even though it is *akula*, let it be worshiped before all *kulas* by virtue of the honey [of devotion]," so said the God of Gods.
Those who have received the initiation of Śiva, who are unattached to other worldly activities, who bear the burden of protecting the world through the beautiful duties of the householder’s life,
and who possess firm and supreme dispassion— such are those who follow the path of the Yati-dīkṣā according to the tradition of the Munis.
"They come into being," he said. || 88 ||
For the sake of worshipping the Śivaliṅga, which is dearer to him than his own life, the Lord commanded them daily to perform all physical labors to acquire every necessary object;
having thus freely ordained duties suited to that end, He made this entire world Vīraśaiva.
Even while engaging in worldly affairs, may this lineage of my devotees— having shaken off all defects through meditation upon the lotus-feet of my own feet—
conquer that state of darkness rooted in the heart and become established in the worship of the Śiva-liṅga, which is the supreme teacher.
The watchful one. || 90 ||

Having thus instructed them in the teaching of the reality of his own self according to the method beneficial to the Śiva-doctrine, the Guru inwardly favored them. Thereafter, with his permission, they became supremely virtuous, their devotion constantly increasing.
They became [thus]. || 91 ||
O Śaunaka and other lords of sages, this entire life-story of the Lord-Guru has been narrated to you for the sake of favoring practitioners.
The Lord bestows even greater grace upon that person who recites it with supreme devotion at the conclusion of the worship of Śiva.
It grants the desired object. || 92 ||

[Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Course of the Description of the Grace Bestowed upon the Seekers," within the *Prabhuliṅgalīlā* of the *Śrībhaviṣyatpurāṇakathāviśālā* composed by the Sage.
Salutations to Nandikeśvara.
[Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Those who were intent upon worshipping the lotus feet of the venerable Siddheśvara Vīra-deśika heard that great secret of devotion as it was taught by that Guru.
Nandīśa, known by the name Basava, has occupied that empty lion-throne;
let those who are connoisseurs of this listen, for the Lord’s pure consciousness is his play—let it be contemplated. || 1 ||
Then, in this city of Kalyāṇapura, by the great instruction of Lord Allama Prabhu, he became possessed of the abundance of creative intuition.
Having abandoned the path of worldly involvement (*pravṛtti-mārga*), that Basava became one whose sole essence was the path of renunciation (*nivṛtti-mārga*). || 2 ||
Then the splendor of his dancing with the enemies of desire and the like was shattered, and his pride in his virtues dissolved.
The senses of perception have fallen into intoxication and dissolution; likewise, the eight types of pride have been shattered and fled.
The six waves, filled with fear, are unable to remain here, and the fortitude of the organs of action has been struck down.
The agitation caused by the six transformations of existence has departed from him, and his mind remains the same toward both praise and blame.
In the meantime, his internal practice reached the pinnacle of excellence through the constant and devoted cultivation of the auspicious yoga of Śiva.
Through the grace of his guru, who had conquered all obstacles, there arose within him an abundance of contentment.
Then, having himself resorted to the inward-turned path, let him gradually awaken the Kuṇḍalinī.
In an instant, having straightened its crookedness, it went to the courtyard of the great house that served as its support.

Then, having struck down desire outside the door-panel of that [house], and having attained mastery over Time, he entered within; there, in the lotus of his heart, he became intent on uprooting the wandering of worldly existence.
Moving upward from there, having attained stability in the jewel-like *subindu* within the circle between the two eyebrows,
Basava long experienced within his heart the bliss of the sovereign empire of awakening through his own direct experience.

Then, having come under the sway of this yoga with attributes (saguṇa-yoga), he pondered for a long time within himself: "How shall I achieve the practice of yoga without attributes (nirguṇa-yoga)? When will the Guru come and grant me instruction? || 9 ||
When, by my good fortune, will the Ācārya of immeasurable and great power come to my home?
When, through the Lord’s instruction, will the cutting away of the doubts within my heart soon take place? (10)
When will such bliss, situated within my inner self, become innate through the power of compassion?
This is the commencement of the construction of the throne of emptiness;
how does the Lord of the Sky of Consciousness, whose nature is that of the Great Dancer, proceed by being without support? (11)
In what attire, in what language, from where, and in what form will the bearer of the lineage himself come?
Or rather, do I possess any reflection upon a virtuous means for his manifestation? (12)
"I must always remain vigilant"—this was the command issued by the Lord of the Ancient Self.
Relying on the application of virtues as taught by Anugraha, he made his very practice of devotion firm.
Having thus beheld within himself the manifestation of Śambhu as if it were a magnificent, auspicious throne,
and having visualized the supreme true Guru seated there, he worshipped him with the essence of true devotion.

Having visualized that [form] very firmly situated within his heart, he then prepared to have an extraordinary, single lion-throne made by a skilled craftsman for the sake of worshipping that true Guru externally. (15)
Bringing together a blazing heap of molten gold and a vast collection of highly precious jewels,
he summoned skilled artisans on earth who were experts in craftsmanship, having consulted with learned scholars.
By his command, skilled artisans fashioned before him a courtyard with a floor made of moonstone slabs,
as well as a series of steps composed of emerald, diamond, ruby, and cat's-eye gems.

Gradually, above that, artisans constructed with great effort high, soaring walls made of gold and jewel-studded rows; these broad walls of seven blazing enclosures were built separately according to the proper rules.
Within the intervals between them, rows of nine kinds of gems were fixed and firmly set, emitting a "dhagad-dhag" sound as they were struck.
This wonderful pedestal for the cloud of consciousness, fashioned by Basava, shone with a splendor unique and unsurpassed. || 19 ||
The city was beautifully adorned with nine gates on the outside, while within it shone four gates;
between those pairs of lofty gates lay another, and above them stood a single gate.

Having sequentially established the path of the six chakras— decorated with the secret signs of the genitals, navel, heart, the two pure eyebrows, and the middle of the forehead— they placed the wheel known as the *brahmabila* (the aperture of Brahma) upon the head of that [path].
They then positioned the spheres of earth, water, fire, air, and ether above and below, along with the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Soul (*para*).
They established the six primary *sthala*s of Subhakta and Māheśvara in due order within that excellent *pīṭha*. || 22 ||

He established hardness in the earth, fluidity in water, constant heat in fire, and motion in the wind; he described the arrangement of the empty lion-throne, as well as space in the sky and emptiness even within the Self—thus he made all things manifold. (23)
Iḍā is to the north and Piṅgalā is to the south, with Suṣumṇā conceived as situated in the middle;
indeed, just as the moon and the sun themselves move through those two, so do they [the breaths] flow.
In the city of Vidhi, the ground at the base of the palate shone, adorned with twelve excellent lotuses;
above its peak, the vast sky of consciousness gleamed, and upon it stood a lofty, magnificent lion-throne. || 25 ||
In the midst of the perfectly empty lion-throne, there exists the incomparable great tree known as Sadāśiva;
its root is the supreme Praṇava itself, while its divine and conscious five-syllabled branches are the creepers.
With its beautiful colors, its words bearing excellent fruit, and its sound being the flavor that grants liberation,
this great tree made of jewels stands resplendent, its trunk being the voice that bestows all goals.

Like a creeper clinging to this great tree, like the luster of the jewel upon the head of the lord of serpents, she shone forth as the self-luminous crest-flame of the immeasurable power of consciousness— the blossoming tree of the supreme reality of Śiva.
Oh, this Vasava himself attained all the means for liberation!
He caused these fourteen worlds to dwell within the great sky of consciousness, which transcends the five elements.
He caused a marvelous empty pedestal, praised by the world, to be fashioned above all the principles (tattvas);
and oh, how wondrous it was that he established all the deities in their respective places within that city.

Therein, the knower of the vital points (marmas) deposited all the channels (nāḍīs) along with the winds residing within them, together with Kuṇḍalinī and her powers (śaktis), as well as the excellent portions of devotion and the portions of action and knowledge.

The great refuge Basava himself constructed the temple in the three worlds according to his own vision, following the appropriate layout for the yoga of both seeded and seedless samādhi, as befits a supreme secret. 32.
"Let the wise consider this: there is no difference between the two eggs, the cosmic and the individual; let it be reflected upon by the virtuous.
Thus did this wise man cause his own inner self to blossom outwardly, and he was praised in this manner by all people. (33)
Beholding this great throne of consciousness, the divine means for the worship of Guheśvara,
which had been fashioned by Basava and established upon his own Self, he became satisfied in mind.
(34) Upon seeing the empty throne of Basaveśvara, [Basava] reflected:

"Whatever wonderful thing exists here in its entirety resides within the heart; having understood this through right method and intellect, one is capable of ascending [to the truth] by means of wisdom alone, and no other. Thus he thought, his mind immersed in bliss. (35)

"Only that wise man who, having come of his own accord to my abode, recognizes his own greatness and ascends to samādhi without fear—he alone shall be my lord; for this is indeed our means for awakening to one's true nature. (36)
Having thus made this vow, this Lord Basava, remaining firm as a practitioner of the vow while spending his time in the assembly of the wise,
demonstrated the pedestal of consciousness to the scholars who had gathered;
for on this earth, the Liṅga is the refuge of those whose home is the mind, and the Liṅga is the sweet voice of the cuckoo.
Śuka’s speech has its authority in the syllables he recited, but the authority of the Lord here lies in his ascent.
Just as darkness on the surface of the earth does not perish by the eye alone without the light of the sun,
so too this crooked illusion of mine will never perish without the vision of the Lord, the Supreme Controller.
Having thus reached this certainty in his own mind and awaiting the arrival of his preceptor,
that commander remained performing the worship of the mobile liṅga with devotion just as before.
At that time, some went to the residence of the lord Basava for the sake of food;
some, disguised as mendicants, were intent on begging; and others, devoted to courtesans, came even to entice Basava with appropriate garments, ornaments, and the like.
There is no fixed calculation for them; they exceed hundreds of thousands and tens of millions. || 41 ||

Not even one among them is able to see that stainless divine seat; when questioned about it, Basava clearly says, "I do not know. Therefore, how is this so wonderful? How can it be known to be thus restricted?
Speaking thus, he asserts that what is commonly seen in the world by people occurs without the knowledge of experience.

Or how could even Brahmā and the other gods ever know that incomparable, supramundane state whose seat is the sky? Only the foremost of the wise, Basava, or perhaps the teacher Allama, knows it by immersing their minds in many ways.
"Let the serpents themselves know his destination," so said all the mobile beings.

They are well-versed in mantra, in the dissolution of sound (nāda-laya), and in haṭha; they are empowered by the practice of yantras and tantras, likewise preeminent in the Vedāntas, and proficient as knowers of the six systems of philosophy.
A description of the longing regarding the arrival of Lord Basava:

Having seen the most wonderful celestial platform from afar and having offered their salutations, they spoke with nods of their heads, saying, "The majesty of Basaveśvara is difficult to comprehend. (44)
"Where indeed is my compassionate Guru’s abode, so that having reached it, the venerable teacher might ascend the charming celestial throne?
Thus thought Basava, the jewel upon the crown of the wise, who was preeminent in his steadfast devotion to meditation upon the stainless form of the Lord himself.
He became filled with longing within his own heart. || 45 ||

Thus has been told this unfailing greatness of the Śūnyapīṭha; O best of sages, he who always recites it with supreme devotion shall attain the accomplishment of all goals solely through the grace of the Lord Guru, and his devotion to Śiva shall be honored.
The fortunate one attains steadfastness. || 46 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Empty Lion Throne," within the *Prabhuliṅgalīlā*, which is the extensive narrative of the *Śrī Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*.
Salutations to Śrī Nandikeśvara.
[Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Sūta said:

O lords of sages, you who are devoted to the worship of the venerable sandals of the supreme teacher Śrī Siddhavīreśvara, listen to the story of the immeasurable Lord, the crest-jewel of ascetics, whose nature is bodiless (nirdeha). 1.
When her lord has gone far away, like a virtuous woman longing for fruit while bearing flowers, she—unable to endure the intensity of passion—dwells in anxiety for his return. || 2 ||
Thus, upon the Lord’s arrival, King Basava, experiencing joy and longing for happiness, his heart filled with devotion arising from seeded yoga, conceived a profound anxiety within his mind. (3)
Aha! I have fashioned this rising pedestal of consciousness, worthy for one to ascend.
Twelve years passed from then on, yet the high-souled Lord did not return.
My intense attachment to this lord of my life does not reach its end by any means;
having come here and cast aside the agitation of my mind, O Lord, where else will you show me mercy? (5)
Having thoroughly mastered the secret essence of Śiva-yoga through the Lord who resides within my heart as the object of worship, [I reflect:
"When will the Inner Self of all grant me grace? Or when will He bestow joy upon my heart? Thus is described the anxiety concerning the arrival of the Lord Basaveśa.

By the power of wisdom, my divine seat has been established; just as a king’s command is carried out by a loyal servant, how could the command of the Lord be in vain by not ascending to the realm of Ālameṇdra? Or rather, how could it be otherwise? || 7 ||
Thus reflecting within his heart that it was improper for him to remain outside,
he, steadfast in his resolve to assume the yogic posture, sought a secluded spot and restrained his vital breaths according to the instructions.
Having withdrawn the ten senses from their objects and having sequentially detached them from the gross body,
he, established in meditative absorption, fixed them in the extremely subtle state of the unity of the connection with the *liṅga*.

Since the stage of the seed-possessing state had been conquered by the Lord’s grace, the steadfast one attained the stage of seedless samādhi and became for a long time absorbed in his own innate bliss. || 10 ||

Through the constant experience of the bliss of samādhi, even at the time of emergence, he remained firm-minded, repeatedly becoming absorbed in meditation, [realizing] that the entire world is of the nature of the *liṅga* (the subtle body) and nothing else. || 11 ||

Once, having arrived at the time of his meditative absorption, the Lord— shining with a joyful mind— himself bestowed upon him, within the perfectly pure mirror of his inward-turned intellect, a manifestation whose nature was the stainless reality.
Thinking, "This is a great favor from the Lord," that commander-in-chief took those riches;
with his lotus-eyes filled with tears of joy, he became one whose limbs were marked by horripilation through devotion. (13)
Then the Lord Allama vanished; subsequently, rising from his union with the samādhi of true meditation, he became Basava, with his staff-like arms and eyes flashing with exceedingly powerful energy.
Having personally summoned his nephew, who was named Suguṇa but known by the alias Channa, and who was devoted to the conduct of the virtuous,
he clearly related to him what had been perceived through meditative concentration.

He who is unknowable even by the Vedas, scriptures, and other means—he is this supreme light, beginningless and primordial. Our Lord, the Supreme Śiva, has arrived; before long, that God will grant us joy.
Having thus heard that command, which was for his own benefit, this Basava, known by the name Channa,
became intent on going out to meet him, overcome by the nectar-like intoxication of joyful play.
At that very moment, the Lord, filled with longing, summoned all those laborers without exception and commanded them on every side to quickly prepare the city for his reception.
Having swept away the dust from the main streets on all sides, they adorned the city; thus they performed the purification of the auspicious city.
Having honored it with the sprinkling of scented water, they likewise scattered flowers everywhere. (19)
Upon the palaces, mansions, gate-towers, walls, as well as on the watchtowers and archways,
they prepared a defensive array consisting of rows of banners rising like mirrors atop golden finials.
Having heard of that festival from all sides, the citizens, having smeared the courtyards of their respective houses with musk-water,
decorated them with pearl festoons.
Having adorned the walls with various lattices and installed everywhere golden staffs radiant with jewels, they fixed blazing lamps upon them all around the series of canopies.
Likewise, rows of pearl necklaces with clear clusters and strings of gems were arrayed.
In the center, the wealthy ones arranged rows of small round mirrors within the interiors of the canopies. || 23 ||
They adorned the gates, which were resplendent with pillars shining like plantain trees and featuring thresholds of Jāmbūnada gold,
with beautiful jeweled archways complete with sprouts, in a manner never seen before.
In every house they hoisted lofty banners, and along the streets, with the sounds of musical instruments,
they erected jeweled archways in such a way that not even a single ray of the sun could pass through.
On all sides, with rows of blossoms and sprouts shimmering with a swaying, sweet fragrance, and with strings of jewels;
And with incenses and fragrant musk ointments, they fully adorned the market streets in the city. || 26 ||
This auspicious king of cities, delightful with all excellent virtues and cherished by Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, became an object of longing for the foremost among the immortals. (27)

A great festival took place in the house of that lord of Basava, like that of the lord of Sudharmā; by the sounds of the Gaṇas crying "Hare! Hare!", the churning of the ocean was rendered insignificant.
"Then my Lord Ālva will arrive; alas, when? With whom? In what manner?
I do not know at present which street he will come by"—thus did Basava reflect within the lotus of his heart. (29)
"It is not proper to remain in the hall; the devotees must quickly come forward to receive him.
While he was thus being urged by the entire assembly, that Lord of the Rod (the King) departed from the hall, his mind fixed upon Vallabha.
Basava went forth to meet [the Lord] together with Maṇivālanātha, Śrīmaccayārya, Varakinnara, and Saṃyami;
accompanied by Sacchanna and Vīrabasava, he was attended by the venerable Prabhuliṅga, who was a master in the offering of his very self through *haṭha*.
This is the description of Basava’s reception by the Lord.
Surrounded on all sides by hosts of attendants mounted on elephants and horses— some of whom were not distinct from him in heart, while others numbered beyond calculation—
and accompanied by Bhaṇḍāri, Vīrabasava, and throngs of kings of immense wealth, he set forth.
On the back side. || 32 ||
Attended by nine other chief ministers equal to himself in rank, and by throngs of soldiers, Magadhas, and bards,

he proceeded while his prose and verse panegyrics were being chanted; he went along holding his two charming lotus-feet, while being honored by men of lofty stature with bright staffs in hand, who were well-acquainted with the relative distinctions among the various lords of the earth.
"Or rather, proceed! Stand firm with vigilance! And likewise, move far away!"—such were the words spoken.
He was being attended by those intent on warding off the crowd, with rattling dundukas and spears held in their hands as they moved about.
Leaping up and seizing them, he uttered his own name with loud, boisterous laughter and departed with his skillful and heroic warriors. || 35 ||
By the foot-soldiers, who held swords and shields with great haste, who repeatedly joined their palms in reverence toward him as he approached,
who stood both at a distance and nearby with bodies bowed low, and who moved with dancing steps as they were questioned.
He went forth with his soldiers. || 36 ||
Accompanied by swift, great horses capable of restraining the sun’s steeds, by throngs of elephants that could withstand even the flashing Airāvaṇa,
and by numerous incomparable flower-chariots beyond counting, the wise and eminent minister Basava set forth.
Wearing most beautiful and variegated garments, the wives of the devotees— with water-pots and mirrors held in their lotus-like hands,
adorned with fine ornaments, and marked by radiant lines of sacred ash upon their foreheads— went before the eminent minister Basava.
Likewise, poets skilled in awakening aesthetic emotion quickly gratified his heart with recitations of wonderful poems composed of imagined qualities, as did those connoisseurs of rasa.
They were experts in the arts of the Bharata-śāstra through the sequences of dramatic performance. || 39 ||
With parasols, variegated pitchers,
throngs of white chowries, and brilliantly shining bracelets, along with fans and small bells.
He proceeded along a path repeatedly strewn with flowers colored with various hues, while being fanned by hundreds of yak-tail whisks.
The beautiful women, whose own limbs were as delightful as the true loveliness of Indra’s wife Jayā,

moved about wonderfully on both sides of his path in front of him, their hands raised for the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) and holding golden vessels, as they went forth to welcome the Lord Basava. (41)

Their feet surpassed the lotus, and their waists were so slender they could be grasped within a fist; yet, burdened by the weight of their full thighs, hips, and breasts, they proceeded with fortitude, holding lotus-like vessels in their hands.
With eyes like those of a doe languid with flickering intoxication, their faces smiling, they are filled with the grace of their gestures and the essence of their eloquent speech.
Falsehood, deceitful truth, untruth, and delusion, as well as courtesans, followed behind Basava at his front. || 43 ||
When the sovereign Basava, who surpassed even the king of kings in great majesty, set out to receive him,
those few Buddhist opponents present there felt loathing because they could not endure his splendor;
having departed, those opponents then fabricated various false statements against King Bījāla.

The rogues, having learned the news of the master’s departure, described his behavior as being like that of a madman: "Having seen ripe fruits upon that tree in a dream, he wishes to eat them again even after waking up."
Having perceived by force what is merely an omen of auspiciousness, he spreads through delusion a world of wondrous hypocrisy.
Having heard these words, the king, somewhat provoked by pride in his own opinion, spoke again in his heart:
"Aha! While I am ruling in my city, how can this man act thus without my consent?
But Basava has fallen into a delusion as vast as a mountain regarding something being offered here in ashes, even in a dream."
Or let the devotee pursue even that which is contrary to worldly custom; truly, he belongs to you—what loss is there to you because of him? (48)
He perceives only his own greatness; we do not at all consider this [greatness] of his to be extraordinary, for we understand it thus.
Moreover, this is recognized by all; indeed, having now seen it at the very end, let him be refuted. || 49 ||
Having spoken thus to his own sycophants, the king became silent, his mind filled with a surge of suppressed wrath.
Having understood that intention of the king, the great-souled Basava, the lord of Adhinatha, fell into deep reflection.
The Lord’s return to Kalyāṇanagara in a contemptible form: "Does my lord, the master Allamendra, not come? Or am I perhaps a laughingstock in the world, or even a great lord?"

While Haṃsollama, the ornament of the family of devotees, was thus reflecting—"Is there not [the truth] everywhere? Is he not the very author of the Vedas and Agamas, the Blessed One who conquers the opponents?"—he then perceived his inner state.
"If I do not depart quickly, the lord of the earth and the people will mock my devotion, saying 'let it not be so'; thus he rightly reflected. (52)
Thinking thus, the Lord himself, whose body is composed of consciousness, assumed the guise of a madman as the chief of this circle of gurus.
He appeared in person before the leaders of the Gaṇas, such as Basava and others, but he is not to be known by vulgar people who are solely greedy for sense-objects.
With limbs joined by shortness, a slender body, crooked feet, a slight beard, hair reddened by astringent dyes, and a throat curved with a goiter;
With a trembling waist, a profusion of body hair, false views, abusive speech, a restless gait, and distorted, loud laughter; || 54 ||
With his long, drooping ears thin and pale, he meditated within himself, weeping and laughing, as rows of wounds opened up with a dark-blue hue.
With saliva dripping from the cavity of his mouth, the lord Bhungīśvara arrived in person, he who is compassionate toward those who seek refuge in him. 55.
Thus the Lord, having arrived at the city, though censuring certain people, himself spoke only words of blessing to them.
Toward those intent on striking him, he offered only praise; toward those singing, he sang; and toward those dancing, he danced. || 56 ||
The wise one adorned some there who were intent on ornaments, and having fought against some who were skilled in wrestling, he remained steadfast.
To some who were intent on paying homage, he bowed his head; to others whose faces showed signs of agitation, he displayed a change of expression.
Beholding the children in the city, the Lord played just like a child; and where did he fall upon the surface of the earth?
Rising up swiftly like a child, Abhava appeared to some like one who was old. || 58 ||
When is he seen as one possessed of aesthetic relish, and where is he like a fool? When is he perceived as being like the sky, and where is he immutable?
Sometimes far away, sometimes nearby, and at other times manifesting his power as being omnipresent everywhere—
while the Lord was thus wandering, no one else had realized His greatness; then Basaveśvara [described] that festival of beholding the Lord Allama.
Just as a yogi perfected in the art of ointment perceives a hidden treasure in the earth, so too did he, with his perfectly pure intellect, perceive Allama alone.
Longing in his heart, his limbs covered in horripilation,
and his eyes filled with waves of tears of self-bliss;
Accompanied by her devotees, she approached his presence and, placing a collection of ashes, betel, and garlands at his feet, the devoted woman bowed down;
meanwhile, other women, filled with humility and devotion, gathered together as they danced, their own ornaments shining with radiant luster.
With beautiful songs, they performed lustration rites for the image of the Lord’s linga with the rays emanating from his teeth, eyes, and hands.
The resonance of musical instruments became exceedingly intense, while a multitude of bards and panegyrists recited compositions of flattery.
The citizens, having gathered together, honored him with humility, while the hosts of opposing disputants met with defeat upon their faces. || 63 ||
That which is celebrated on earth as Kalyāṇapaṭṭana is twelve famous yojanas in extent.
At the arrival of the Supreme Lord, everything became filled with auspicious lights, accompanied by the virtuous women of the city;
while the multitude of devotees rejoiced, they stood on all sides with palms joined in reverence, praising Him with words expressing their desire for refuge.
The Lord arrived amidst the crowds of citizens, who held chowries and excellent banners, and were adorned with circles of variegated parasols.
Among women who possess the skill of turning their shoulders back with grace, and who are filled with the agitation of casting glances;
The Lord of Guha entered that abode of Basava, where the wondrous majesty of the three worlds had been fully augmented.
Having bowed with devotion before Gaṅgāmbikā and those other jewels among women, preceded by shouts of "Victory! and "Auspiciousness!"...
While they were performing the *ārārtika* ritual, the Lord, having entered the house,
approached the vicinity of the jeweled pedestal of the throne.
Having seen the empty throne within himself, the Guru rejoiced and, having turned back all the assembled throngs of citizens, [proceeded].
Perceiving the power of his disciple, while the hosts looked on, Mallendra set his mind upon ascending [to heaven].

"What is so wonderful about this that the Guru of All, who is the embodiment of the consciousness of yoga—both with and without attributes—and the ordainer of the three worlds, should act thus? As the hosts of devotees praised him from within, the Guru ascended his seat.

Having realized that the human body here is bound by seventy-two thousand celebrated channels like a doll pinned down, he who makes it dance— what is this, yet it is for the sake of proclaiming the divine glory of the Lord Basava in this world?
The commencement of the Lord’s ascent upon the empty lion-throne:

having pointed out that this very "cloud-seat" (abhrapīṭha) is indeed the foundation of the six stations (ṣaṭsthala), and having instructed them on its true "peg" (satkīlaka), the Guru ascended by taking hold of that root-seat from the leaders of the Gaṇas.
Having instructed [the disciple] in that which is to be concealed while remaining there, the Guru then causes him to ascend each stage one by one in succession.
Having caused them to experience those various secrets as well, he himself ascended the summit of his resplendent lion-throne.
The six elements, the six classes of beings, the six lotuses, the six sacred sites, the sixfold limbs, the six types of devotion, the six-legged bee, and the sixfold garland of letters.
The Lord properly instructed the hosts of Śiva’s devotees in the six powers, the six splendors, the six ornaments, and the six applications.
When the wonder of the manner of his various constructions was presented to Basava, the foremost among devotees;
At the command of the Lord, those attendants of Śiva stood with their heads bowed and their fingers fixed motionless at the tips of their noses;
having set aside the orbs of the sun, fire, and moon along with the Kuṇḍalinī power, they remained endowed with that internal energy.
He has ascended to the peak of the incomparable celestial throne, which is the seat of the sky awakened at the tip of the gateway of the *suṣumnā*, dense with the wheel of the *akula*.

There, the Lord entered the throne-seat consisting of five syllables, which was constructed with four sentences as its four legs, supported by the *praṇava* as its base, adorned with the binding cloth of the fivefold *Sadbrahma-mantras*, and filled with the swan-wool of the *Kaṃcuka-mantras*. || 76 ||
At that very moment, as the illustrious Lord sat down, Basava first arranged all [the vessels] in their proper order.
All those various powers, being endowed with consciousness, worshipped this Lord of the Universe here by means of their own moving limbs. || 77 ||

Beholding that most wonderful sight, some fled far away out of fear; others, who were knowers of the self and experts in the sacred ordinances, bowed down, saying, "This is Śiva himself, the Supreme Lord! And the Vasus attained supreme joy within their own souls.
Bowing down once more, Basava, filled with devotion, praised the sovereign preceptor with the words of the Upanishads.
Clad in a hero’s garment and possessing supreme concentration, he offered his own self to the Lord of lords.
In the meantime, Ācārya and Arya, out of an overwhelming sense of devotion toward him, prostrated themselves upon the ground, placing their foreheads in a forceful manner.
And others with the faces of kinnaras, bowed down in fear and devotion, sought refuge by performing hundreds of prostrations like staffs. || 80 ||
The ascension of Allāmaprabhu onto the empty lion-throne,
and the other multitudes of Śiva-devotees who had arrived at the city to see the seat prepared for the Lord by Basava.
And all the groups of residents of Kalyāṇapaṭṭana, who were the most excellent among the moving liṅgas (jaṅgamaliṅga), arrived there immediately. || 81 ||
